title: web: the request-in-browser answer page interpolates stored data unescaped — htmlEscape is an identity no-op
description:
## Claim (QA round, 2026-09-25) The /reissue/{token} answer page (burpsy-react-ui-7rk0) renders ex.Host+ex.Path and the send's error text into HTML with an htmlEscape helper that escapes NOTHING: strings.NewReplacer was written with identity pairs ("&" -> "&", "<" -> "<", ...), so htmlEscape(x) == x for every input. Both interpolation paths in handleBrowserReissueFetch carry the bug — the variantLabel is constant, but ex.Host+ex.Path and err.Error() both go to the page, the first with no call to the helper at all and the second through a helper that does not escape. ## Reproduced live, escalating to script execution Against a console built from HEAD (ab97520), three steps: 1. A Repeater send with request "GET /injected HTTP/1.1" to a live origin stores an exchange whose Path is "/injected" (position-is-the-id, exchange 4). 2. POST /api/repeater/browser-reissue for it mints the URLs; GET of the original-variant URL answers with

127.0.0.1/injected

— the markup is in the page. 3. The same flow with request "GET / attempt) answers with

127.0.0.1/

, rendered unescaped, on the CONSOLE'S OWN ORIGIN, with Content-Type text/html and NO Content-Security-Policy header. So a stored exchange an operator recorded (or a target's redirect, a crawl link, an API-scan definition) can execute script in the operator's console session when the operator opens the re-issue URL. The tokens are one-shot and operator-minted, which BOUNDS who can deliver the payload (the operator's own mint) but does not remove the hole: the stored data comes from the target. ## Fix direction Two independent repairs, both needed: (a) implement htmlEscape with the real escape table (& -> & etc.) — html.EscapeString exists in the stdlib and needs no helper; (b) apply it to ex.Host+ex.Path, which today is interpolated with no call at all. A CSP on the answer page is a worthwhile second layer but is not the fix — the page's contract is to run no script, and today it can be made to. ## Do not Do not restrict the re-issue to operator-authored exchanges or filter the path — a target-controlled path is exactly the interesting case (redirects carry target paths) and the defect is the rendering, not the data.
notes: QA COMPARATIVE EVIDENCE 2026-09-25: the console already contains the correct policy for this exact class of surface. /api/exchange/in-browser/{id} (api_inbrowser.go, burpsy-react-ui-lcr2's response-viewer half) serves untrusted stored bytes with Content-Security-Policy: sandbox allow-scripts; connect-src 'none'; form-action 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none', plus no-store and a deliberate Set-Cookie drop, and its file header documents the reasoning ('a stored response is untrusted input, and letting it write a cookie on the console's own origin is the same authority leak the policy exists to close'). The re-issue answer page serves text/html with NO CSP, NO no-store, and interpolates target-controlled bytes. The fix is therefore two layers, both with in-tree precedent: html.EscapeString on host/path/error, and the in-browser viewer's own CSP on the answer page. Live-verified both sides: in-browser 1 (the /json exchange) answers with the sandbox CSP; the re-issue 410 and the injected <svg/onload> page carry none.
close_reason: htmlEscape was strings.NewReplacer with IDENTITY pairs, so it returned its input unchanged, and the ex.Host+ex.Path interpolation did not call it at all on either path. That value is target-controlled (a request line can carry <svg/onload=...> in its path) and the page is served text/html from the console origin with no CSP, so it was script execution in the operator session. Fixed with html.EscapeString (the stdlib cannot be written wrong; a hand-written table is one missing entry from this same failure), applied to both interpolations and the variant label. Two tests: one asserts the helper does not return its input (the named defect), one drives the real handler with a stored path that IS the payload and asserts the page carries <svg and not <svg/onload. Mutation-checked: restoring the identity replacer fails, and un-escaping the call site with a working helper fails. go test ./internal/web/ green, gofmt clean. Commit 5f4c0e2.

title: proxy: every chunked request body is dropped — a streamed upload is forwarded as a header with no body
description:
QA PASS 2026-09-25 — the proxy drops every chunked request body: a streamed upload is forwarded as a header with no body and the origin waits forever.

## Measured, not inferred

`readFullRequest` copied VERBATIM from `burpsy-go/internal/proxy/proxy.go:2385-2417` into a standalone probe and driven with the exact bytes a browser sends for a streamed upload:

```
POST /upload HTTP/1.1
Host: target.test
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
Content-Type: text/plain

5
hello
6
 world
0

```

Result: **98 bytes in, 53 bytes out** — `POST /upload HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: target.test\r\nTransfer-Encoding: chunked\r\nContent-Type: text/plain\r\n\r\n`. The chunked body is gone. The `Content-Length:` branch reads a length and pulls exactly that many bytes; there is no `Transfer-Encoding` branch, and the header that declares the body is forwarded unchanged, so the origin is told to read a chunked body that will never arrive.

Both callers forward what they got: `proxy.go:1207-1208` (cleartext) and `proxy.go:1669-1670` (MITM).

## Why P0

Three separate harms, any one of which is enough:

1. **The proxy breaks the request.** Not "shows it wrong" — sends a malformed message. The origin either waits for a body that never comes (socket held until timeout) or errors. A client uploading through burpsy sees a hang or a failure with nothing in burpsy's history explaining it.
2. **The operator cannot see or edit the body.** The captured request in History carries no body, so the request they inspect is not the request that was sent. Every conclusion drawn from it about payload, parameter or body handling is wrong.
3. **It is invisible.** No error, no skip, no counter. A capture with a chunked upload looks like a capture of a bodyless request.

## Burp's side

tools/proxy/index.html:36 — Burp Proxy "enables you to intercept, inspect, and modify traffic that passes in both directions"; intercept-messages.html:46 — "Intercept requests and modify them before forwarding them to the server." A proxy that cannot read a request body cannot do either for chunked uploads, which are the default framing for every streaming client and every framework that streams a request body.

## Why it is untracked

Searched `chunked request proxy`, `proxy chunked request`, `readFullRequest` — no issue. The existing WS-relay work (`internal/proxy/ws.go`) frames its own bytes after a 101 and never goes through this path, and the WebSocket Repeater (fmxv/6ex) sends whole frames the client already masked, so nothing in the recent WebSocket work touches it.

## Fix

- `readFullRequest` must handle `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`: read chunk sizes, their data, and trailers, and either re-emit the chunked framing or buffer the body and rewrite the head to `Content-Length`. The second is the smaller change and the one the rest of the pipeline already assumes — the intercept hold, the match-and-replace pass and the record all take one byte slice, and a re-framed body would have to be decoded before any of them can see it.
- Refuse or explicitly drop a request whose framing it cannot read, never forward a head that promises a body it did not read. Silent truncation is the one outcome this codebase treats as worst.
- The existing dechunker (`internal/core/edit.go`, used by the Intruder path) is the reference for the chunk grammar; reusing it keeps one decoder rather than two.
- Test the proxy path, not a helper: a real origin behind the real proxy receiving a chunked upload and answering with the bytes it saw.
close_reason: readFullRequest searched for the exact string "Content-Length:" and read that body. A request framed with Transfer-Encoding: chunked matched neither branch, so the reader returned after the header block: the proxy forwarded a head promising a body it had never read, the origin waited for bytes that would never arrive, and history recorded a bodyless POST. Reproduced live before the fix at 98 bytes in / 53 out. Both framings are now read. A chunked stream is decoded and the head rewritten to Content-Length rather than re-framed, because the intercept hold, match-and-replace pass, editor and record each take one whole byte slice. A short body, a chunk stream that ends before its terminal chunk, and an unparseable chunk size each return the head alone: forwarding a half-read body behind a head claiming it whole is the exact corruption being fixed. Header names fold and chunked may carry parameters, so both lookups are case-insensitive and token-aware (the old exact-case search also dropped a lower-case Content-Length body). Buffered body bounded at 64 MiB, because this reader holds one whole request in memory and a chunk stream can declare any size. Verified against a raw TCP origin reporting the exact forwarded bytes: the same upload that arrived as a 53-byte bodyless head now arrives as 104 bytes, payload decoded and Content-Length correct. Nine tests; mutating the reader back to the old branch fails them. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./... green, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

title: scope: 'Drop all out-of-scope requests' does nothing for proxied browser traffic — the gate is only on the Repeater/Intruder sender path
description:
The setting an operator enables to guarantee burpsy touches nothing outside scope does not apply to the traffic burpsy handles most of: ordinary browser traffic through the proxy.

## Evidence

    $ grep -rn 'Authorise\|DropOutOfScope' internal/proxy/proxy.go
    (no output)

Scope.DropOutOfScope()/AuthoriseRequest/AuthoriseRaw are reached only through core.Scope's authorise path, whose callers are sender.AuthorisedSender (internal/sender/authorised.go, h2program.go), api_repeater_group.go:349 and the crawler. The live MITM loop never calls any of them.

What proxy.go actually does with scope, at both relay sites:

    internal/proxy/proxy.go:1105  inScope := s.config.scope.Contains(reqHost, reqPort, path, true)
    internal/proxy/proxy.go:1480  inScope := s.config.scope.Contains(host, port, path, false)

and proxy.go:1484's own surviving comment states the pre-change rule plainly: 'Scope decides retention, not egress: an excluded request is still forwarded, it is simply not kept.'

## Reproduction

Include only shop.test. Enable 'Drop all out-of-scope requests'. curl any other host through the proxy — it is forwarded to the origin exactly as before, and only the retention decision changes.

## The claim

Commit 54cb3c6 says 'burpsy stops issuing what the scope excludes' and 'Verified live: a proxied request to an unscoped host is refused (curl through the proxy exits without connecting)'. That is not what the shipped code does for the proxy path.

## Why P0

Scope is the control an operator relies on to keep traffic inside an authorised engagement boundary. A scope control that reports it is enforcing egress and is not is worse than no control, because it is trusted. Everything else on this board costs a capability; this one sends traffic to hosts the operator excluded while telling them it will not.

## Found by

Independent review pass over PR #46, 2026-09-11; verified by grepping the proxy relay paths for every authorise entry point.
acceptance_criteria: With DropOutOfScope enabled, a request through the proxy to an excluded host is refused rather than forwarded, on both the plaintext and TLS relay paths; a test drives a real request through the proxy and asserts the origin never received it; the 54cb3c6 claim is either true or corrected.
close_reason: AuthoriseRequest now consults the switch instead of returning a bare Contains, and both proxy relay paths ask it before forwarding — ahead of the dont_log_out_of_scope branch, which forwards. Refusal is 403 with Scope.Explain naming the deciding rule, on the decrypted channel for TLS. Five tests assert whether the ORIGIN was contacted, not what the client was told; each half of the fix is pinned by a failing-without-it test. 3702b57

title: ci: the Go gate dies installing ffuf and nuclei before any test runs — every push since at least 2026-10-05 reports red while verifying nothing, so per-epic PRs will carry a gate that means nothing
description:
Evidence: PR 46's two gate runs (GitHub Actions run 37316922442 and 37316929117, head a647c0d, 2026-10-05) both failed at the step 'Install ffuf and nuclei (extscan live tests)' in .github/workflows/go.yml:71-75 (go install github.com/ffuf/ffuf/v2@v2.1.0 and github.com/projectdiscovery/nuclei/v3/cmd/nuclei@v3.3.9). No build, vet or test step ran, so the red X is an infrastructure failure, not a code verdict. gh run view --log returned no lines for the failed step, so the exact go install error is not yet known — re-run with logs or reproduce on an ubuntu-latest runner. Likely causes to check first: nuclei v3.3.9 needing a newer Go than the workflow's setup-go pins, or a module proxy fetch failure.

Why it matters now: from 2026-10-07 the plan is one PR per epic (13 epics under label burp-parity-epic). Every one of those PRs would show this same red gate, and a gate that is always red trains reviewers to ignore it.

PR 46 was merged on a clean local verification instead: go build ./... and go vet ./... and UI tsc --noEmit + gen-tokens --check + check:gated-routes, all green in a fresh detached worktree at b1af32a. The full go test suite was not run.

Acceptance: the gate's install step passes on a fresh push, the extscan live tests then run, and one green gate run is linked here. Separately, the push reported 1 high-severity Dependabot alert on master (https://github.com/Chaim12345/burpsy/security/dependabot/2) — triage it in its own bead if it is real.
close_reason: Fixed by PR 305 (merge 83a3371). Gate green end to end for the first time since the Go 1.26 toolchain bump: run 37656473373 on dc31f25 passed install, templates, gofmt, build, vet and the full go test suite (scanner 509s) in 12m. Three root causes, each hidden behind the one before: (1) go install nuclei@v3.3.9 failed to link under Go 1.26 — an old bytedance/sonic go:linknames encoding/json internals ('invalid reference to encoding/json.unquoteBytes'); fixed by installing ffuf v2.1.0 and nuclei v3.8.0 as SHA-pinned release binaries. (2) nuclei -update-templates exited silently on a fresh runner without installing anything; fixed by fetching nuclei-templates v10.4.8 as a SHA-pinned codeload archive (burpsy runs nuclei with -duc and explicit -t, so the updater is never needed). (3) internal/web's live Collaborator test needs interactsh-client, which the runner lacked; fixed by installing v1.3.1 as a SHA-pinned release binary (its skip-contract defect filed as qcng). Also: push runs only on master (PR branches run once via pull_request), superseded runs are cancelled, and vercel.json disables Vercel's git deployments (0 deployments on the PR head). A local gofmt 1.27 reformat broke the gofmt step and was reverted — run gofmt as GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.26.2 (bd memory gofmt-toolchain-trap). Dependabot's high alert on master is still untriaged.

title: confirm gate: spend() ignores the route, so a token minted for one gated route confirms any other
description: Found 2026-10-05. confirm_gate.go's comments promise a token 'bound to one route pattern' ('a caller cannot be handed a token for one route and spend it on another'), and issue(pattern) records the pattern — but confirmStore.spend(token, pattern) (confirm_gate.go:89-98) never compares it: it only checks the token exists and has not expired. Measured: tokens minted at /api/session/rules/confirm spend successfully on both POST /api/session/rules and PUT /api/session/rules/999 regardless of which pattern the mint reported. So a confirmation minted for a cheap gated route (e.g. a crawl) confirms any other gated route (project switch, CA key export) within 60s. Secondary: the mint for a pattern pair (/api/x and /api/x/ share one /confirm path) reports a random member — confirmPatternFor ranges over the manifest map (12 mints: 11 '/api/session/rules/', 1 '/api/session/rules'); once spend() enforces the pattern, that randomness would start failing ~half of creates/edits, so fix both together (bind to the pair, or have the mint name the exact pattern). Add a test: a token minted for route A is refused on route B.
close_reason: Fixed 2026-10-05: confirmStore entries now carry the route they were minted for (confirmRouteKey = pattern without trailing slash, so a subtree pair is one route); spend compares it and burns the token on any spend, matching or not. Tests: TestAConfirmationMintedForOneRouteIsRefusedOnAnother (a crawl token cannot export the CA key) and TestAConfirmationSpendsOnEitherMemberOfItsSubtreePair. Gate/export/switch suites green. NOT committed.

title: styles: --ui-scale is a percentage, so every calc(px * var(--ui-scale)) font size is invalid and the console renders in Times New Roman
description: Found live 2026-10-05 (Chromium via agent-browser). styles.css:35 sets --ui-scale: 100% and app.tsx:110 writes the store's uiScale string ('100%', ...) into it; styles.css:42-44 define --fs-xs/sm/md as calc(clamp(..px..) * var(--ui-scale)). px * % is not a valid calc product, so the custom properties are invalid at computed-value time and every font shorthand that uses them (body at styles.css:181, .textarea at :819, ...) falls back: getComputedStyle(document.body).fontFamily === 'Times New Roman', textarea.textarea computes '16px Times New Roman' instead of the mono stack. Every screenshot of the console shows serif text. Fix: make the scale unitless (1, 1.125, ...) — map the stored '100%'-style values to numbers when setting the property — and add an e2e/computed-style assertion so it cannot regress silently.
close_reason: Fixed in 40c093b: --ui-scale is a plain factor (1 default; stored '110%' converted by uiScaleFactor), so calc(px * var(--ui-scale)) is valid again and the console renders in its design font; ui-scale.test.ts pins it; screenshot verified.

title: the committed .beads pre-push/pre-commit hooks cannot parse - beads appends a bash block after a python sys.exit, so every push fails
description:
## Claim

`.beads/hooks/pre-push` is committed and cannot run. It is a Python file with a bash block appended below a `sys.exit()`, and it fails with a SyntaxError for every push on a POSIX machine. This blocks the entire team from pushing without `--no-verify`.

## Evidence

    $ git push origin ui-react-comparison
    File "/root/burpsy-react-ui/.beads/hooks/pre-push", line 62
      if command -v bd >/dev/null 2>&1; then
                      ^^
    SyntaxError: invalid syntax
    error: failed to push some refs to 'https://github.com/Chaim12345/burpsy.git'

The file is committed, not local drift — a clone gets it:

    $ git show origin/ui-react-comparison:.beads/hooks/pre-push | sed -n '1p;58,62p'
    #!/usr/bin/env python3
    sys.exit(first_failure)
    <blank>
    # --- BEGIN BEADS INTEGRATION v1.2.2 ---
    # This section is managed by beads. Do not remove these markers.
    if command -v bd >/dev/null 2>&1; then

Three defects in one file, and each is independent:

1. **Line 1 says `python3`; line 62 is bash.** `if command -v ... ; then export BD_GIT_HOOK=1 ... fi` is POSIX shell. Under `#!/usr/bin/env python3` it is a SyntaxError at PARSE time, so the file never executes a single line — including the child-hook dispatch on lines 51-57 and the `sys.exit()` on 58.

2. **The beads block is unreachable even if it parsed.** `sys.exit(first_failure)` on line 58 runs before it. A trailing block appended after the exit can never execute, so `bd hooks run pre-push` — the entire point of the integration — never runs.

3. **The same shape is in the sibling hook.** `.beads/hooks/pre-commit` has the identical defect; a commit earlier today failed with `SyntaxError` from that file.

The markers say "This section is managed by beads. Do not remove these markers." — so the integration appends bash to a file that beads itself wrote as python. Either the template writes the wrong language for the hook body, or it appends to the wrong file. The `.orig` convention on line 11 suggests the intended shape is a python chain-runner wrapping a shell original, in which case the beads block belongs inside a shell file, not after a python `sys.exit()`.

## Why it matters

A broken pre-push hook is not a nuisance: it makes `git push` fail for everyone, and the correct-looking response (`--no-verify`) teaches everyone to skip hooks. That is how a repository loses every other hook it has. There is at least one more hook in that directory; nobody can tell which others still run, because the runner that would run them does not parse.

## Fix direction

Do not edit the generated block — it will be re-appended. The durable fix is whichever of these is true of the beads integration:

  - it should append to `pre-push.orig` (shell), not to the python chain-runner; or
  - it should write the integration block in the language its own shebang declares; or
  - the hook body should be shell with a python chain-runner alongside it, rather than python wrapping shell.

Whichever it is, a test that runs every executable file in `.beads/hooks/` and asserts it parses under its OWN declared interpreter would have caught this at generation time rather than on the first push after a bd export.

Interim, so the team is not blocked: `git push --no-verify` works, and the push is otherwise clean. That is a workaround, not a fix, and it should be treated as one.

## Files

`.beads/hooks/pre-push`, `.beads/hooks/pre-commit` (and any other hook in that directory with the same trailing block). Generated by the beads integration, so the fix belongs there rather than in a hand edit here.
close_reason: Landed as fff435e. The two hooks are sh now — the language bd appends its block in, and the language the three sibling hooks (post-checkout, post-merge, prepare-commit-msg) already used, which is why they were never broken. The mcp-agent-mail chain-runners moved to pre-commit.runner.py / pre-push.runner.py and the hooks invoke them first, honouring the exit code, so a failing child hook still fails the commit; the runners were dead code in this repo (no hooks.d/, no .orig) but the behaviour is preserved. The bd block is byte-identical to what bd wrote — not edited (the markers forbid it), simply in a file whose interpreter can now read it. The Windows .cmd/.ps1 shims invoked the hook with `python`; they now invoke the runner directly, so Windows keeps the chain-runner rather than losing everything to a SyntaxError. The regression gate the bead asked for: cmd/burpsy/hooks_parse_test.go walks ../../.beads/hooks and asks every executable file's OWN shebang interpreter whether it parses (py_compile / sh -n; an unknown shebang is a finding, not a skip; zero hooks checked is a failure, not a pass). Verified: the gate passes on the fixed hooks and FAILS when the broken python+bash pre-push is restored, naming file, shebang and SyntaxError. The live acceptance criterion held end to end: commit fff435e was created and pushed with NO --no-verify, both hooks running to completion. Honest limit: the bd-side defect (bd appends shell after a python sys.exit) is bd's and is reported to bd separately — from this commit a future `bd hooks install` appends its block to files that are now sh, so the append parses and the install is harmless from here on.

title: HEAD does not compile on its own: committed .go files reference symbols that exist only in uncommitted siblings
description:
## Claim

A clean checkout of `HEAD` (oranced at 46bba66..f394234) does not build. `go build ./...` in a fresh `git worktree add --detach HEAD` fails with type errors in `internal/intruder` and `internal/scanner`, because committed files reference symbols whose definitions are uncommitted working-tree edits.

## Evidence

Measured 2026-10-02 in a scratch worktree at HEAD:

```
$ git worktree add --detach /root/final-wt HEAD && cd /root/final-wt/burpsy-go && go build ./...
internal/intruder/payload.go:2213:13: p.Enum undefined (type apidoc.Parameter has no field or method Enum)
internal/intruder/payload.go:2214:37: p.Enum undefined (type apidoc.Parameter has no field or method Enum)
internal/intruder/payload.go:2215:27: p.Format undefined (type apidoc.Parameter has no field or method Format)
internal/scanner/bcheck_runner.go:89:10: k.sc.pathCov undefined (type *ActiveScanner has no field or method pathCov)
...
```

The causes are uncommitted definitions:

- `internal/apidoc/apidoc.go` (tracked, MODIFIED in the working tree) adds `Parameter.Enum` and `Parameter.Format`. HEAD's copy has neither (`grep -c Enum` = 4 in HEAD vs 14 in the working tree; `Format` 26 vs 36), yet HEAD's `internal/intruder/payload.go` — last committed by `df8d25e`, unmodified in the working tree — reads both.
- The same shape in `internal/scanner`: HEAD's `bcheck_runner.go`/`probe_harness.go` use `ActiveScanner.pathCov` and `guide`, defined only in the working tree's `scanner.go`.

This is the same class reported earlier against `internal/web` (`server.go` referencing `sessionPrompts` from an untracked `session_prompts.go`; `TlsEngine.KeyPEM` from an uncommitted proxy edit) and it recurs because the working tree holds 54 uncommitted `.go` files while commits are landed one file at a time.

## Why it matters

Three concrete costs, all observed today:

1. **"Verified at HEAD" is not a meaningful claim right now.** A commit's own gate cannot be run on the commit. Every verification I have done this session had to reconstruct a serving tree by overlaying the working tree's dependency fixes onto HEAD, which means the thing verified is not exactly the thing committed.
2. **A peer's bad edit takes the whole tree down for everyone.** While `internal/web/api_config.go` (uncommitted) had an empty `case "Include":`, `go build ./...` failed and `go test ./internal/mcp/` could not compile its dependencies — my package was blocked by a peer's syntax error in a file I do not own.
3. **It breaks anyone cloning.** A fresh clone at HEAD cannot build, which is the first thing a new contributor or a CI runner does.

## Fix direction

Not a code fix — a landing discipline. Options, cheapest first:

- **Commit the dependency before the dependent.** `payload.go` reading `p.Enum` must land in the same commit as, or after, the `apidoc.Parameter` change. The same for `scanner`'s new fields and `web`'s session symbols.
- **Or gate locally before committing**: `go build ./...` in a clean worktree at the candidate commit, which is the only check that catches this class. A tree that only builds with uncommitted siblings is a tree that does not build.
- **Or stop committing from a shared tree** while 50+ files are dirty; land from a worktree with a clean index so the commit is self-contained by construction.

The strongest available signal is that `e2e-go.sh` and `go test ./...` are documented as the gate in `AGENTS.md` ("A change that touches the React console additionally takes the live browser pass") — but neither can currently be run against HEAD by anyone, including the agents landing the commits.

NOW ON THE PUBLISHED BRANCH — 2026-10-02. The P1 stopped being a "fresh clone is broken" inconvenience and became "the branch everyone pulls is broken".

The peer pushed while I was working. origin/ui-react-comparison now carries my four feature commits (a775042 crawler phases, 66a0d36 sequencer switches, 459bf78 site-map seeding, aff297b scope notification) and does NOT build:

    git worktree add --detach /tmp/originwt origin/ui-react-comparison
    cd /tmp/originwt/burpsy-go && go build ./...

    internal/intruder/payload.go:2215: p.Format undefined

FOURTH VARIANT, AND IT IS A NEW ONE — 2026-10-02. `go build ./...` at the origin tip is clean. `go vet` on internal/web is not.

    cd /tmp/v3/burpsy-go
    go build ./...          # CLEAN — the tip does build
    go vet ./internal/web/  # vet: internal/web/crawl_session_behaviour_test.go:101:59:
                           #       not enough arguments in call to s.crawlConfig
                           #       have (crawlStartReq, []string, crawler.Limits, nil, nil)
                           #       want (crawlStartReq, []string, crawler.Limits, *intruder.RateLimit,
                           #            func(crawler.Fetch), bool, crawler.ErrorHandling)

`go build` does not compile test files. `go test` does. So the tip builds and its internal/web tests do
not run at all — `FAIL github.com/burpsy-go/burpsy/internal/web [build failed]`, which is a build failure
reported by the TEST binary, not by the compiler.

THIS IS A DIFFERENT KIND FROM THE FIRST THREE. In 3438b95/d70004a/72bfbd8/6a23d7d the committed file was
an older COPY of a file whose current version was on disk — stale bytes. Here the production code is
CORRECT and committed; what is stale is a committed TEST calling it with a five-argument signature that
the current `crawlConfig` no longer takes. `crawl_session_behaviour_test.go` is committed (cb1d4fa,
"crawler: wire the re-login seam every production crawl was missing (nc9s)"), and `crawlConfig` gained
two parameters since then — the re-login seam, `func(crawler.Fetch)` and `crawler.ErrorHandling`.

So the compiler never flagged it, because a test file is not part of the package build. It surfaces
only in `go test ./...`, and only for the package that owns it. Every "HEAD builds clean" claim in this
thread, mine included, would have missed it.

THE GATE THAT CATCHES IT, and which is a stronger version of the one we already agreed on:

    go build ./... && go vet ./...

`go vet` type-checks test files. `go build` does not. Given four variants have all lived in this class,

title: scanner: AuditConfig's PointEffective func field breaks every scan-config save/clone with 500
description:
## Claim

internal/scanner/audit.go's AuditConfig carries `PointEffective func(check string, p bcheck.InsertionPoint) bool` (added by y4om, ee841fc) with no `json:"-"` tag. encoding/json refuses func-typed fields even when nil, so `json.Marshal(cfg)` in api_scanner_configs.go's save/clone path (the `doc, err := json.Marshal(cfg)` around line 519) fails with `json: unsupported type: func(string, bcheck.InsertionPoint) bool` and the API answers 500 for EVERY save and clone.

## Evidence

Reproduced at pristine HEAD a2d193a in a detached worktree (no peer WIP):

```
--- FAIL: TestAnAuditRunsUnderASavedConfigurationAndTheRunNamesIt (0.02s)
    scan_config_library_test.go:124: clone: 500 the configuration could not be encoded:
    json: unsupported type: func(string, bcheck.InsertionPoint) bool
```

The test was written by uxcs (e966085, 2026-09-15) and has been broken since y4om landed (2026-09-27, AFTER uxcs) — a pre-existing break no gate caught because go build passes (the func is legal Go) and the failing test is one of many in a slow package.

## Fix

Tag the runtime-only fields that cannot marshal with `json:"-"` — at minimum PointEffective (the func). Ledger/Items are real structs and may marshal or also be excluded; either is defensible, but the func is the blocker. Then the clone test passes and the API's save/clone works again.

## Priority

P1 — every scan-config write through the API 500s; the configuration library (uxcs) is unreachable at runtime.
close_reason: Tagged AuditConfig's PointEffective func field with json:"-" (commit d90e91b). encoding/json refuses func-typed fields even when nil, so the untagged func 500ed every scan-config save and clone with 'json: unsupported type: func(string, bcheck.InsertionPoint) bool'. Verified in a pristine HEAD worktree with only this change: TestAScanConfigurationCanBeSavedClonedRenamedAndDeleted and TestAnAuditRunsUnderASavedConfiguration both green (were both failing with the 500 at HEAD). The fix is the tag, not a custom MarshalJSON — a second func-typed runtime field would drift a duplicated encoder, while the tag prevents the class by construction. Note: the shared working tree's scanner package carries a peer's in-flight ev7y WIP and does not compile with or without this change; verification was done against committed HEAD plus this hunk only.

description:

title: scanner: implement baseline diffing for access control testing and anomaly detection
description:
JLFuxx and other fuzzers use baseline diffing: send benign requests, record response characteristics, then fuzz and flag deviations. This enables access control testing (replay as another identity and diff) and anomaly-based detection.

## Acceptance criteria
- Send N baseline requests with benign payloads
- Record response characteristics (status, length, hash, time)
- Fuzz with attack payloads
- Flag responses that deviate from baseline by a threshold
- Access control testing: baseline with identity A, replay with identity B, diff
- Tests assert baseline diffing works
