title: web console: no authentication and no CSRF/Origin check — a page the operator visits can drive burpsy's attacks (rebinding/CSRF)
description:
## Claim

The web console has no authentication and no cross-site request protection. Every mutating API route is reachable by any page the operator's browser loads, and burpsy is a tool that sends attacks — so a malicious page (or a DNS-rebinding attack against the loopback console) can drive burpsy's proxy, scanner, and Repeater without the operator's knowledge.

## Threat model

The console binds to 127.0.0.1:8081 by default (cmd/burpsy/main.go:42), which stops other hosts reaching it — but not the operator's own browser, which visits hostile targets all day while burpsy runs. Two live paths:
- **CSRF:** a page the operator visits issues cross-origin requests to http://127.0.0.1:8081/api/... . With no CSRF token, no Origin/Sec-Fetch check, and no enforced JSON content type, a simple form or fetch can start an audit, add a scope rule, or send a request.
- **DNS rebinding:** a hostile domain rebinds to 127.0.0.1, defeating the loopback bind entirely, and then talks to the API as same-origin.
- **Non-loopback bind:** `-web 0.0.0.0:8081` (a documented, supported flag pattern, cf. -blindxss) exposes the whole console to the network with no auth at all. This case is P1.

## Evidence

burpsy:
- No auth middleware: `grep -rniE 'middleware|Unauthorized|401|requireAuth|apiKey'` over internal/web/*.go (non-test) finds none. `netauth` is credentials to authenticate TO targets, not auth ON the console (server.go:179-185).
- No CSRF/Host/Origin/Sec-Fetch validation: `grep -rniE 'r\.Host|Origin|Sec-Fetch|SameSite|csrf.?token|rebind'` over internal/web/*.go (non-test) returns only the SSE per-origin connection limit (api_events.go:22) and unrelated "original"/"Origin" strings. No mutating route checks the requester's origin.
- The server is a plain http.Server with Addr from the flag (server.go:1116-1117).

External precedent: Burp's own REST API requires a generated key; Caido added authenticated HTTPS for remote access in 2026. Both treat "the local API is powerful, so gate it" as core.

## Fix direction

1. Origin / Sec-Fetch-Site validation on every mutating (non-GET, or non-riskRead) route: reject cross-site requests. This is the minimum and stops CSRF and rebinding.
2. Require a per-instance token (printed at startup, or set via flag/env) that the UI sends and the server checks, so a non-loopback bind is not wide open.
3. Enforce a JSON content type on mutating routes so a simple HTML form cannot trigger them.

This pairs with the runtime risk/confirm gate bead: the gate decides WHICH operations need confirmation; this decides WHO may call them at all.

## Why it matters

burpsy can send attack traffic on command. An unauthenticated, CSRF-open control plane means a page the operator merely visits can weaponise their own burpsy against a third party, or an attacker on the LAN can when the console is bound off-loopback. This is the control plane of an offensive tool with no lock on the door.
acceptance_criteria: Every mutating route rejects cross-site requests (Origin/Sec-Fetch check) and non-JSON content types; a per-instance token gates access so a non-loopback bind is not open; a CSRF PoC against /api that starts an audit or edits scope is refused.
close_reason: RESTORED CLOSE 2026-09-27: this was reopened by accident earlier in the session (an unclaim attempt used '-s open'). The fix is landed and verified present in the tree: internal/web/api_sameorigin.go (187 lines) implements the cross-site gate — Host must be loopback (the rebinding defence), Sec-Fetch-Site must be same-origin/same-site/none, and Origin when present must match Host — wired into server.go with internal/web/api_sameorigin_test.go covering it. Commit 66ee44a closed and exported it. No reopen was warranted.

title: crawler: the crawl-config key table lists sections Burp never ships and hides the 3-of-46 figure
description:
## Claim

burpsy's crawl-config loader reports "nothing to apply" for a configuration whose crawler half is largely loadable, and its section table is keyed on names Burp does not use — so the real coverage figure (3 of 46) is never visible and three listed sections are fabricated.

## Burp-side evidence (build 51467/2026.7.1, verified 2026-09-27)

- Every shipped file nests under the section names `crawl_limits`, `crawl_optimization`, `error_handling`, `login_functions`, `customization`, `crawl_project_option_overrides`, `live_passive_crawl` — `Preferences/CrawlDefaults.json` (35 crawler.* keys, all under `crawler.`), `Preferences/LivePassiveCrawlDefaults.json` (10 keys under `crawler.live_passive_crawl.*`), `BuiltInConfigs/*.json` (21 distinct crawler.* keys). **Total distinct: 46 crawler.* keys.**
- Keys are spelled **with underscores** (`"crawl_optimization": {"crawl_strategy": "fastest"}`), nested one level under the section.
- **Correction to bead 3ok6's evidence:** it cites `map_root.tsv:12473-12478` and claims "10 keys across them" in the shipped configurations. That range is six rows, all `crawl_limits`; the shipped set is 21+ distinct keys across four sections in the BuiltInConfigs, plus the Preferences files.

## burpsy-side evidence (verified 2026-09-27)

- `internal/crawler/burpconfig.go` `burpCrawlConfigKeys` applies exactly **3** keys (`crawler/crawl_limits/maximum_crawl_time`, `maximum_unique_locations`, `maximum_request_count`).
- `burpCrawlConfigSections` lists six sections: `crawl_limits`, `optimization`, `crawl_scope`, `exclusions`, `inclusions`, `crawl_optimisation`. **None of the last five is a section Burp ships** (zero hits for `crawler.crawl_scope` / `exclusions` / `inclusions` in map_root.tsv or any shipped config). The real `crawl_optimization`, `error_handling`, `login_functions`, `customization`, `crawl_project_option_overrides`, `live_passive_crawl` are absent from the table and land in `UnknownSections`.
- Net: of 46 shipped keys, 3 apply and 43 are reported — but the report an operator reads ("unrepresentable: N keys, unknown sections: M") does not distinguish "Burp shipped this and I cannot apply it" from "this section name does not exist".

## Classification

CONFIRMED, and it falsifies the section table in bead 3ok6 while confirming its direction.

## What an operator cannot do

Importing `Crawl strategy - fastest` (one key: `crawl_strategy`) reports zero applied keys and an unknown section, when the honest answer is "1 key, and burpsy has no crawl-strategy concept". An operator auditing a migration cannot learn that the donor applies 46 keys and the receiver honours 3.

## Acceptance criteria

1. `burpCrawlConfigSections` lists exactly the section names Burp ships (verified against `CrawlDefaults.json` + `LivePassiveCrawlDefaults.json` + `BuiltInConfigs/*.json`), with the fabricated five removed.
2. Every shipped key is either applied or named in `UnrepresentableKeys`; no key is ever silently dropped.
3. `CrawlConfig` carries `ShippedKeyCount` and the report renders "3 of 46 applied", so the figure is on the operator's screen.
4. A test driving the **real** `BuiltInConfigs/*.json` and `Preferences/CrawlDefaults.json` files asserts 0 dropped keys and 3 applied.

## Priority

P1 — it is the honest-counting defect the project is organised against, it makes 3ok6 unclosable as written, and it is a pure data-table fix that unblocks the speculative-links, API-discovery and error-handling beads (their keys are all in the sections currently mis-tabulated).
notes: RELEASED 2026-09-27 15:57: a peer session is actively landing this bead (their uncommitted WIP directly implements the section-table correction, the 46-key list, and the coupled error_handling family from o0c5 — insertion.go, crawler.go, limits.go, audit.go, audit_config_keys_test.go, audit_engine.go, audit_items.go, scanner/burpconfig.go, check_contract.go, checks_injection.go, probe_harness.go, api_crawl.go all modified within the last 30 minutes, errorhandling.go created 15:29). Do not implement independently.
close_reason: Verified complete. burpCrawlConfigSections lists exactly 7 real Burp sections, ShippedKeyCount=46, AppliedKeys/UnrepresentableKeys partition every key. Tests pass against real transcribed keys with 0 dropped.

title: crawler: implement the error_handling family — follow-up passes, timeout pause thresholds, auth-failure escalation
description:
## Claim

Burp's crawler has a four-key error-handling policy. burpsy has **no** retry, no follow-up pass, and no timeout escalation: a failed request is counted (`SkipSendFailed`) and the crawl moves on. Two of Burp's shipped configurations depend on these keys by name, so today importing either one is a silent no-op that burpsy honestly reports as "unapplied" — the exact failure `3ok6` was filed for, unfixed.

## Burp-side evidence (build 51467/2026.7.1)

- `Zf9w.java:29-32,37-40` — `crawler.error_handling.pause_task_requests_timed_out_count`, `pause_task_requests_timed_out_percentage`, `consecutive_authentication_failures_before_pausing_task`, `number_of_follow_up_passes`. Record `Zhrp.java:12-27` (four ints). UI `Zrfv.java:157` "Handling repeated timeouts during crawl", `:164`, `:227`, `:257` "follow-up passes to retry requests that timed out.", `:109` "Only values between 1 and 10 are allowed" (auth-failure cap). DOC crawl-settings.html:167-186.
- **Shipped values:** `Never stop crawl due to application errors.json` sets all three pause thresholds to **0** and `number_of_follow_up_passes: 1`; `Crawl and Audit - Deep.json` sets `number_of_follow_up_passes: 1, pause_task_requests_timed_out_count: 30`. Defaults: `consecutive_authentication_failures_before_pausing_task: 2`, `number_of_follow_up_passes: 1`, `pause_task_requests_timed_out_count: 15`, `pause_task_requests_timed_out_percentage: 0` (`CrawlDefaults.json`).
- **The `0` problem:** `pause_task_requests_timed_out_count: 0` is Burp's shipped way to say "never pause", and burpsy's crawl-request ints use `if n > 0` (`api_crawl.go:279-281`, the documented reads-zero-as-unset trap). A naive port would read 0 as "use the default", producing a crawl that *pauses* where the operator explicitly disabled it.

## burpsy-side evidence

Zero hits for a retry/follow-up/backoff mechanism in `internal/crawler/`; `SkipSendFailed` (`skip.go:142-145`) and `SkipResponseUnreadable` (`:146-150`) are the whole failure vocabulary. The engine has `suiteGate` (crawl-wide pause, `crawler.go:1090`) but nothing per-request. Bead `5efx` covers the **audit** side's follow-up passes and does not touch the crawler.

## Classification

CONFIRMED.

## What an operator cannot do

A flaky target yields a crawl that reports N transport failures and simply has a hole in its coverage, with no way to ask for a second pass over just those requests. Nor can they cap how long the crawl keeps hammering a refusing host, or ask the crawl to stop after repeated authentication failures.

## Acceptance criteria

1. All four keys are `*int` on `crawlStartReq` so **0 is expressible**; all four land in `AppliedKeys` on config import.
2. When the crawl finishes, a follow-up pass re-issues exactly the requests that ended in `SkipSendFailed`, up to the configured count, through the ordinary `perform` path (re-authorised, re-captured, re-scanned).
3. Crossing the consecutive-timeout or auth-failure threshold sets the existing `suiteGate` for the crawl's task row and records a distinct, named stop so the report says the crawl was **paused by policy**, not finished.
4. A test that a config setting all three thresholds to 0 produces a crawl that never pauses.
5. A test that a follow-up pass recovers a request that failed once.

## Priority

P1 — two shipped configurations depend on these keys by name (silent no-ops on import), and the uncovered-retry case is a real coverage hole.
notes: 2026-10-05: wired and tested. The landed engine half (errorhandling.go, runFollowUpPasses, checkPauseThresholds) was never called — noteFailure/checkPauseThresholds were dead code. Done: failures recorded at the SkipSendFailed site (timeout classified via net.Error/DeadlineExceeded), consecutive streaks reset on a response / restored session, auth failures counted from failed re-logins (session_gate.go), thresholds checked after every visit and inside follow-up passes, follow-up skipped after a policy pause. THREE DEFECTS FIXED in the landed code: (1) follow-up budget used lim.Requests, which reads 0 all crawl, so retries could spend a second full MaxRequests — now rep.Fetched (mutation-tested: disabling it re-sends 12x vs 2); (2) percentage threshold divided by lim.Requests so could never fire — now fetched+failed; (3) retry loop aliased c.followUp[:0] while appending. Failed now counts requests that ENDED failed (partition preserved); new Report.follow_up_recovered. AC1: four *int request fields under Burp names on crawlStartReq, 0 expressible, crawler.ErrorHandling.Validate shared bounds (auth<=10, pct<=100, >=0). DEVIATION from AC3 wording: a tripped threshold ENDS the crawl with the named StopPaused* (as the landed StopPaused* docs define) rather than calling suite-wide PauseAll, which would freeze every other running task; dash has no per-task pause. Tests: internal/crawler/errorhandling_run_test.go (6), internal/web/crawl_progress_test.go TestCrawlRequestTakesTheErrorHandlingKeysAndZeroIsAnAnswer. UI fields queued to frontend agent.
close_reason: Done: error_handling wired end to end (see notes: three defects in the landed engine fixed — follow-up budget, percentage threshold, slice aliasing; mutation-tested). Four *int request fields under Burp names, 0 expressible, shared Validate. Stops now serialise by name (j5j7 backend). Deviation recorded: a tripped threshold ends the crawl with a named StopPaused* rather than suite-wide PauseAll. Crawl dialog Error handling group; live: auth=11 refused with the server text. UI completed and driven live 2026-10-05 by the frontend-ux agent (tsc clean, bun test src/lib 802 pass, build ok, Go reachability tests ok). Full Go module build+vet+tests green. NOT committed. Stop rendering in the UI tracked by j5j7 (in flight).

title: crawler: add the speculative/hidden-link discovery phase (comments + JavaScript), with a per-crawl cap
description:
## Claim

Burp runs a distinct crawl phase that extracts URLs from HTML **comments** and **JavaScript** and follows them, bounded by a configurable maximum. burpsy declines `onclick` outright (`internal/crawler/discover.go:281-294`) and never scans comments or script bodies. The setting is **on by default in Burp** (1000 links), so the default burpsy crawl is narrower than the donor's today.

## Burp-side evidence (build 51467/2026.7.1)

- Phase: `Zrbx.java:80` — `return "SpeculativeLinksCrawlPhase";`, enqueued as a first-class phase in `Zc16.java:73-75` (`this.Zk.add(new Ziuo(this))`). Action kind `Zb8w.SPECULATIVE`, filtered by `Zia6.java:130-132` / `Zmor.java:89-91`.
- Config: `Zxcp.java:116-117` → `crawler.customization.request_speculative`, `crawler.customization.maximum_speculative_links`.
- UI: `Zrfu.java:160` "Follow hidden links in comments and JavaScript", `:168` "Maximum hidden links to follow:", `:307` "must be between 1 and 50,000". Default **1000** (`Preferences/CrawlDefaults.json`, `crawler.customization.request_speculative: true` + cap). DOC crawl-settings.html:300. Phase literal: `map_root.tsv` → `Zb29.java:18` `super("AddingSpeculativePageToGraph")`.
- **Caveat carried forward:** burpsy's stated reason for declining `onclick` ("Burp's own handling of an inline handler is not recoverable from the evidence base") was correct in 2026-08; it is now **falsified** by the shipped configs, which make the setting reachable without any JS heuristics. The comment should be re-worded when this lands.

## burpsy-side evidence

`discover.go:281-294` states the refusal. No `request_speculative` field exists in `crawlStartReq` (`internal/web/api_crawl.go:219-320`) or in `burpCrawlConfigKeys` (`internal/crawler/burpconfig.go:77-81`).

## Classification

CONFIRMED on both sides.

## What an operator cannot do

Cannot ask burpsy for the endpoints a JS app hides in a `<script>` block or an HTML comment — the exact place single-page apps and comment-leaked admin paths live. `request_speculative` is reported **unapplied** when loading any Burp configuration, so a migrated config silently loses it.

## Acceptance criteria

1. `POST /api/crawl` accepts `request_speculative` (bool) and `max_speculative_links` (int); both appear in the run record's view JSON.
2. Burp config files carrying `crawler/customization/request_speculative` and `maximum_speculative_links` land in `AppliedKeys`, not `UnrepresentableKeys`.
3. The engine extracts candidate URLs from HTML comments and script bodies and admits them through `enqueue` (so they pass scope, destructive and query gates) — never as privileged seeds.
4. `MaxSpeculativeLinks` is honoured; exceeding it records a new named stop + skip reason and is reflected in `Unfetched`/`Caveat`.
5. A test that a comment-borne URL is fetched when on, and recorded as a counted decline when off.

## Priority

P1 — cheap, self-contained, and the default crawl is narrower than the donor's today.
close_reason: Speculative-hidden-link phase shipped: parsePage mines HTML comments and script bodies for URL-shaped candidates (absolute http(s) + root-relative paths, trailing punctuation trimmed) and admits them through the same admit/enqueue gates as navigational links — never privileged (a comment-borne /logout still hits the destructive gate, a cross-host candidate still hits scope). Config.RequestSpeculative + Limits.MaxSpeculativeLinks (default 1000 = Burp's shipped default) with a crawl-wide cap checked last in enqueue, so the cap counts what the crawl FOLLOWS not what it saw. New StopSpeculativeLinks + SkipSpeculativeLimit + LimitReport.SpeculativeDropped (folded into Unfetched + Caveat). API: crawlStartReq accepts request_speculative + max_speculative_links (pointer, 0=admit-none); Burp config keys crawler/customization/{request_speculative,maximum_speculative_links} land in AppliedKeys via a new configField row kind. Also wired faadff0's half-finished eh (o0c5 error-handling overlay) through crawlConfig — it was a write-only variable blocking the whole web package build. Tests: 7 new (comment/script fetched-on vs unfetched-off, cap honoured+named, destructive+scope gates, extractor unit, Burp config parse). Full crawler + web suites green (one pre-existing web failure: another agent's func-field config encode).

title: scanner: max_items_in_progress, parallel_crawl_and_audit and logging_enabled ship in Burp's defaults and are absent from burpsy's key table
description:
## Claim

Burp's shipped audit defaults (`out/clean/jdt_src/burp/Zeuc.java:41-47`, build 51467/2026.7.1) set three keys that burpsy's pinned `burpShippedScannerKeys` list (`internal/scanner/audit_config_keys_test.go:21-77`, 55 keys) does not contain — verified directly 2026-09-27:

```java
public static Zg4q ZD() {
    Zxm6 var0 = new Zxm6();
    var0.Zn("scanner.audit_optimization.max_items_in_progress", 10);
    var0.ZB("scanner.audit_optimization.parallel_crawl_and_audit", true);
    var0.ZB("scanner.audit_optimization.logging_enabled", false);
    return var0;
}
```

`grep max_items_in_progress|parallel_crawl_and_audit|logging_enabled audit_config_keys_test.go` → 0 hits for all three. The test at `:82-98` only asserts shipped→row for the keys it lists, never shipped→present, so a key absent from the list is invisible to it: **a test that claims completeness passes while the claim is false.**

## Burp-side evidence

- `max_items_in_progress` is a **live admission cap**, not a config row that does nothing: `Zm58.java:88-98` — `ZS()` computes `this.ZD.Zii() - this.Zp.Zg()` (cap minus in-flight) and refuses to admit when ≤ 0; `Zp(int)` at `:188-206` admits N items. Default 10 per `Zeuc.java:43`. It bounds how many audit items a run keeps in flight — a queue-depth cap entirely distinct from worker concurrency, and the thing that bounds memory on a large scan.
- `parallel_crawl_and_audit` (default **true**): `Zc16.java:170` wires the crawl↔audit parallelism; `Zhd_.java:42,56` read it.
- `logging_enabled` (default false): the audit request-log switch, `Zhd_.java:44`.

## burpsy-side evidence

- `audit_config_keys_test.go:21-77` — 55 keys, none of the three present.
- `burpconfig.go:30-41` (`burpConfigSections`) lists `audit_optimization`, so an operator's file naming `max_items_in_progress` reaches `apply()` (`audit.go:92-99`) with no row and lands in `UnrepresentableKeys` as a bare name — or worse, an inner-key miss with no name at all.
- The audit engine has no in-flight admission cap: `audit_engine.go:1026-1031` sizes one global worker pool from `MaxConcurrency`; budget enforcement at `:1081-1090` is time/requests only.

## Classification

BUG (an enumeration that is incomplete, so a checked claim is wrong) + CAPABILITY GAP.

## What an operator cannot do

They cannot cap how many audit items a run keeps in flight, and — because the key is invisible — they cannot even learn Burp has the control. An operator who lowers the cap on a big site to bound memory has nothing to lower. An exported Burp config naming any of the three keys silently loses it.

## Acceptance criteria

1. The key re-derived against `in/extract/resources/BuiltInConfigs/*.json`'s `scanner.audit_optimization.*` leaves (not extended by hand — extending by hand is what missed it) and added to `burpShippedScannerKeys` with a row reading Burp's default of 10.
2. `parallel_crawl_and_audit` and `logging_enabled` either get rows or explicit declined rows with a reason naming what is missing.
3. `AuditConfig.MaxItemsInProgress OptUint32` enforced as an admission cap at the point an item is claimed for dispatch — a cap applied after claim still allocates.
4. The cap's effect observable: a run with the cap at 2 must never have more than 2 items concurrently past admission, pinned by a test that counts the overlap rather than reading the field.
5. The shipped-key test extended to assert the pinned list **is** the shipped set (bidirectional), so this defect class cannot recur.

## Priority

P1 — it is the one gap in this pass where a test claiming completeness is passing while the claim is false; the fix is small; memory behaviour on a large scan is the operator-visible harm.
close_reason: Verified complete. burpShippedScannerKeys contains all 3 missing keys (max_items_in_progress, parallel_crawl_and_audit, logging_enabled). MaxItemsInProgress OptUint32 enforced as admission cap. Bidirectional shipped-key test. Overlap-counting test pins cap at 2.

title: crawler: the re-login machinery is complete, tested and never wired — no production crawl sets SessionCoordinator, so an operator-launched crawl goes unauthenticated from the first expiry
description:
## Claim
`internal/crawler/session_gate.go` is complete and tested (SessionCoordinator seam, expiry detection, bounded re-login) — but NEITHER production crawl sets it: `api_crawl.go:425-447` and `api_apiscan.go:205-231` build their `crawler.Config` without `SessionCoordinator` or `LoginPagePattern`. Every operator-launched crawl is therefore the unauthenticated one, silently. `gaps.md:1083-1092` declared this closed in 2026-08 on the strength of the mechanism; the caller never landed.

## Evidence
- Burp: `Zgjj.java:131` (`crawl_using_provided_logins_only`), the `Zrl5`/`Zrbs`/`Zrlw` login phases — a crawl uses the project's session handling by default.
- burpsy: `api_crawl.go:425-447` and `api_apiscan.go:205-231` — config literals omitting the coordinator; `server.go:64,755` — `Server.sessionCoordinator` exists and is never passed; `session_gate.go` — the unused seam.
- This is the same defect class as bead fddb (a closed bead whose mechanism landed without its caller) and s9ma.

## Fix direction
Pass `s.sessionCoordinator` (and the login-page pattern when the operator supplied one) into both `crawler.Config` literals; add a test that fails if a production crawl's config has a nil coordinator while session rules exist. Then re-measure: a crawl behind a login page should follow the session, and the crawl report should say when a re-login happened.

## Why it matters
A crawl of an authenticated app stops at the login redirect and reports whatever the public pages yielded — with no signal that the session was lost. The operator gets a confident, empty result.
close_reason: internal/crawler/session_gate.go was complete and thoroughly tested -- five session-recovery tests in crawler_test.go, a fakeCoordinator, a status-flip rule, a login-page rule, a bounded re-login budget with its own stop reason, and a report that surfaces re-login health. gaps.md:1083-1092 declared it closed in 2026-08 on the strength of the mechanism. Neither production caller ever passed it: api_crawl.go:425-447 and api_apiscan.go:205-231 built their crawler.Config literals without SessionCoordinator or LoginPagePattern, so crawler.go:1260's 'if c.cfg.SessionCoordinator != nil' short-circuited on every operator-launched crawl. The consequence is the bad one: a crawl of an authenticated app follows the login redirect and reports whatever the public pages yielded, with no signal that the session had been lost. The operator gets a confident empty result and a re-run gives the same one. Both literals now carry s.crawlSessionCoordinator() and req.LoginPagePattern. It is the coordinator every other tool already routes through -- Repeater, Intruder, the proxy -- so a crawl uses the project's session handling the way Burp's crawl_using_provided_logins_only describes, and there is no second, drift-prone way to think about re-login. The API scan gets it too: it walks the same routes in a different mode, and a scan that loses its session enumerates the login redirect as though it were an endpoint. login_page_pattern is new on both request types, because the status-flip rule alone only half-closes this. An application that serves its shell with a 200 for every route -- the common SPA shape -- never flips a status, and the crawl would sit there authenticated-in-name-only. Empty keeps the status flip, so the field is optional; a malformed pattern is a 400 from crawler.New before any task row exists, which is the rule the rest of the request already follows. A pattern that silently never matched would be a control reporting a dead session as a live one. crawlSessionCoordinator returns nil for a server without a coordinator, and nil MEANS nil: a typed nil in that interface is a non-nil value holding a nil pointer, which is the shape that panics on first use rather than at the call -- worse than the original defect, because it takes the process down instead of quietly doing nothing. The two config literals are extracted into crawlConfig and apiScanConfig for a reason worth recording: my first wiring test called the helper directly and PASSED against the unwired shape. The helper was right and nothing called it, which was the entire defect. A field missing from a struct literal nobody inspects is invisible -- the same shape as the Params field's own note that 'the store kept the set, the console rendered it, the test asserted it, and the wire shape in between silently dropped it'. Reading what production actually BUILDS is the only assertion that detects this class. 8 tests, mutation-checked both ways: unwiring both literals fails 2, and a typed nil fails the real-nil test -- its message shows the trap exactly, printing <nil> for a value that is not nil. There is a behaviour test too, against a target that genuinely expires the session mid-crawl, so the claim is not only that the field is set. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./internal/web + internal/crawler green, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

title: build: iosv's last mile is uncommitted — the scannerlaunch UI half and the rebuilt bundle sit in the working tree while the bead is closed
description:
## Claim (QA round, 2026-09-25)

burpsy-react-ui-iosv is closed and its engine + tests landed (e7f42a2, 38894bc), but the feature's UI half exists ONLY as uncommitted changes in the shared tree:

- burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/pages/scannerlaunch.tsx — the LiveAuditCard badge and gaps now render behind_for_ms ("behind 40s" / "behind 2m") and batch_limit ("sweeping 400/tick"), the entire operator-visible point of the catch-up work. git log -S "behind_for_ms" over that file returns NO commit: no branch tip carries it.
- burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/dist/app.js — rebuilt with the change ('behind_for_ms' present in the working-tree bundle), also uncommitted.

The file also carries 419/410 insert/delete whitespace churn (the real delta under --ignore-all-space is 12 lines: the two badge/gaps edits), which is the edit-tool indent-strip signature this repo has hit before — it makes the honest 12-line change LOOK like a rewrite and would make any review of the eventual commit noisy unless -w is used.

A reset or a careless checkout loses the feature's last mile with no bead saying it is missing: the tracker is closed, so nothing would resurface it.

## Same class, second file

burpsy-go/gaps.md carries an uncommitted 1300-line rewrite (a new gaps ledger format: G-reflected-xss-header-reach, the 21/23 xsschallenge measurement). Also uncommitted, also invisible to the tracker. Whose WIP this is belongs to its author to land or park, but a QA round has to say it exists, because "uncommitted in a shared tree" is how closed features go missing.

## Fix direction

Commit the scannerlaunch + bundle delta (with -w reviewed so the churn is not what lands), and gaps.md separately as its own change. If gaps.md is deliberately being rewritten by an in-flight effort, that effort should say so on its own bead; today it is unattributed working-tree state on a 1300-line tracked file.
close_reason: Both halves landed as separate commits. (1) The gaps.md ledger-replacement was reverted to HEAD and the genuinely new G-reflected-xss-header-reach entry appended under the existing structure: pure addition, 9->10 h2 sections, corpus section and all closed-gap evidence intact, diff zero removed lines - commit 56041fd. The 1300-line rewrite had deleted the ledger's entire history; both sessions' QA rounds flagged it independently and the fix was agreed in coordination. (2) The iosv UI half - scannerlaunch's LiveAuditCard rendering behind_for_ms and batch_limit - landed as 12 lines in 2 hunks with the file otherwise byte-identical to HEAD, because the working-tree copy carried 419/410 edit-tool whitespace churn under it: reviewed with git diff -w first, then rebuilt from HEAD so the commit IS the change - commit 3ad5480. Bundle rebuilt (behind_for_ms + batch_limit verified in dist/app.js), tsc clean, bun test:lib 711/0. A reset can no longer lose either.

title: ui: the detached exchange window opens on #history and never mounts its page — DetailWindowPage is unreachable from the action that claims to open it
description:
## Claim (QA round, 2026-09-25)

Burp's "Show details in new window" shipped as burpsy-react-ui-wvcl (commit 3f597eb), but the action never lands on the page it opens: openDetailWindow (pages/detailwindow.tsx:60) builds

    `${location.pathname}${location.search ? location.search + "&" : "?"}exchange=${id}#history`

so the new window's hash is #history. The router (app.tsx useHashRoute) maps the hash to a NAV_LEAF id and mounts that leaf: #history mounts HistoryPage. The DetailWindowPage leaf is registered as id "exchange-detail" (nav.ts:145), and nothing in the codebase writes that hash — grep finds it only in nav.ts's registration and the route test. openDetailWindow's ?exchange=N query param is read by exactly one function, detailExchangeId, which only DetailWindowPage calls — and DetailWindowPage is never mounted by the URL the action builds.

Net effect: "Show details in new window" opens a second window showing the ordinary HTTP history table, with no exchange selected. The page the bead delivered — the editor, the Inspector, the parameter/cookie/attribute tabs, the Close button — is dead code reachable only by hand-typing #exchange-detail.

## Why the shipped tests did not catch it

detail-window-route.test.ts pins that the leaf exists, is hidden, belongs to Proxy, and that leaf ids are unique — every assertion is about the leaf, none is about the JOURNEY: no test asserts that the URL openDetailWindow builds contains the hash that routes to the leaf. The close reason records the gap honestly ("NOT live-verified: the window as rendered (browser host down)") — the one check that would have caught it is the one that never ran.

## Fix direction

Either the URL ends #exchange-detail (and the router needs no change — it matches leaf ids exactly), or openDetailWindow keeps #history and HistoryPage reads the exchange param and mounts DetailWindowPage in its place. The first is the smaller change and matches the registered leaf. The test to add is the missing one: assert the constructed URL's hash equals the detail leaf's id — that is the assertion whose absence is this bug. Also worth stating: the fallback path navigates the SAME tab with navigateToHistoryWith, which builds '#history?exchange=N' — the same miss in the same-tab fallback, so the operator who had the popup blocked ALSO gets plain history.
close_reason: One-line fix: openDetailWindow built the URL with #history, and the hash is the route, so the window mounted HistoryPage and DetailWindowPage was reachable only by hand-typing #exchange-detail. Now #exchange-detail, with a route test that READS the real URL builder out of the source and asserts the hash - a test that restated the expected hash would have passed against the bug. Verified live against a real console: /?exchange=1#exchange-detail mounts the detail page (heading GET /alpha?q=1, Request/Response/Inspector editors, Close window button, 12 message tabs); 5/5 route tests, tsc clean.

title: history: a blind CONNECT tunnel shows message 0 — another exchange's request — under its own Request label
description:
QA PASS 2026-09-25 — a blind CONNECT tunnel in HTTP history shows another exchange's request bytes as its own, because message id 0 is a real message.

## The chain

1. `burpsy-go/internal/proxy/proxy.go:1582-1628` creates the blind-tunnel `core.Exchange` with no `Request` and no `Response` — correctly, because a blind tunnel has no bytes to record. Both fields stay at their zero value.
2. `burpsy-go/internal/web/api_types.go:227-235` emits that zero to the UI unconditionally.
3. `burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/lib/data.ts:268-273` establishes that **message id 0 is a real, fetchable id** — the store is a dense counter from zero.
4. `burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/ui/variant-picker.tsx:53-64` — `variantMessageId(edited, …)` returns `edited` for the "edited" reading, and `history.tsx:703` passes `selected.request`, which is `0`.
5. `useMessage(0)` fetches message 0 and the pane renders it under the label **Request** for the selected tunnel.

## What the operator sees, and why it is P1

A row whose bytes belong to a different exchange, presented as this row's. A blind tunnel is the one case where an operator deliberately has no request bytes, and that absence is Burp's documented state: `map_root.tsv:10859` says pass-through connections have *"No details about requests or responses ... available in the Proxy ... history"*, and http-history/index.html:149-152 promises a selected item shows *"the request and response messages for the item"*. burpsy shows *a* request message — just not this item's.

This is evidence corruption rather than a missing feature. An operator reading a CONNECT row to see where a client went is looking at the first request captured in the project, labelled as the tunnel's own. Every conclusion drawn from that pane is wrong, and nothing on screen marks it.

## Why it is untracked

Searched `blind tunnel`, `message 0`, `request id 0` — no issue. The related work (`mr4p` server-IP, `10e` delete, `c05` edited-message readings) does not touch the zero-id case. The bug is a missing discriminator between "no message" and "message number zero", and the store's dense-counter design is exactly what makes the two indistinguishable at the wire.

## Fix

- Make absence explicit at the wire. The cheapest correct change is a pointer or an explicit `has_request`/`has_response` on the exchange view, so a client can tell a tunnel from the first message. `omitempty` on a plain number cannot do it, because 0 is a legitimate id.
- Then render the absent case as the absent case: a pane that says "This tunnel is blind — no request or response bytes were captured", which is the truth and is more useful than either a wrong pane or a blank one.
- Until the wire carries the flag, `history.tsx` can at least stop fetching id 0 for a row whose `variants` are all absent AND whose `request` equals the store's first message — but that is a heuristic, and the pointer is the real fix.
- A test: seed a blind tunnel AFTER at least one real exchange, select the tunnel row, and assert the request pane does not contain the other exchange's bytes. That test fails today, which is the point.
close_reason: A blind CONNECT tunnel has no request bytes to record and the proxy builds that row with no Request, but the message store's ids are a dense counter from ZERO, so 0 is the first request the project ever captured and exchangeView emitted that zero unconditionally. The UI read it as 'this row's request is message 0' and the detail pane rendered the project's first request under the label Request for a tunnel that has none -- another exchange's bytes, with nothing marking it. That is evidence corruption, and Burp's own account agrees the absence is the honest state (map_root.tsv:10859: pass-through connections have no details about requests or responses available in the Proxy history). The fix is in the model: core.Exchange.Request is now a *MsgId mirroring Response, which has always been a pointer for the same reason -- a bare MsgId cannot say 'no request' because its zero value IS a real request, so the distinction was unrepresentable anywhere. core.Occurrence, which mirrors the same pair for finding attribution, changed with it. Four sites that silently read the zero as an id are fixed: AddExchange indexed a request-less row under byRequest[0] (Restore could reintroduce it), the variant resolver returned message 0 as the ORIGINAL reading of a row with no request, and api_search scanned ex.Request unguarded -- the same defect reached through search, its response half already having the guard the request half lacked. Two limitations stated rather than hidden: the durable store's request column is NOT NULL and SQLite cannot relax that with ALTER TABLE, so a request-less row persists as 0 and Restore normalises it only when message 0 is absent from the restored set; and about 200 construction sites were converted mechanically using the compiler as an oracle, the only judgement calls being the four above. On the UI side fetchRaw takes number|null and REFUSES with a message naming the reason rather than fetching message 0, and a context-menu plugin is handed message: undefined. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./... green with the test cache cleared, tsc clean, bun test:lib 711/0 plus 4 new, check:tokens green, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

comments.author: burpsy
comments.text:
REPRODUCED LIVE 2026-09-25 against a real console (ui-live.sh fixture, proxy 18280 / web 18281):

1. Seeded five real exchanges, then opened a blind tunnel by CONNECTing through the proxy to an external host. The proxy answered 'HTTP/1.1 200 Connection Established'.
2. /api/history then contains the tunnel row: id=6 method=CONNECT request=0 response=None. Message 0 is the FIRST seeded exchange's request.
3. Selecting that row in the browser, the Request pane renders 'GET /zebra HTTP/1.1 Host: 127.0.0.1:18299 Connection: close' - exchange 0's bytes, from a different exchange, under the label 'Request'. The Response pane correctly says 'No response was captured for this exchange.'

The blind tunnel therefore shows another exchange's request as its own, and the asymmetry (Response correct, Request wrong) is exactly the zero-id collision the code reading predicted: the response field is a pointer in the wire view and the request field is a bare number.

title: scanner: light/medium/intrusive tiers collapse to one switch while the key matrix reports all three as applied
description:
QA PASS 2026-09-25 — Burp's light/medium/intrusive scan tiers collapse to one switch, and the key matrix reports all three as applied.

## What the code does (and says)

`burpsy-go/internal/scanner/audit_engine.go:132-140` states it without hedging: *"burpsy has no per-check intrusiveness ranking, so Burp's light/medium/intrusive active tiers collapse to one gate: every tier the configuration sets to false turns the active check families off, and any tier set to true leaves the base switch set alone."* The approximation text is shown beside the resolved configuration, so an operator reading the preview learns the difference.

That disclaimer is the right behaviour, and this bead is **not** about a hidden lie. It is about two things the disclaimer cannot fix.

## Why it still matters

**1. The configuration key matrix says all three tiers apply.** `internal/scanner/audit.go:984-1005` marks the three tier keys `applies=true` while the engine collapses them. A preset importer or a settings review reads the matrix as "this key is honoured" — which is the claim a key matrix exists to make. `t2s`/`oco4` landed that matrix; `jvyw` closed with the tiers marked applied. The matrix and the approximation note now say opposite things about the same keys.

**2. A light-only request is not a light scan.** Burp's auditing.html:80-101 defines light, medium and intrusive as separate check sets and warns the aggressive tiers "may trigger alerts, log users out, or cause data loss". An operator who loads a Burp light preset, sees the three keys reported as applied, and disables intrusive and medium is still running the intrusive checks. The approximation note is one sentence in a configuration preview, and the damage (an account locked out mid-scan) is not something the operator was warned about at the moment they launched.

## What the operator loses

The ability to run a genuinely non-aggressive scan. Every active check is all-or-nothing, so a careful operator either accepts Burp's most aggressive tier or runs no active audit at all. That is the safety valve Burp's tiers exist to provide, and its absence is why "run a light audit" is not expressible in burpsy.

## Already-tracked correction

`burpsy-react-ui-jvyw` is CLOSED and marked the three tier keys applied. The collapse is documented in the engine, so the close reason overclaims the matrix, not the code.

## Fix, in the order that matters

- **First, make the matrix honest.** A key that changes no behaviour must not be reported as `applies=true`; report it as approximated and point at the note. This is a one-line correction to a claim the matrix makes, and it is the part that can mislead a preset review.
- **Then the capability.** Tiering needs a per-check intrusiveness rank in the check registry — a field, not a rewrite, because every check already has a registry row. Light then means "active checks ranked light", and a preset's three keys select three sets as Burp intends. The approximation note disappears when the three are independent.
- **Meanwhile, warn at launch.** A configuration that collapsed the tiers should say so in the confirmation, where the operator decides to send traffic, not only in the preview.
close_reason: The three scan_type_*_active keys all reported applies=true while the engine ran one gate: activeTiersAllOff asked only whether every tier was off, and any single tier set true left the whole base switch set alone. A preset enabling light and refusing intrusive still ran the intrusive checks. Each check now carries a CheckInvasiveness rank declared in the registry beside the request it makes: passive (43, exempt from all three keys since it sends nothing), light (155, one probe read back), medium (13, effect outlives the response -- cache entries, request pairs sharing server state), intrusive (15, plants state someone must undo -- stored canaries, OOB collaborators, XML entity expansion). The default is TierLight so a descriptor that forgets its rank is admitted by the lightest tier rather than silently excluded. An unset tier key says nothing about its tier; nil-versus-empty carries 'inherit' apart from 'every tier off'. Measured light-only 116, medium-only 43, intrusive-only 58 against a 131-check base -- three distinct sets where the old gate produced one. Two tests hold the matrix to the engine's actual behaviour, and three mutations (disabling the rank filter, dropping the passive exemption, severing the rank's path from descriptor to dispatch table) each fail. The approximation note loses the tier sentence; the launch warning the issue asked for is unnecessary once there is no collapse left to warn about. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./... green, e2e-go.sh 24/24. Commit c73b5dc.

title: network: platform credentials reach the sender but not the proxy, so browser traffic is proxied unauthenticated
description:
QA PASS 2026-09-25 — configured platform credentials reach the sender but not the proxy, so browser traffic is proxied unauthenticated.

## What is wired, and where it stops

`burpsy-go/cmd/burpsy/main.go`:
- The **sender** gets them: `httpSender := sender.NewSender(egressSenderConfig(upstreamPolicy, platformAuth, clientCerts))` (`main.go:494`), where `egressSenderConfig` sets `config.PlatformAuth = auth` (`main.go:988-991`), and credentials are restored from the store at startup (`restoreNetworkAuth`, `main.go:1017-1045`).
- The **proxy** does not: `proxyServer := proxy.NewServer(proxyConfig)` (`main.go:477`) is built from `proxyConfig`, which is assembled earlier and carries client certificates and the upstream policy but no platform-authentication source. `grep -rn 'PlatformAuth' burpsy-go/internal/proxy/` finds nothing.

So an operator who configures Basic, Digest or the NTLM codec under Settings → Network → Platform authentication gets authenticated Repeater sends, authenticated scanner probes, and an **unauthenticated browser through the proxy** — which is where most of their traffic is.

## The raw-path exclusion is not the issue

`internal/sender/sender.go:90-98` deliberately withholds PlatformAuth from `SendRawOutcome`, and the reasoning is correct: *"SendRawOutcome's contract is that it sends what the caller wrote, verbatim, and the desync and smuggling probes this tool exists to send depend on that byte-for-byte fidelity."* That reasoning is about **operator-authored probe bytes**, and this finding is not about that path. Browser traffic arriving through the proxy is not a byte-fidelity probe — it is a real request the operator is relaying, and Burp's own model (connections.html:55-60, "These settings enable Burp to carry out automatic platform authentication to destination web servers") treats platform authentication as a property of the connection to the destination, not of a particular tool's send path.

## What the operator loses

Any target behind integrated authentication (NTLM/IWA) that the operator has configured credentials for: the browser through burpsy gets a 401, Repeater sends with the same request succeed, and the difference between the two paths is invisible. troubleshooting.html:97 is the case Burp calls out — platform-authenticated applications fail *through Burp* and the fix is to configure Burp to handle it.

## Already-tracked correction

`burpsy-react-ui-sel6` (the one still-open issue in the tracker) covers the missing **NTLMv1 / Negotiate scheme implementations**. It does not cover applying the credentials that DO exist to the proxy leg, and it is a P3 about absent schemes rather than a P1 about a configured setting being silently inert on the main traffic path.

## Fix

- Give `ProxyConfig` a platform-auth source and consult it on the browser-facing leg, with the same per-host matching the sender uses (`netauth.Credentials` is already an interface the package can depend on).
- Keep the raw-byte exclusion exactly as it is, and say in the setting's own help that platform authentication applies to Repeater, scanner probes and proxied browser traffic — so an operator can see the coverage rather than infer it.
- The NTLMv2 codec landed in `3fb2ce1`; this wiring is what makes it reachable for a browser, which is the point of having built it.
close_reason: An operator who configured Basic or Digest under Settings > Network > Platform authentication got authenticated Repeater sends, authenticated scanner probes, and an UNAUTHENTICATED browser through the proxy -- where most of their traffic is -- while the panel said the rules were stored. The NTLMv2 codec landed in 3fb2ce1 and was unreachable for the traffic that needed it. The same *netauth.Credentials the sender holds is now handed to ProxyConfig, so one set of rules governs every leg. The edit is a header insert at the request head's terminator, not a request rebuild: the proxy relays bytes, and rebuilding one to attach a credential would mean parsing it, re-serialising it, and hoping the round trip is byte-identical for everything the parse did not model. The browser's own Authorization header always wins, case-insensitively. There is no retry, deliberately -- a 401's challenge is learned as each response head arrives so the NEXT request authenticates, across a new connection, because re-sending a request the browser did not ask to repeat against a refusing host is how an account gets locked out. GET /api/network/auth now reports presented_on_proxy beside presented_on_egress, because a Server can be assembled with one leg and not the other. Verified live through a real console against an origin that refuses unauthenticated requests: the same browser-shaped request answered 401 with no credential configured and 200 after one was added through the console's own API. Mutation-checked four ways: dropping the operator-header-wins rule, moving the insert past the blank line (which put every credential at the front of the body), removing the attach at the forward, and removing the challenge learning. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./... green, tsc clean, bun test:lib 711/0, check:tokens green.

title: proxy: enabling interception silently forces HTTP/1.1 upstream, moving every h2 target off the protocol under test
description:
QA PASS 2026-09-25 — turning interception on silently keeps every HTTP/2 browser connection off the interception path. This is a deliberate policy, and the bead is to decide whether it should stay one.

## What the code says, in its own words

`burpsy-go/internal/proxy/alpn.go`: *"When interception is enabled only http/1.1 is offered, because the hold queue is HTTP/1-shaped: an intercepted request is held, shown and possibly edited as HTTP/1 bytes, so offering h2 upstream would negotiate a protocol the intercept path cannot represent."* And the file header: *"What stays here is the one decision that is the proxy's and not a general one: interception forces http/1.1."*

`AlpnOffer(clientOffer, interceptionEnabled)` filters to HTTP/1.1 whenever interception is on, so the negotiated protocol cannot become h2, and the h2 path (`h2_relay.go`) only relays and records — it has no intercept hold.

## Why this is a decision and not a bug

The reasoning is sound and stated in the source: an HTTP/1-shaped hold queue cannot represent an h2 request, so offering h2 would negotiate a protocol the intercept path cannot honour. The alternative — accepting h2 and then being unable to hold it — is worse. **Nothing here is misreported, and this bead must not be filed as a defect.**

But the consequence is large enough to be an operator's decision rather than an implementer's:

## What the operator loses

Burp defaults to HTTP/2 and lets the Inspector override the protocol for an individual intercepted request (settings/network/http.html:194-205, intercept-messages.html:167-169). In burpsy, **the moment an operator enables interception, every HTTP/2 target silently drops to HTTP/1.1** — and most modern TLS sites are HTTP/2-first. The operator sees traffic that negotiated a protocol their browser would not have used, with nothing on screen saying the interception switch changed the protocol. That is a real fidelity cost: an HTTP/2-specific behaviour (h2-only security headers, HPACK, server push, stream priorities) is never exercised through burpsy at all.

## The decision

- **Keep HTTP/1-only interception, and say so.** Cheapest and honest: the interception switch's own help should state that enabling it forces HTTP/1.1 upstream, and the Protocol column / a per-exchange note should make the downgrade visible. An operator who knows is making a choice; one who does not is being silently moved off the protocol they came to test.
- **Or add an h2 intercept path**: the hold queue would need to represent a stream, and a per-stream hold/forward model is a substantially larger change than this policy. That is a scoping decision, not a fix.

The first option is available now and removes the deception; the second is the roadmap item. What should not remain is the current state, where the switch changes the negotiated protocol with no indication anywhere.

## Already-tracked correction

None found — searched `http/2 intercept`, `h2 intercept`, `relay not intercepted`. The existing force-H2 beads (745, 57yk, 6i4) concern the Repeater's per-request protocol override, not the proxy's interception-time offer.
close_reason: Enabling interception makes AlpnOffer return only http/1.1 because the hold queue is HTTP/1-shaped, and it was invisible: every intercepted record stamped ProtocolHTTP1 unconditionally, so a downgraded row and an HTTP/1.1-only target were identical and the operator could not tell the protocol under test was never exercised. The protocol field keeps answering what carried the exchange (HTTP/1.1 is truthful); the missing second fact now rides on the rows -- DowngradeNote writes 'client offered HTTP/2; interception carried this over HTTP/1.1', computed once per tunnel from the client's offer and the negotiated value, and withDowngradeNote joins it with a row's existing note rather than overwriting it. Surfaced in three places the operator meets the decision: the Intercept switch hint (turning it on now states intercepted traffic is carried as HTTP/1.1 including clients that offered HTTP/2), and both the history detail head and the detached detail window, which show a warning-toned 'HTTP/2 downgraded' beside the protocol badge. Verified end to end through a real console: an h2-capable client requested an h2 origin via an interception-enabled proxy, the origin reported serving HTTP/1.1, the client saw HTTP/1.1, the history row carried the note and the detail head showed both badges; the switch hint was confirmed in the browser. Mutation-checked: computing the note without attaching it fails, and dropping the note from the response record site fails. The WebSocket handshake record deliberately keeps its ProtocolHTTP1 constant -- reaching that line already proves http/1.1 and no test could reach a variable there without a TLS WebSocket fixture. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./... green, tsc clean, bun test:lib 711/0, check:tokens green.

title: proxy: an open-ended response is never forwarded — the client gets nothing until the response ends
description:
QA PASS 2026-09-25 — the proxy has no streaming response path, so an open-ended browser response hangs with no bytes delivered.

## What Burp provides and why it matters

settings/network/http.html:96-104 describes the store-and-forward problem and Burp's answer in one breath: waiting for a response to end before forwarding any of it means that for an open-ended response, **"none of the response is ever forwarded"**, and the fix is that **"The Proxy passes these responses straight through to the client in real time."** burpsy has a per-host "declare this host open-ended" setting for the *sender*, so the concept is understood — it is simply not applied to the proxy.

## What burpsy does

- `burpsy-go/internal/proxy/proxy.go` has no streaming path: `grep -n 'Flush\|stream'` finds no response flush, and the response is fully read by `readHTTPResponse` before anything is written to the client (`proxy.go:2632-2648`).
- `burpsy-go/internal/httputil/httputil.go:122-231` reads an unframed response until EOF with **no timeout**, so an open-ended response does not merely delay the client — it holds the proxy's connection to that host indefinitely.

## What the operator loses

Server-sent events, long-poll, AI-token streaming, and any endpoint that keeps a response open. The browser client waits; nothing arrives; burpsy's history shows nothing; the proxy's connection to the target is pinned. This is a common shape for exactly the modern applications an operator is testing, and unlike the chunked-body P0 it is not visible as an error — it looks like a slow target.

## Why this is a gap and not a defect

Nothing in burpsy's code claims streaming. The sender HAS the declaration and an open-ended read path, which is the right place for it; the proxy leg simply never got the same treatment. There is no misleading claim to correct, only a capability the proxy lacks while the tool that sends through it has it.

## Fix

- Detect an open-ended response the way the sender does (a host declared open-ended, and/or a response whose framing is absent) and stream it: write the head, then copy chunks to the client as they arrive, flushing per chunk.
- Record the exchange incrementally so History and Logger show the partial response rather than nothing, with the same "no terminal framing" caveat the sender's open-ended path already carries.
- Undeclared open-ended responses still need a bounded read, or one hostile target can pin every proxy connection; the sender's `OpenEndedTimeout` is the reference for the bound and for saying so in the UI.
close_reason: Every response was buffered to completion before the client saw any of it. On a response that does not end -- an SSE feed, a long-poll -- httputil's ReadResponseBody copies an unframed body until EOF and EOF never comes, so the client received no bytes at all until the connection's own deadline fired, which it reads as a hung target. Three legs buffered and all three are fixed: the HTTP/1 plaintext path (handleHTTP now hands the request to streamPlainResponse, which owns the upstream connection for the life of the stream, which is why the branch sits before forwardRequest rather than after it), the HTTP/1-over-TLS intercept loop (streamTLSResponse, with the read deadline set on the upstream leg from the policy window), and relayH2Stream, which did io.ReadAll on the response body -- the same defect on the protocol nearly every TLS origin negotiates. The predicate is deliberately not 'is this response frameless': a real event stream is chunk-framed and never sends its terminal chunk, so testing for missing framing classified every genuine SSE feed as ordinary and buffered it. What distinguishes them is whether the framing completes, known only once the read has run. A framed response is never streamed: Match & Replace and the hold are entitled to see the whole message before any of it reaches the client. A streamed response is forwarded live then recorded and is NOT held -- a rule cannot rewrite a byte the client already has. Both record paths gained an alreadyWritten flag rather than a second recording function. The window comes from the same Settings > Network list the sender reads; the proxy had no access to it, so the panel described a list only Repeater obeyed. A negative window is refused rather than clamped. Verified live through a real console against a real h2 SSE origin: first event at +60ms while the origin was still sending, second at +6.01s on release; before the fix both arrived together at the end. Mutation-checked four ways: buffering instead of streaming, the predicate off, the record dropped, and the settings push to the proxy removed or losing the operator's window. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./... green, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

title: repeater: a group send labelled Parallel is goroutine fan-out, not a synchronized send
description:
QA PASS 2026-09-25 — a parallel group send is ordinary fan-out, so a group labelled "Parallel" cannot test a race condition.

## Why this is the worst of the batch

Burp's parallel mode is not "send N requests at once"; it is *"Repeater synchronizes parallel requests to ensure that they all arrive in full at the same time"* (tools/repeater/send-group.html:151-162). For HTTP/1 it withholds each request's LAST BYTE and releases those bytes down the connections simultaneously; for HTTP/2 it uses a single-packet attack. The point of the feature is that request N does not leave at 10:00:00.001 because Go scheduled it there. The same doc says the response pane shows the order in which responses arrived (1/3, 2/3) — the measurement of the thing the feature exists to produce.

burpsy has `sync.WaitGroup` and one goroutine per item (`burpsy-go/internal/web/api_repeater_group.go:255-278`). No barrier, no held final byte, no arrival ordinal in the result (`api_repeater_group.go` reports tab/status/response size/framing/read state), and the Repeater group table has no arrival column (`burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/pages/repeater.tsx:1665-1748`).

## Why the UI label is the problem, not a missing feature

An operator reading "Parallel" reasonably believes arrival is simultaneous. The setting exists to test a race condition — a double-click handler, a session rotation, a balance check — and under Go's scheduler the requests can land arbitrarily far apart, so a race that only fires within a microsecond is **invisible**. The tool reports a successful parallel send for a test that did not test anything, which is this project's stated worst outcome: a result that reads complete and is not.

## Already-tracked correction

`burpsy-react-ui-03z` is CLOSED with a reason claiming parallel mode landed, and its own scope note mis-associates the last-byte synchronization with the single-connection mode (where it does not belong — `sender.SendKeepAlive` writes in order on one socket, and no synchronization is needed or wanted there). The close reason therefore overclaims: fan-out is not parallel send.

## Fix

- Hold the final byte of each HTTP/1 request; write head, then release the held bytes through one barrier so the last byte of every request goes out together. `sender.SendKeepAlive` and the single-connection path are the wrong place for this — a barrier needs a separate connection per request, which is what parallel mode already opens.
- Add the arrival ordinal to each item result and a column in the group table, so the feature reports the ordering it is for. Burp's own docs make the ordinal part of the feature.
- Until the barrier lands, rename the mode. A label that promises a property the engine does not provide is the defect, and it is cheaper than the barrier.
close_reason:
Closed as fixed in 43a53dc (+ the wtov types restoration in 732c14a, which
this landing required to land on a green gate).

The Parallel group is now a synchronized send, not fan-out. Every member
dials its own connection and writes its request minus the final byte
(sender.SendSynchronized, new); the orchestrator collects one ready signal
per member — a dial failure counts as an arrival, so one dead port cannot
hang the group — then closes the release channel and every held byte goes
out together. HTTP/1 is pinned for the whole send (ProtocolPreferenceHTTP1,
alpn egress offer excludes h2): there is no "final byte of the raw" once
the h2 path frames it, and the honest h2 equivalent is the single-packet
attack, a separate mechanism. The pin is visible in each result's protocol.

The response pane part of the bead is landed too: results are ranked by the
moment their response's first byte was read (ties by tab order) and the
ordinal ships as `arrival` on Parallel items only — 0/absent for a member
that never answered and for the sequence modes, whose order is tab order by
construction. The UI group-outcome table gains the "Arrived" column (#n)
for parallel sends.

Honest limits, stated rather than papered over:
- Cross-member arrival ORDER is not asserted by any test. With one live
  member, tab order and wire order coincide, so an ordering assertion
  would be vacuous; a multi-member wire-timing double was measured this
  session as unreliable on loopback (three handler goroutines' wake
  order masquerading as the wire). The hold itself IS mutation-checked at
  the sender level: removing the barrier fails the test with the final
  byte queued at the readiness signal, and a cancelled hold returns the
  cancellation error instead of hanging teardown.
- The bundle commit at 6c62d5c already carries this page change (it was
  built from the shared tree); rebuilding at 43a53dc is byte-identical,
  so no separate dist commit exists for ajp6.

title: proxy parity test fails: core.Exchange.RequestFP has no exchangeFieldRules entry
description:
`go test ./...` is red at `internal/proxy/parity_test.go:205`:

```
--- FAIL: TestTheProxyAndTheCrawlerRecordTheSameShapeOfExchange (0.02s)
    parity_test.go:205: core.Exchange.RequestFP has no parity rule: say whether the proxy and the crawler must populate it identically, and add it to exchangeFieldRules
```

Cause: `af5ca79` ("scanner: the audit ledger keys on request content - changed requests re-audited, not silently deduped", bead 6n4d) added `RequestFP uint64` to `core.Exchange` (`internal/core/store.go:429`) and its producer (`internal/scanner/capture.go:279`, `RequestFP: core.RequestFingerprint(x.Request)`), but did not add a rule to `exchangeFieldRules` in `internal/proxy/parity_test.go`. That test deliberately hard-fails on any unclassified field - its message is the contract, not an oversight - and it also asserts `len(exchangeFieldRules) == reflect.TypeOf(core.Exchange{}).NumField()`, so the file cannot be fixed by deleting the check.

Both files are committed and unmodified in the working tree (`git status --porcelain -- internal/core internal/proxy` is empty), so this is committed breakage on the branch, not local WIP.

Fix: classify `RequestFP`. It is an FNV-1a of the recorded request bytes, and the two legs do not record the same bytes - the parity test's own UserEdited comment states the proxied leg is the one that strips Proxy-* headers and corrects framing, and the crawler authors its own request rather than relaying a client's - so the honest rule is `ruleMayDiffer`, with the comment saying why: a fingerprint of each producer's own bytes is not a claim the two must agree. Whoever lands it should confirm that reading rather than copy it - the alternative is that both legs are expected to fingerprint identically for a same-URL fetch, which the Proxy-* stripping contradicts.

Surfaced while running the Go gate for burpsy-react-ui-whr, which touches no Go files.
close_reason: RequestFP classified as ruleMayDiffer in internal/proxy/parity_test.go. Measured: ruleIdentical fails (proxy 13582984474493235635 vs crawler 579827216269916262), ruleAbsent is false because both legs compute it at scanner.Capture.Record. go test ./internal/proxy/ green in 44.3s.

title: scanner: the coverage harness never seeds stored render pages - every stored row is unreachable in the runtime suite
description:
runtime_coverage_test.go seed() (lines 538-602) stores one exchange per vulnapp.Endpoint. The row loop at :817-818 skips entries with an empty Row, and vulnapp_stored.go declares render pages exactly that way: /st/notes (:162), /st/feedback/list (:138), /st/account/activity (:143), /st/profile/card (:149), /st/support/tickets (:154), /st/theme/page (:166), /st/bookmarks (:183), /st/forms (:195), /st/widgets (:206), and the /safe variants.

Consequence: those pages never enter rt.exchanges or s.store.Exchanges(), so storedRefetchTargets (internal/scanner/stored_refetch.go:208) - which builds its candidate list from s.store.Exchanges() - cannot list them, RefetchStoredTargets never requests them, and ObserveStoredCanaries never sees a body carrying a planted canary. Every stored row whose evidence comes from a render page is therefore structurally unreachable in this suite; the suite reports them as missed even though the row and matcher are correct.

Measured: TestTheScannerDetectsWhatTheTargetDeclaresItIsVulnerableTo reports 159 of 160 rows demonstrated, 1 missed - the missed row is Cross-site scripting (stored) via /st/note?text=seed, and the target IS vulnerable (its Note says the note is inlined unescaped into a <script> literal by /st/notes on a later request).

The production path differs: storedRefetchTargets iterates REAL captured traffic, so in an operator scan the render page is reached because the crawl captured it. The gap is specific to the coverage harness.

FIX DIRECTION: seed each empty-Row manifest entry the same way as the row entries (a GET captured into the store), or add an explicit render-page seeding step. Acceptance: the stored row fires in the coverage suite and the count moves from 159/160 to 160/160, with no change to the scanner packages. This is the fix that unblocks 1a3z and tqyf; do NOT add a stored row or a new matcher for it.
close_reason: FALSIFIED BY MEASUREMENT 2026-09-18. The bead claims the coverage harness never seeds stored render pages. That is false: runtime_coverage_test.go:173-179 iterates vulnapp.Vulnerabilities() and calls seed() for every entry with NO Row filter, and seed() stores each exchange (rt.store.AddExchange(ex), rt.exchanges[e.Path] = ex.ID). The empty-Row skips at :757, :817-818, :970, :1013 govern which rows are AUDITED, not which are seeded. Proven directly by instrumenting the refetch: completion.Refetch printed "324 of 324 known GET targets re-fetched; 1 canary sighting(s), 1 planted canary(ies) never surfaced anywhere (refused=0 failed=0 observed=1 outstanding=1)" for /st/note?text=seed. Observed=1 means the render page WAS re-fetched and the canary WAS sighted there. The real cause of the stored-row miss is recorded on tqyf: storedRenderNotes renders the value into an unbreakable single-quoted JS string literal. Closing this bead as filed on a false premise; the tracking continues on tqyf.

title: scanner: FinishScan is never called by any web audit path — deferred stored-DOM claims never settle in operator-launched scans
description:
The scanner's stored re-fetch pass (stored_refetch.go:58-88 FinishScan), the browser render pass (stored_dom_render.go:113-184 RenderStoredTargets, MaxStoredDOMRenders 120, storedRenderConcurrency 4) and the pending-claim registry are FULLY BUILT and tested in isolation (runtime_coverage_test.go:321-391, stored_lifecycle_test.go:40-73) — and have ZERO production callers. Verified by grep over internal/web for FinishScan|RenderStoredTargets|RefetchStoredTargets: the only hit is a coincidental substring in the minified ui/dist/app.js. Only cmd/xsschallenge/main.go:294 and scanner tests call it.

Consequence: any stored-DOM claim deferred during a web-launched audit (POST /api/audit/{id}, /api/audit/selected, crawl-audit, API scan) is registered in the PendingRegistry and NEVER settled — no re-fetch, no browser render, no second ask. domStoredCheck's deferDOMStoredClaim (checks_dom.go:340-367) returns errCheckInconclusive so the row reads 'undecided, not clean' — honest, but the evidence to confirm it never arrives.

## Context
Found by the browser/crawler integration research scout 2026-09-17. The xsschallenge binary is the only caller today — proof the machinery works when invoked. FinishScan mutates shared scanner state: read stored_refetch.go:58-88 carefully for idempotency before choosing the call site.
acceptance_criteria: 1. FinishScan is called at the end of runBulkAudit (api_scanner_audit.go:361 tail) and runAudit (:212 tail). 2. Call placement respects concurrent audits — PendingRegistry mutation is scanner-wide; the xsschallenge pattern (FinishScan once after the batch) is the model; if two audits run concurrently the second call must not double-settle. 3. A deferred stored-DOM claim from a web-launched audit settles within the same task's outcome. 4. e2e or web test proving the wiring. 5. Full gate.
close_reason: Wired and verified. FinishScan now runs at both web audit tails: runAudit (single exchange, synchronous — reply carries a deferred ScanCompletion block) and runBulkAudit (selections/crawl-audit/API scans — settlement lands on the same task row with a dashboard event naming settled and outstanding counts). Guard: new ActiveScanner.PendingCount() reads claims WITHOUT creating the registry (Pending() would self-register, making the guard lie), so a claim-free audit sends no second-pass traffic at all. Load-bearing ordering found by the failing test: the bulk paths' context is the task's own and Handle.finish calls the task's cancel, so the deferred phase MUST run before task.FinishWithNote — first draft ran after and the re-fetch died 'context canceled' with 0/3 targets re-fetched (observed via stderr probe). Tests: 3 new in audit_deferred_test.go against the real vulnapp — bulk (30 claims settle, finding lands on the store, registry drains), single (deferred block in reply, registry drained), guard (static audit: no second-pass traffic, no deferred block). Mutation check observed: both guards disabled -> bulk times out waiting for claims, single reports missing deferred key; guard test keeps passing as it should. Gates: internal/web 38s ok, internal/scanner 431s ok, e2e-go.sh 24/24, vet/gofmt clean, whitespace audit clean. Committed 29463f4.
