title: netauth: ParseScheme refuses the NTLMv2 it implements — the codec landed and is unreachable
description:
## Claim

`internal/netauth/netauth.go` `ParseScheme` refuses `"ntlmv2"` at parse time (`case "ntlm", "ntlmv1", "ntlmv2", "negotiate", "kerberos": return "", fmt.Errorf(...)`), and `SupportedSchemes()` offers only Basic/Digest. But `internal/netauth/ntlm.go` implements **NTLMv2 only** — full NTLMSSP codec + MS-NLMP response algorithm with MIC — and its own header says so. The two files disagree: the codec exists and nothing can select it.

## Burp-side evidence

Burp's platform authentication offers Basic, Digest, NTLMv1, NTLMv2 and Negotiate (`Zgwy.java:205` "Authentication type:", `Zgq4.java:28-33` `use_negotiate_auth_scheme` on the upstream credential). Build 51467 tree; behaviour verified against the running 2026.7.3 jar.

## burpsy-side evidence

- `netauth.go:ParseScheme` — the refusal is the load-bearing half: an NTLMv2 credential cannot be configured at all.
- `netauth.go:UnsupportedSchemes()` returns `["NTLMv1","NTLMv2","Negotiate"]` — **stale**: it names NTLMv2, which is implemented.
- `ntlm.go:4` — "This file implements **NTLMv2 only**."
- `net_auth_pattern_parity_test.go` pins the codec.
- Bead `trcy`'s close reason says "The NTLMv2 codec landed in 3fb2ce1 and was unreachable for the traffic that needed it" — the intent was always to wire it; the refusal is the remaining defect.

## Classification

BUG — a landed capability made unreachable by its own selector, plus a stale refusal list that tells the UI the codec is absent.

## What an operator cannot do

Configure an NTLMv2 credential for a target that demands it, even though the full codec (NTLMSSP negotiate/authenticate messages, MS-NLMP response computation, MIC) is in the tree and tested at the codec level.

## Acceptance criteria

1. `ParseScheme` accepts `"ntlmv2"` (keeping NTLMv1/Negotiate/Kerberos refusals with their reasons — those are genuine: NTLMv1 is DES-only, Negotiate needs a KDC credential).
2. `SupportedSchemes()` adds NTLMv2 so the UI panel offers it.
3. The per-connection affinity the proxy leg needs is stated honestly: NTLMv2 handshake state must persist per upstream connection; if the proxy opens a fresh socket per request, the rule either pins a connection or the scheme is wired sender-side first — a test drives a real 401 challenge/response round trip through whichever leg lands.
4. A codec-level test proving a captured negotiate/authenticate pair verifies (the MS-NLMP response algorithm) — already exists; extend it to the selection path.

## Priority

P2 — a landed, tested codec that nothing can reach; the fix is the selector plus one wiring decision.
close_reason: Wired the NTLMv2 the codec implements, both legs: ParseScheme accepts ntlmv2, SupportedSchemes adds it, UnsupportedSchemes drops the stale name, NewCredential accepts SchemeNTLMv2. ntlm.go gained the wire session (ntlmChallengeBlob decodes and validates the WWW-Authenticate: NTLM b64 payload; ntlmAnswer drives MS-NLMP 3.3.2 end to end — NTOWFv2 from the password, the domain decoded back from the MsvAvNbDomain AV pair's UTF-16LE, the v2 response computed once over the target info as sent, MIC over negotiate+challenge when MsvAvFlags asks). Credentials.Authorization sends NEGOTIATE preemptively and the AUTHENTICATE on the bounded one-retry flow; Learn accepts the NTLM blob and refuses re-learning the same challenge bytes (same shape as the Digest repeated-nonce refusal); the ntlm cache is keyed by host like the Digest one and forgetMatching drops both. Acceptance 1+2: scheme parses and is offered. Acceptance 3: state lives in the credential store keyed by host, not a socket — TestAnNTLMv2ChallengeIsLearnedSoTheNextRequestAuthenticates proves the learned challenge reaches the second request on a SEPARATE proxy connection, and Test_a_configured_ntlmv2_credential_completes_the_three_leg_exchange drives a real server that verifies the AUTHENTICATE's NTProofStr with an independent MS-NLMP recomputation (acceptance 4's selection-path extension). The two stale tests pinning ntlmv2-as-refused were updated to pin the new behavior; the web API test pins ntlmv1 as the refused Burp scheme. Verified: build/vet/gofmt clean, netauth+sender+full proxy suite green, web network-auth tests green in a pristine HEAD worktree. Committed 5a8df0c.

title: api: the risk classification is test-only — no runtime server-side confirm gate, so a direct/MCP/agent caller bypasses the UI dialog on attack routes
description:
## Claim

burpsy classifies every API route by a risk class (riskRead / riskLocal / riskAttack / riskAsset), but that classification is enforced only by a TEST and by doc comments — there is no runtime server-side gate that makes a caller confirm before invoking a riskAttack route. The only confirmation that exists is a UI dialog, which any direct API caller (a script, an MCP client, an agent, or a CSRF/rebinding request) bypasses completely.

## Evidence

burpsy:
- The taxonomy exists only in the test: `route_manifest.go` does NOT exist; only internal/web/route_manifest_test.go does, and `type riskClass string` and the riskAttack/riskRead values live there. Confirmed by `ls internal/web/route_manifest*` (one file) and `grep -rn 'riskClass' --include=*.go | grep -v _test` (only doc comments in api_compare_sitemaps.go:51, api_passive_branch.go:22-26, api_scanner_audit_items.go:336).
- The test's own comment states the intent as unmet: route_manifest_test.go:52 — a manifest so that "a single server-side check CAN enforce confirmation, rather than 21 facades each deciding for themselves." "Can", not "does".
- The only runtime confirmation is UI-side: crates/web/src/lib.rs:393 — "the UI puts a confirmation in front of it." That is a browser dialog, not a server gate; a non-browser caller never sees it.
- No runtime gate: `grep -rniE 'require.*confirm|needsConfirm|unattended|X-Confirm'` over internal/web/*.go (non-test) finds nothing.

## Fix direction

Turn the test-time classification into a runtime manifest the server owns, and add one middleware that consults it:
1. Promote the route→riskClass table out of the test into a real internal/web/route_manifest.go the server registers against (the test already wants this; it fails a route that is not in the manifest).
2. A single server-side check: a riskAttack (and destructive riskLocal) route requires an explicit confirmation signal — a header/param the caller must set, or a two-step confirm token — before it executes. The UI supplies it after its dialog; an unattended caller must supply it deliberately.
3. Keep riskRead/riskAsset ungated.

## Why it matters

This is the enforcement primitive I wrongly assumed already existed when filing the MCP-transport (q31t), agent-loop (x40l) and scan-MCP (wflj) beads. Those all depend on it: exposing burpsy's routes to a model or a remote caller WITHOUT a server-side gate hands every attack route out with only a browser dialog — which the model never sees — standing between a prompt and live attack traffic. The gate has to exist before any of them is safe. It also backs the console-auth bead: auth says who may call; the gate says which calls need a deliberate confirm.
acceptance_criteria: A runtime route manifest owned by the server maps each route to its riskClass; one middleware requires a deliberate confirmation signal before a riskAttack route executes; a direct API call to an attack route without the signal is refused; riskRead/riskAsset stay ungated.
notes:
The manifest half was already done by acdv (route_manifest.go is production code, not test-local), so this was the gate alone.

internal/web/confirm_gate.go, wrapped as s.sameOriginOnly(s.confirmationGate(s.mux, confirmMux)):
- needsConfirmation gates mutating verbs on the four classes: scope, attack, credential, destructive. Reads and assets pass through -- gating GET /api/scope would mean the console cannot show the operator what they are about to confirm, which is the dialog this backs up.
- One-time tokens from crypto/rand, bound to the route pattern, 60s TTL, swept on issue so a console left running does not grow unbounded. A header not a body field: the gated routes take their payload in the body, and a confirmation smuggled into that body is a field an attacker sets as easily as the confirmation.
- 428 Precondition Required, and the refusal names the route, the risk and how to confirm -- safe only because the origin gate is OUTER, so reaching the 428 already means the caller is not a hostile page.

Three ordering/joining bugs found by tests, each a gate that silently forbade routes or leaked:
1. Mint endpoints on a separate mux. On s.mux, Test_every_route_pattern_is_a_literal (correctly) refuses the derived pattern, and a gated route could shadow its own /confirm.
2. TrimSuffix before appending, or a subtree pattern '/api/x/' yields '//confirm' -- a path no caller types, so the endpoint 405s. Plus dedupe: the manifest holds both '/api/pools' and '/api/pools/', and registering both panics ServeMux.
3. The mint check must run BEFORE the risk resolution. '/api/sequencer/capture/confirm' resolves by longest match to the riskRead subtree '/api/sequencer/capture/', so checking risk first let the mint fall through to the main mux and 405. Same for /api/tools/log.

Gate order is the security argument and is tested: with sameOrigin INSIDE, a cross-site caller got the 428 and learned which header to try next. Caught by four existing same-origin tests.

12 new tests. go build ./... go vet ./... gofmt -l clean. internal/web green except the pre-existing /api/session/prompts manifest failure from another agent's untracked WIP (reproduces with my change reverted).

Not in scope, and the refusal says so: a caller that can POST /x/confirm without a human present can satisfy the gate itself. That needs console auth, which is a separate bead. What this guarantees is that the dangerous call is never reached by accident, and never by a tool acting on the operator's earlier unrelated instruction.
close_reason: Closed

title: crawler: parse API definitions (OpenAPI/Swagger, SOAP WSDL, GraphQL) as crawl discovery sources
description:
## Claim

Burp's `parse_api_definitions` / `parse_soap_wsdls` / `perform_graphql_introspection` / `guess_hidden_graphql_endpoints` make an API document encountered *during* a crawl into a source of endpoints. burpsy reads JSON `url`/`href`/`next` members but parses no API *document*.

## Burp-side evidence (build 51467/2026.7.1)

- `Zrf0.java:3627-3637` — panel "API crawling" (3633) with four checkboxes: `guess_hidden_graphql_endpoints` (3627), `perform_graphql_introspection` (3622/3632), `parse_api_definitions` (3634), `parse_soap_wsdls` (3630/3637); description 3631: "Configure how Burp detects and explores APIs when crawling your site." Test button 3629 "Test common GraphQL endpoints". Action kinds `Zb8w.API` (11), `Zb8w.SOAP` (28), `Zb8w.GRAPHQL_INTROSPECTION` (26), `Zb8w.DISCOVERED_GRAPHQL_OPERATION` (27). DOC crawl-settings.html:243-259 — "Test common GraphQL endpoints … only available if Perform GraphQL introspection is selected." Defaults: all `true` except `guess_hidden_graphql_endpoints: false` (`CrawlDefaults.json`).

## burpsy-side evidence

`crawler.go:1745` `consumeJSON` is the only non-HTML extractor; `discover.go` has no document parser. `burpconfig.go:77-81` applies 3 keys, so these four are reported unrepresentable. Bead `93o4` covers the *launcher*, not the crawler phase — it does not dedup this.

## Classification

CONFIRMED.

## What an operator cannot do

A target publishing `/openapi.json` or `?WSDL` yields **zero** extra locations from a burpsy crawl even though the file is fetched, stored, scanned and discarded. GraphQL endpoints are never introspected and never guessed.

## Acceptance criteria

1. Four `crawler/customization/*` keys land in `AppliedKeys` when present.
2. A JSON/YAML body recognised as an OpenAPI/Swagger document yields its `paths` operations as frontier items (method + path + declared parameters).
3. A WSDL body yields its `<operation>`/soapAction endpoints.
4. A GraphQL endpoint receives an introspection query when the key is on, and its operations become locations.
5. A parse failure is a distinct counted skip (`SkipAPIUnparsed`), never "0 locations".

## Priority

P2 — high value on API targets; each of the four parsers is a discrete unit of work.
notes:
PARTIAL in commit b4855ae. Acceptance criteria 1, 2, 3 and 5 are met; criterion 4 is NOT.

MET: (1) the four crawler/customization/* keys land in AppliedKeys — the census test moves 9 -> 13 applied, 37 -> 33 unrepresentable; (2) a JSON or YAML OpenAPI/Swagger document yields its path operations with method, declared parameters and operationId; (3) a WSDL yields its <operation> endpoints (identity + POST, no invented path); (5) an unparseable definition is SkipAPIUnparsed, a new counted reason, never '0 locations', and  present-but-unreadable is a failure while  absent is a legal skeleton.

NOT MET: (4) GraphQL. The two keys perform_graphql_introspection and guess_hidden_graphql_endpoints land in AppliedKeys and are recorded on the report, but NO introspection query is sent and no hidden GraphQL endpoint is guessed. A caller reading the report would see those two keys applied and could reasonably conclude the behaviour exists; it does not. That is the dishonest-counting shape this repository treats as a defect, so it is stated here rather than left for someone to discover.

Also partial: a WSDL operation contributes its identity and POST only. The service path lives in the port's <soap:address>, and this reader refuses to guess it rather than inventing an endpoint, so a WSDL's operations are counted and not fetched. GraphQL introspection is the natural next step and is unstarted.

Verified: 20 new tests green; three mutations each fail a named test (WSDL subtree consumption, the malformed-paths distinction, the YAML fallback). go build/vet/gofmt clean and the full internal/crawler suite passes. Files: internal/crawler/{apidoc.go,apidoc_decode.go,crawler.go,skip.go,burpconfig.go} + three test files.
PARTIAL in commit b4855ae. Acceptance criteria 1, 2, 3 and 5 are met; criterion 4 is NOT.

MET: (1) the four crawler/customization/* keys land in AppliedKeys — the census test moves 9 -> 13 applied, 37 -> 33 unrepresentable; (2) a JSON or YAML OpenAPI/Swagger document yields its path operations with method, declared parameters and operationId; (3) a WSDL yields its operation elements (identity + POST, no invented path); (5) an unparseable definition is SkipAPIUnparsed, a new counted reason, never "0 locations", and a `paths` key present-but-unreadable is a failure while `paths` absent is a legal skeleton.

NOT MET: (4) GraphQL. The two keys perform_graphql_introspection and guess_hidden_graphql_endpoints land in AppliedKeys and are recorded on the report, but NO introspection query is sent and no hidden GraphQL endpoint is guessed. A caller reading the report would see those two keys applied and could reasonably conclude the behaviour exists; it does not. That is the dishonest-counting shape this repository treats as a defect, so it is stated here rather than left for someone to discover.

Also partial: a WSDL operation contributes its identity and POST only. The service path lives in the port's soap:address, and this reader refuses to guess it rather than inventing an endpoint, so a WSDL's operations are counted and not fetched. GraphQL introspection is the natural next step and is unstarted.

Verified: 20 new tests green; three mutations each fail a named test (WSDL subtree consumption, the malformed-paths distinction, the YAML fallback). go build/vet/gofmt clean and the full internal/crawler suite passes. Files: internal/crawler/{apidoc.go,apidoc_decode.go,crawler.go,skip.go,burpconfig.go} plus three test files.
COMPLETE in commits b4855ae (documents) + 1124259 (GraphQL). All five acceptance criteria are now met.

  1. The four crawler/customization/* keys land in AppliedKeys (census 9 -> 13, 37 -> 33 unrepresentable).
  2. A JSON or YAML OpenAPI/Swagger document yields its path operations with method, declared parameters and operationId.
  3. A WSDL yields its operation elements (identity + POST).
  4. A GraphQL endpoint receives an introspection query when the key is on, and its operations become locations (1124259). The query goes through perform(), so it is scope-authorised, rate limited, captured and counted like every other crawl request; the request bound is checked before the send.
  5. A parse failure is a distinct counted skip (SkipAPIUnparsed, SkipGraphQLUnparsed, SkipGraphQLIntrospection), never "0 locations".

Four defects were found by this session's own tests, and each is worth recording because the symptom in every case was "the feature silently does nothing" rather than an error:

  - The GraphQL hook was installed against res.Raw, which is the whole raw HTTP response including the status line and headers, so every probe read the head and never the body. A hook placed one step too early compiles, looks correct, and never fires.
  - looksLikeGraphQLEndpoint matched any `data` key, which every JSON API response has; it would have POSTed an introspection query to every JSON endpoint a crawl touched. Now requires `__schema` or `errors`. Found by a mutation: the existing test seeded an HTML page, where the probe is false for a different reason, so a looser probe passed it.
  - lim.Requests reads zero throughout a crawl (it is assigned from rep.Fetched only after the loop ends), so the bound check was checking nothing. Now reads rep.Fetched.
  - The two GraphQL bookkeeping maps were never initialised; the first envelope reached panicked on a nil-map assignment.

Verified: 29 new tests green across the two commits. Nine mutations each fail a named test (WSDL subtree consumption, malformed-paths distinction, YAML fallback, the GraphQL probe loosened two ways, request bound removed, meta-fields yielded, introspection-disabled flattened to zero). go build, go vet, gofmt and the full internal/crawler suite clean.

Standing limitation, deliberate and stated rather than fixed: a WSDL operation yields its identity and POST only, because the service path lives in the port's soap:address and this reader refuses to guess it. WSDL operations are counted, not fetched.

This session added b579e39: two crawl-level tests the committed suite lacked — an unparseable introspection answer records SkipGraphQLUnparsed (never a silent zero) and a guessed path is probed once per origin. Three mutations each fail a named test. Verified: go build/vet/gofmt clean, full internal/crawler suite green at HEAD.

title: scanner: no per-host throttle interval or resource-pool concurrency — audit pacing is a global budget only
description:
## Claim

`fkl8` closed the 429/503 backoff half of Burp's resource pools. The other two pool knobs — `throttle_interval_millis` (+`throttle_random_enabled`) and `concurrent_request_limit` per pool — have no bead and no burpsy representation. A run is paced by a session-wide time and request budget (`internal/scanner/audit.go:517-526`) and by `ScanConfig.MaxConcurrency` (`audit_engine.go:1026-1031`), which is global: one slow host consumes the whole pool and every other host stalls behind it.

## Burp-side evidence (build 51467/2026.7.1)

`project_options.resource_pools.*` — `out/strings/map_root.tsv:17469-17504` (default pool) and `:23192-23213` (custom pools): `concurrent_request_limit` (+ enabled), `throttle_interval_millis` (+ enabled, + `throttle_random_enabled`), and the backoff family fkl8 took. Runtime state keys confirm per-pool granularity: `scan_resource_pool_in_progress_requests` (`map_root.tsv:28564`), `scan_resource_pool_latest_request_time` (`:13895`), `request-queue-%d` (`Zr9n`, `:28563`).

## burpsy-side evidence

`AuditConfig` (`audit.go:516-668`) has no throttle or per-host concurrency field. `audit_engine.go:1026-1031` sizes one global worker pool from `MaxConcurrency`. Budget enforcement is at `audit_engine.go:1081-1090`.

## Classification

CAPABILITY GAP.

## What an operator cannot do

Scan a target at a polite fixed rate (the standard courtesy and the standard WAF-evasion case), and cannot scan two hosts at different rates in one run. Six related beads describe the *consequences* of the global pool (6urp per-host pacing, ajp6, a4ng, i4fa's pool-driven attack quality); none asks for the knob.

## Acceptance criteria

1. A per-host rate limiter on the audit dispatch path: minimum interval between probes to the same host, with an optional randomisation matching `throttle_random_enabled`.
2. A per-host in-flight cap, distinct from the global worker count, so a slow host cannot consume the whole pool.
3. Both surfaced on `/api/scanner/config` and honoured by the live sweep, which shares the dispatch loop.
4. A test driving two hosts where one is deliberately slow, asserting the other completes rather than being blocked — the same shape as 6urp's symptom, asserted at the fix.

## Priority

P2 — real operator need, well-located Burp evidence, and it unblocks the family of pacing beads.
close_reason: Closed

title: scanner: scan_speed and scan_accuracy are per-check payload-set and token-count selectors in Burp, not run-level pacing
description:
## Claim

Two rows at `internal/scanner/audit.go:1317-1320` (scan_accuracy) and `:1323-1326` (scan_speed) are reported unapplied on the reasoning that Burp's presets "change which checks run per issue type" / "trade check coverage for time". Both readings are wrong about the mechanism, and the truth is the more portable one: **both are per-check mutation-set selectors**, a shape burpsy already has (`CheckInvasiveness`, `check_contract.go:105-118`).

## Burp-side evidence (build 51467/2026.7.1)

- `scan_speed` → `Zsv7.java:7-62`: `FAST, NORMAL, THOROUGH` with `int speed` and ordered predicates `Zi(o) = speed >= o.speed`, `ZS(o) = speed < o.speed`. Threaded into **check construction** and gates payload-set membership: `Zbxl.java:42-46` (`if (this.Zq == Zsv7.THOROUGH) add HTTP_MIXED_CASE_PREFIXED_URL_PAYLOAD; if (!https) add HTTPS_PREFIXED_URL_PAYLOAD`), `Zch1.java:19-29` (FAST adds `}}`, `%}`, random+`%>`; THOROUGH adds `%]` and `;//';";%>?>`), `Zc99.java:29-32`, `Zeoh.java:93-96,117-122,171-174`, dispatched from `Zey.java:31-43`.
- `scan_accuracy` → `Zgnf.java:7-43`: `MINIMIZE_FALSE_NEGATIVES, NORMAL, MINIMIZE_FALSE_POSITIVES` with `int accuracy`. `Zs_2.java:8` is the whole mechanism: `Map.of(MINIMIZE_FALSE_NEGATIVES, 4, NORMAL, 8, MINIMIZE_FALSE_POSITIVES, 10)`, consumed by `ZN():90-98` and looped per check at `Zk():62-88` — a **mutation-token count**. Separately `Zc4i.java:7` is a third accuracy member, `FALSE_POSITIVE_REDUCTION`, attached to the scan *type* (`Zh7v.java:9-11`).
- Shipped: scan_speed in 6 of 29 configs, scan_accuracy in 3.

## burpsy-side evidence

- `audit.go:1317-1326` (both rows `applies: false`). The per-check tier infrastructure is `CheckInvasiveness`/`TierLight`/`TierMedium`/`TierIntrusive` (`check_contract.go:105-118`), selected by `activeTiers` (`audit_engine.go:245-253`) — a three-value rank selector that a second independent rank axis would slot into without new machinery.

## Classification

CAPABILITY GAP + UX DIVERGENCE (two shipped presets, `Minimize false positives.json` / `Minimize false negatives.json`, currently load as silent no-ops).

## What an operator cannot do

Neither of Burp's two headline accuracy presets — the ones a reviewer actually hands to someone — changes anything burpsy sends. And no burpsy check can offer a cheap-and-wide versus thorough-and-narrow mutation set, the single biggest lever on a large audit.

## Acceptance criteria

1. A `CheckSpeed` axis (three values) on `CheckDescriptor`, set per check family, independent of `Invasiveness`. A check with no declared speed inherits the configured level's base set.
2. A run-level `ScanSpeed OptUint32` honouring Burp's three `uiName` spellings (`fast`/`normal`/`thorough`, `Zhd_.java:61-63`) so an exported Burp config loads by name.
3. A run-level `ScanAccuracy OptUint32` honouring `minimise_false_negatives`/`normal`/`minimise_false_positives` (`Zhd_.java:65-74`) that bounds a check's mutation attempts to Burp's 4/8/10.
4. Both rows leave the "not applied" bucket; `audit_config_keys_test.go:112` counts move.
5. A test that loads `Minimize false positives.json` through `ParseBurpConfig` and observes the **set of probe requests actually sent** differ from the same run under `Audit coverage - maximum.json` — the count, not the config row.

## Priority

P2 — two shipped presets that are currently silent no-ops is the sharpest operator-visible harm here; the axis is a small extension of machinery that exists.
notes:
REOPENED 2026-10-05 by the same audit. The close reason claims 'CheckSpeed (FAST/NORMAL/THOROUGH) and CheckAccuracy (MINIMIZE_FALSE_NEGATIVES/NORMAL/MINIMIZE_FALSE_POSITIVES) axes added to CheckDescriptor' plus 7 new tests.

At HEAD: CheckSpeed 0 files, CheckAccuracy 0 files. ScanAccuracy appears in exactly 1 file, so a fragment of the plumbing may exist while the two axes the bead is actually about do not. CheckDescriptor itself is real (scanner/audit.go) and has neither field.

Partial-or-absent rather than cleanly absent, so whoever takes this should read the one ScanAccuracy site first and decide whether it is a leftover from this work or belongs to something else.
close_reason: Landed in 0c01842, after being closed once describing CheckSpeed/CheckAccuracy that existed in zero files (found by the 466-bead audit). All five criteria: (1) CheckSpeed axis on CheckDescriptor, independent of Invasiveness, zero value = every run; (2) ScanSpeed loads by Burp's fast/normal/thorough NAMES — the values are strings in a section the parser treated as numeric, so Burp's own files would have been rejected; (3) ScanAccuracy bounds mutation attempts to Burp's 4/8/10 table; (4) both rows left the unapplied bucket, coverage pin moved 38/4/16 -> 40/4/14 loudly; (5) the two shipped presets now send DIFFERENT payload counts (10 vs 4), asserted against the exact JSON Burp ships. 13 tests; 7 mutations, 6 killed — including the one that caught the config->harness wiring gap, which is what 'closed but never landed' looked like here. NOT done and recorded: no built-in check declares a Speed yet, so the axis is enforced but selects nothing; ranking the corpus needs Burp's per-check payload-set mapping and guessing it would put invented rankings behind an operator-visible control.

title: scanner: skip_ineffective_checks is a live per-insertion-point gate in Burp; the key row calls it unimplementable
description:
## Claim

`internal/scanner/audit.go:1329-1332` reports `scanner/audit_optimization/skip_ineffective_checks` as *"not applied: this engine infers nothing about a check's effectiveness, so it has nothing to skip on."* That reason is false. Burp's effectiveness oracle is **per insertion point**, not per check, and it is reachable here.

## Burp-side evidence (build 51467/2026.7.1)

- `Zfhb.java:81-83` is the per-insertion-point dispatch filter:
  ```java
  private boolean lambda$doPerInsertionPointChecks$2(Zuit var1) {
      return var1 != null && (!this.Z_.Zip() || var1.Zh()) && this.Zs.ZA(this.Zc.Zt());
  }
  ```
  `Zip()` is `skip_ineffective_checks` (declared `Zcsr.java:12`, fed from `Zhd_.java:38`). When the key is ON the predicate reduces to `var1.Zh()` — the point's own effectiveness. `Zh()` bottoms out in `Zb42.java:63-66` → `Zcgg.Zw(point)` (`Zcgg.java:12-14`) = `point.Zp(new Zc3c())`, a probe returning true for one message class and false for the other.
- Ships in 3 of 29 shipped configs (`Audit coverage - thorough.json:13`, `Minimize false positives.json:13`, `Minimize false negatives.json:13`).
- **Confidence:** the gate's existence is CONFIRMED (I read all four files); the exact effectiveness metric inside `point.Zp(...)` is UNKNOWN from this tree — `Zc3c` itself is two trivial cases (`Zc3c.java:4-10`), so the interestingness is computed on the point, not precomputed.

## burpsy-side evidence

- `audit.go:1329-1332` (the row). The engine has a per-point verdict seam it never uses for this: `bcheck.InsertionPoint` carries `Kind`/`Name`/`BaseValue` and `bcheck.Enumerate` returns `Declined` rows with a `What` (`internal/bcheck/insertion.go:322-333, 704-713`) — the exact shape a point-effectiveness decline takes.
- `audit_config_keys_test.go:112` pins the row as reported-unapplied.

## Classification

CAPABILITY GAP + a false statement in an operator-facing table (the 86le-class precedent for treating that as more than cosmetic).

## What an operator cannot do

An operator who loads Burp's "Minimize false positives" preset is told the key did nothing. In Burp it drops the check set at points that provably do not behave interestingly — the largest request saving Burp offers on a 300-parameter form. burpsy pays full price on all of them.

## Acceptance criteria

1. A named `AuditConfig.SkipIneffectiveChecks OptUint32` on the run, defaulting to Burp's shipped default.
2. A per-point effectiveness predicate on the `bcheck` enumerator seam — same position as `lightAuditShouldSkip`, evaluated **per point inside the request**, not per (kind, host) across the run (that is 7bkj's mechanism, a different one).
3. Declined points counted in the item outcome so the partition identity in `audit_engine.go:1222` still holds, with a distinct `What` — not folded into `AuditItemPointSkippedDeclined`.
4. The key row changes from `not applied` to applied-or-partial; `audit_config_keys_test.go:112` counts move.
5. A test that toggles the key and observes the **point-level declined count** differ, not just the row flag.

## Priority

P2 — the Burp mechanism is small and fully located; the burpsy seam exists; the cost is a predicate + a row flip. Not P1 (it removes requests, does not add detections); not P3 (the current `what` is a false statement in a settings surface).
close_reason: Applied, per INSERTION POINT as Burp does (Zfhb.java:81-83 filters the per-insertion-point dispatch on the point's own effectiveness, not on the check's). The old row's 'this engine infers nothing about a check's effectiveness' was the wrong subject — the key never asked about a check. The decision is ported; the exact predicate is not recoverable from the tree (Zc3c is two trivial cases), so the oracle is ours and the row says so: a place is dropped only after THIS RUN probed it twice with nothing found, keyed per (check, kind, name, host) so one check's silence cannot gate another check away from a place. An unprobed place is always probed; a place that answered is retired permanently; a nil oracle skips nothing. Every drop is a bcheck.Declined with its count and its own AuditItemPointStatus. Also fixed: isNumericBurpKey read the whole audit_optimization section as numeric, so a Burp file carrying "skip_ineffective_checks": true was rejected outright. Verified: 8 unit assertions over the decision + a real-session pair (same exchanges, key on vs off: fewer probes, non-zero judged count, and that count absent when off). Key-table pin moved 37/4/17 -> 38/4/16. Full internal/scanner suite green apart from one pre-existing failure owned by 3ymo (its max_items_in_progress key applies and Test_a_configs_reported_keys_are_exactly_what_apply_overlays has not been taught to check it). Commit ee841fc, which also carries 3ymo's in-flight admission cap because the two interleave in three files and a hunk-level split does not compile; the commit message attributes it.

title: extender: a plugin chord can take a key that belongs to the shell, another plugin, or the editor (Ctrl+C/V/Z, AltGr), and auto-repeat re-invokes it
description:
## Context

These are review findings (2026-09-27) on wsu4's UNCOMMITTED diff, for whoever holds wsu4. This is a handoff, not a claim. None of these can happen until the dispatch bug (sibling bead) is fixed, but all of them will once it is.

## Claim

A plugin chord can take a key that already belongs to something else: the shell's own bindings, another plugin's chord, or an editing key inside an input or CodeMirror.

## Evidence

1. **No collision check.** Nothing in the hotkey validation in `internal/extension/host.go` (`case reg.Kind == KindHotKey && NormaliseChord(reg.Chord) == ""`) checks for collisions with the shell keymap or between plugins.
   - A plugin asking for "Ctrl+K" (palette), "Ctrl+R" (Send to Repeater) or "Alt+1" (switch tool) means both actions fire.
   - Two plugins declaring "Ctrl+Shift+K" put `mod+shift+k,mod+shift+k` in the joined list. The library fires the callback twice per press, and `bindings.find` returns the first plugin both times, so plugin A runs twice and plugin B never runs.
   - `actionForChord` (`ui/src/lib/shortcuts.ts`) already does duplicate detection for the shell keymap and is not consulted.
2. **Editing keys are taken.** `usePluginHotkeys` passes `{ enableOnFormTags: true, enableOnContentEditable: true }` and calls `event.preventDefault()`. The host accepts "Ctrl+C", "Ctrl+V", "Ctrl+Z", "Ctrl+B"/"Ctrl+U" (the editor's codec keys) and "Ctrl+Alt+Q", which is AltGr+Q ('@' on a German layout). In the Repeater or Intercept editor, each of these presses would cancel the edit and send an RPC to the plugin instead.
3. **Auto-repeat.** Nothing filters `event.repeat`, so holding a chord sends dozens of `hotkey.invoke` calls and toasts.

## Fix direction

- **Collisions:** refuse, or at least mark conflicted, any chord that `actionForChord` already resolves in the shell keymap, and any chord a second plugin repeats. Pick one policy (first wins with a visible refusal, or both refused) and show it in the Extensions table.
- **Editing keys:** refuse the clipboard/undo/codec chords and Ctrl+Alt combinations (AltGr) at load, or don't fire inside form tags and contenteditable unless the chord is on an allowlist.
- **Auto-repeat:** ignore `event.repeat`.

## Acceptance

Tests for:
- a plugin chord equal to a shipped shell binding,
- two plugins declaring the same chord,
- Ctrl+C pressed inside a CodeMirror editor, where the plugin is not invoked and the default edit happens,
- a held chord, which invokes the plugin once.
acceptance_criteria: Tests: a plugin chord equal to a shipped shell binding is refused or marked conflicted; two plugins with one chord follow a stated policy visible in the Extensions table; Ctrl+C inside CodeMirror does not invoke the plugin and performs the default edit; a held chord invokes once.
close_reason: Closed

title: extender: the chord the host accepts is not the chord the UI binds — two normalisers, last key token wins, unknown keys accepted
description:
## Context

These are review findings (2026-09-27) on wsu4's UNCOMMITTED diff, for whoever holds wsu4. This is a handoff, not a claim.

## Claim

The chord the host accepts is not always the chord the UI binds, and some accepted chords can never fire. The root cause is two independent normalisers, `NormaliseChord` in Go and `normalisePluginChord` in TS, with no test checking that they agree. Neither checks the key against what the keymap can actually dispatch.

## Evidence

The reviewer ran a copy of `NormaliseChord`. Current code, re-read 2026-09-27 11:00, still reproduces all of this:

1. **The last key token wins.** In the `default:` branch of `NormaliseChord`'s loop (`internal/extension/protocol.go`), `key` is reassigned on every non-modifier token; the TS loop does the same. So:
   - `"Ctrl+Page Up"` → `mod+up` (the arrow key)
   - `"Ctrl+Back Slash"` → `mod+slash` ('/' instead of '\')
   - `"Ctrl+K+J"` → `mod+j`

   All three are accepted and bound to a different key than declared, while the doc says "exactly one non-modifier key". The console's own `validateChord` (`ui/src/lib/shortcuts.ts`) refuses a second key.
2. **Key names are never checked:**
   - `"Ctrl+Banana"` → `mod+banana` and `"Ctrl+Equals"` → `mod+equals` (the event code is `equal`). Both are accepted and never fire.
   - `"Ctrl+,"` → `mod+,`. `usePluginHotkeys` joins chords with ',' and the library splits them on ',', so this becomes `mod+` and an empty string.
   - `"Ctrl+>"` hits the library's sequence separator.
   - F13 and above are accepted, even though F1-F12 are refused.
3. **The Go and TS copies already disagree.** Go splits on `"+- "` (`strings.IndexAny`). TS splits on `/[+-\s]/`, which includes tab. `"Ctrl+\tK"` → Go `mod+\tk` (accepted) → TS `mod+k` (installed).
4. **Stale text:** the unknown-kind refusal in `host.go` (`this host implements context-menu, menu and editor-tab only`) omits the two kinds added since, session-action and hotkey. The `Invoke` doc comment ("The three literal method names below") is equally stale. A plugin author who typos `"hot-key"` is told hotkeys don't exist.

## Fix direction

1. Make one source of truth. The host already computes the normalised chord in validate(). Put it on `Registration` (for example a `binding` field), have the UI install that field directly, and delete `normalisePluginChord`. If a TS check is still wanted, run the result through `validateChord`.
2. In `NormaliseChord`, refuse a second non-modifier token instead of overwriting `key`, and check the key against the set of keys the keymap can dispatch; ',' and '>' must be spelled by name or refused.
3. Replace the nested HasPrefix/TrimPrefix chain with a `[]struct{prefix, mod string}` loop. `appendUnique` and `hasModOrAlt` can be `slices.Contains`.
4. Fix the two stale strings.

## Acceptance

A table test on the Go side covering every example above, each either refused or normalised to the key actually declared. Once the TS copy is gone, no separate TS test is needed; until then, one table must drive both.
acceptance_criteria: One normaliser (the host's) whose output is sent on Registration and installed verbatim by the UI; a Go table test where Ctrl+Page Up, Ctrl+Back Slash, Ctrl+K+J, Ctrl+Banana, Ctrl+Equals, Ctrl+, , Ctrl+>, Ctrl+F13 and Ctrl+<tab>K are each refused or normalised to the declared key; the unknown-kind refusal lists all five kinds.
close_reason: Closed

title: extender ui: no plugin hotkey can fire — the handler matches handler.keys, which react-hotkeys-hook strips of modifiers
description:
## Context

These are review findings (2026-09-27) on wsu4's UNCOMMITTED diff, for whoever holds wsu4. `plugin-hotkeys.ts` and `app.tsx` are being edited live, so this is a handoff, not a claim.

## Claim

No plugin hotkey can fire. In `usePluginHotkeys` (`internal/web/ui/src/lib/plugin-hotkeys.ts`), the callback does:

```ts
const pressed = handler.keys?.join("+");
const binding = bindings.find((b) => b.chord === pressed);
if (!binding) return;
```

react-hotkeys-hook 5.3.3 strips modifiers out of `HotkeysEvent.keys`. Its parser does `keys: o.filter((e) => !l.includes(e))`, where `l` is the modifier list (`node_modules/react-hotkeys-hook/packages/react-hotkeys-hook/dist/index.js`, about lines 42-55). For `mod+shift+k` the handler gets `keys = ["k"]`, so `pressed = "k"` never equals `"mod+shift+k"` and the callback returns before invoking anything.

## Evidence

- Library parser: confirmed by reading the dist source above.
- The 6 bun tests in `plugin-hotkeys.test.ts` pass, but they only test `normalisePluginChord` and `installedPluginHotkeys` (pure functions). None of them mounts the hook or sends a keydown, which is how this got through.

## Also in this hook

- **Fetch and staleness:** `usePluginHotkeys()` is mounted in the shell (`app.tsx`), so `useExtensions()` fetches `/api/extensions` on every page. That undoes the `open` gating the palette applies to the same request (`ui/palette.tsx`: `useResource<ExtensionList>(keys.extensions, "/api/extensions", open)`). Nothing re-fetches the list or pushes changes over `/api/events`, so a plugin that crashes after load keeps its chord installed and every press fails with ErrNotLoaded.
- **Memo:** `bindings` is a new array on every render, so the deps array `[chord, bindings, invoke]` never matches.
- **Duplication:** the invoke-and-toast `onSuccess`/`onError` block is a copy of the palette's `runExtension`. Share it.

## Fix direction

Match on `handler.hotkey` (the chord string as installed), or register one `useHotkeys` per binding so no lookup is needed. Refresh the extension list when plugin state changes, whether by event, refetch on load/unload, or a short stale time. Memoise `bindings` on `extensions.data`.

## Acceptance

A test that renders `usePluginHotkeys` with a stubbed extension list declaring "Ctrl+Shift+K", dispatches a real Ctrl+Shift+K keydown, and asserts `hotkey.invoke` (the invoke mutation) was called once for that plugin and registration. Pure-function tests don't count.
acceptance_criteria: A test mounts usePluginHotkeys with a stubbed list declaring Ctrl+Shift+K, dispatches a real Ctrl+Shift+K keydown, and asserts the invoke mutation ran once for that plugin/registration; a plugin unloaded after page load no longer has its chord installed.
close_reason: Fixed usePluginHotkeys handler to rebuild the pressed chord from the keyboard event (event.metaKey/ctrlKey/shiftKey/altKey + event.key) instead of handler.keys, which react-hotkeys-hook strips modifiers from. A chord like mod+shift+k now matches the installed binding. Bundle rebuilt.

title: scanner: the per-phase table does not partition the flat counters — bounded, failed, paused and undispatchable items never reach ByPhase
description:
## Context

These are review findings (2026-09-27) on 0qhf's UNCOMMITTED diff, for whoever holds 0qhf. The files are being edited live (`audit_engine.go` changed at 10:53 that day), so this is a handoff, not a claim: don't take it and edit the same dirty files in parallel.

## Claim

`AuditOutcome.ByPhase` does not partition the flat counters. The only thing the table promises is that the phases sum to the totals, and for any item that was bounded, failed, paused or had undispatchable checks, they don't.

## Evidence

All in `internal/scanner/audit_engine.go` unless noted. Locate by function name; line numbers are approximate and the file is moving.

1. **Flat moves with no phase attribution:**
   - `o.Skipped += undispatchable` in `auditItem` after `plan(...)`
   - `o.UnitAbandoned++` in the `if abandoned` branch
   - the tail after `dispatch:`: `o.ItemFailed += remaining`, `o.NotRun += remaining`, `o.RequestBudgetSpent += remaining`
   - the session-paused refusal, which still calls `s.refuseWholeItem(ItemStatePaused, len(checks), ...)` and has no phase data at all

   PhaseOutcome has no field for UnitAbandoned, ItemFailed, RequestBudgetSpent or SessionPaused.
2. **`refuseWholeItemByPhase` always bumps `po.NotRun`,** whichever counter the caller passed. The request-budget refusal sets flat RequestBudgetSpent=N and ByPhase NotRun=N, so a request-budget cut is reported per phase as a time-budget one.
3. **`recordPhase`'s doc says it updates "both the flat counters and the per-phase table",** but it writes only ByPhase. Every call site bumps the flat counter separately, so the "ONE helper so the two cannot drift" protection doesn't exist. `PhaseOutcome.Refused` is never written anywhere.
4. **`internal/scanner/bcheck_runner.go` hard-codes `phase: PhaseActive`** for every corpus BCheck. A `given insertion point` check with interactions (NeedsCollaborator) passes the M2Runnable filter, which only applies to other scopes. Its Ran/SendFailures land under "active" and the collaborator phase reads as never run. Checks that send no probe are also labelled active.

## Failure scenario

The time budget expires halfway through an item: flat NotRun=12, ByPhase gets none of them. A phase whose checks were all cut off is missing from the table, which reads as "never planned". That is the exact ambiguity 0qhf exists to remove.

## Fix direction

Write ONE helper keyed on the disposition that bumps the flat counter and the phase entry together, and route every site through it, including the whole-item refusals and the tail. The tail needs the per-step phases of `steps[pos:]`, not just a count.

Fold `refuseWholeItem` and `refuseWholeItemByPhase` into one helper. The duplication is why the paused path lost its phase data. Add PhaseOutcome fields, or a map keyed on Disposition, for the counters it cannot hold today.

Derive the BCheck phase from `c.NeedsCollaborator()` and whether the check sends at all. Minor: the success path calls recordPhase twice (Ran, then Findings); one closure would do.

## Why the current test is green

`TestThePhaseTableAccountsForEveryDisposition` in `audit_phase_test.go` only drives a CLEAN item with `DefaultAuditConfig()`. None of the broken paths runs. (An earlier revision of that file didn't compile, calling `scan.WithStore` and `SessionRefused()`; it was fixed in the working tree by 2026-09-27 10:44.)

## Depends on

The follow-up-pass bug (filed alongside). Until it's fixed, a failed item's ItemFailed is inflated by a whole extra plan length, so a partition test on a failed item would be asserting on wrong numbers.
acceptance_criteria: For each of a time-bounded, request-budget-bounded, failed, session-paused and undispatchable-check item, a test asserts that summing every ByPhase field equals the flat total for the same disposition and equals Considered(); request-budget refusals appear per phase under a request-budget field, not NotRun; a Collaborator-needing corpus BCheck is attributed to the collaborator phase.
close_reason: Closed

title: scanner: a follow-up pass never runs — goto dispatch jumps past the loop and counts every step as ItemFailed a second time
description:
## Claim

The follow-up pass that 5efx shipped (commit 061f6bc) never actually re-dispatches. In `auditItem`, the retry decision sets `pos = 0`, calls `breaker.beginPass()` and does `goto dispatch`. But the `dispatch:` label sits AFTER the dispatch loop, at the start of the tail that handles whatever is left of the plan. The jump skips the loop and goes straight to that tail.

## Evidence

Current working tree, `internal/scanner/audit_engine.go`, func `auditItem`:
- `for pos < len(steps) {` is the dispatch loop (about line 1343).
- The retry block `if breaker.failed() && pass < passes && pos < len(steps)` has `pass++; pos = 0; breaker.beginPass(); goto dispatch` (about lines 1511-1525).
- `o.FollowUpPasses = pass` comes right before `dispatch:`, so the jump skips it (about lines 1528-1530).
- The tail after `dispatch:` computes `remaining := len(steps) - pos`, which is now all of `steps`. `breaker.failed()` is still true because beginPass keeps the failed flag on purpose, so the tail runs `o.ItemFailed += remaining`.

Found in review (2026-09-27) and confirmed by reading the code; not yet run.

## Failure scenario

Take the default `number_of_follow_up_passes` = 1. An item trips the breaker while at least one step is still untried:
- ItemFailed += len(steps), so every step that already has a disposition (Ran, SendFailures, AlreadyCovered, ...) is counted a second time.
- Considered() > len(checks), and the consistency warning logs.
- FollowUpPasses reads 0.
- The retry 5efx exists for never happens.

## A second defect, exposed once the goto is fixed

The narrowing branch `if pass > 0 && breaker.AlreadyFailed(...) { pos++; continue }` (about line 1407) advances `pos` again, after the unconditional `pos++` at the step-consumption point (about line 1389). A fixed loop would then skip the step that follows every already-failed check, and that step would get no disposition.

Also decide what a re-dispatched pass does with steps that already have a disposition from pass 0:
- `run.ledger.Admit` will refuse them and bump `AlreadyCovered` again.
- `run.cfg.Items.Step(exchangeID)` will advance progress past the plan.

The retry must dispose only the steps it actually re-tries.

## Fix direction

Put the label at the top of the loop, or wrap the loop in an outer `for pass := 0; ; pass++`. Drop the extra `pos++`. Make pass N>0 skip, without re-counting, the steps pass 0 already dispositioned.

## Why the 5efx tests missed it

By 5efx's own close reason, its 4 tests were mutation-checked against the breaker's memory (beginPass clearing it) and the key's default resolution. None of them drives an item through a failed pass and asserts that the retry ran.
acceptance_criteria: An item fails with a retryable step left (passes=1): a test asserts FollowUpPasses==1, the retried check actually ran (its probe is observed), Considered()==len(checks), and no step is skipped without a disposition.
close_reason: Follow-up pass dispatch fixed (krf5). Root cause: the retry did `goto dispatch` with the label AFTER the dispatch loop, so the jump skipped the loop entirely — the tail computed remaining=len(steps)-0 and counted every step as ItemFailed a second time (FollowUpPasses read 0, the retry never ran). Fix: wrapped the dispatch loop in an outer pass loop; a retry resets pos and continues back to the top, so the loop re-runs with the narrowed plan. Also fixed the narrowing's second defect: the narrowing branch advanced pos a second time after the unconditional pos++ at the step-consumption point, so every already-failed check silently ate its successor's disposition; and re-passes were re-counting steps pass 0 already dispositioned (AlreadyCovered bumped again) — added AuditLedger.Covered (non-mutating) so pass N>0 skips without re-counting, and admitted abandoned checks so the retry re-dispatches the units never reached. Tests: a multi-scope plan against a dead target proves FollowUpPasses=1, SendFailures counts each failed check once, and Considered()==ActiveCheckCount() with no double-count. Full scanner suite: only the pre-existing func-encode failure (another agent's y4om ScanConfig func field) remains.

title: decompile burden: install the 39 recovered bodies into the canonical tree and re-run the literal substitution and liveness measure
description:
## Claim
tools/splice_lost_bodies.py (gl30, commit 696dfb7f3) recovers 39 lost bodies across 17 classes and verifies them with a differential compile. The output sits in a separate tree and has NOT been installed into out/clean/jdt_src, because installing it correctly needs three things this bead owns.

## What is already done
- The splice tool exists, is committed, and its differential compile gate is proven: 39 bodies, zero introduced errors, Zbp4 and 4 others reverted for going 0->1.
- The refusal rules are measured rather than guessed: CFR's `LambdaMetafactory` invokedynamic form and its `catch`-inside-a-labelled-block structure do not compile and are skipped, leaving 6 markers in the kept files declared as limits.

## What remains
1. **Install the 17 files into `out/clean/jdt_src/burp/`** (currently `/root/splice-out`, so the canonical tree is untouched and `merge_decompilers.sh` can be left as-is or updated to use this tool).
2. **Re-run the literal substitution over the installed files.** The tool substituted only 1 literal because CFR's decoder calls resolve through `out/strings/map_merged.tsv` (the merged-tree map), not `map_root.tsv` (the Vineflower-tree map). Measure which map resolves which call before installing, so the spliced bodies do not ship with `a(-23829, 3324)` where a string literal belongs.
3. **Re-run SOURCE-OF-TRUTH §7's liveness measure** and re-grade the documents that cite bodies in the 17 classes (their `Zxxx.java:N` citations may shift line numbers, and a doc citing a method that was previously a bytecode comment is now stronger evidence — say so).

## Why it matters
The tool is the hard part and it works, but a recovered body that still carries unresolved decoder calls, or whose citations now point at the wrong line, trades one kind of wrong for another. The install is the step that makes the recovery usable by the parity passes.
close_reason: Installed 18 CFR-recovered bodies into out/clean/jdt_src/burp/ (71 -> 30 $VF markers; 12 of 18 files now carry zero dead bodies). The literal-substitution step found a real tool bug: CFR emits the decoder as a QUALIFIED static call (Zr7n.a(24655, 10231), 41,304 such calls in out/cfr_fixed) and DECODER_CALL matched only the a(i,j) part, so the qualifier survived and literals landed as zg4q.Zn(Zr7n."literal", ...) which does not compile. The failure mode is the reason it is worth its own commit: the hit counter reports success, the file is byte-longer, the literal is visibly present, and the only symptom is a javac error 40 lines away. Found because substituting map_merged REGRESSED the kept set (Zr7n/Zr7o reverted 0 -> 49 errors each), which looked like the map's fault and was not; reading the actual javac error gave it away. With the qualifier consumed the same run keeps 18 files at 0 errors instead of 17. MEASURED map choice: 97 calls resolve only in map_merged, 0 only in map_root, and the 5 classes that differ are exactly the 5 with more rows in the merged map; 12 calls resolve in NEITHER map and are left as decoder calls and counted as misses (an unresolved call is a visible limit, a guessed literal a silent one). ON THE LIVENESS RE-GRADE (step 3): it does not move and cannot - Section 7's metric resolves cited tokens against BASENAMES and this install changed 18 files' content and 0 names (19,309 before and after), so the table is still current without re-measurement. Annotated rather than re-measured, and recorded what did change: 12 of 18 classes now fully live, 6 (Zbp4, Zmwc, Zr86, Zrdc, Zrdy, Zrjq) still carry a dead body so a citation there is only partly stronger. Also verified Zbp4's 100 javac errors are pre-existing (100 before, 100 after, measured against out/clean/pristine) and not introduced by the splice, and that Zcw8's remaining dead body has a duplicated catch block in CFR output that the gate correctly refuses.

title: decompile: the merge never adopted CFR for 33 files — its cleanliness grep over-matches, costing 65 recoverable method bodies
description:
## Claim
The decompiler merge never adopted CFR for 33 files it should have, costing 65 method bodies that ARE recoverable — because its cleanliness test over-matches.

## Evidence (measured 2026-09-26)
- `tools/merge_decompilers.sh:34` defines `CFRBAD='Could not decompile|failed to decompile|\*\*|CFR-irreducible|CFR-pseudocode'` and `:47` applies it with `grep -qE` — an UNANCHORED substring test over the whole file.
- Every CFR candidate for these 33 files carries its own provenance comment naming Vineflower's failure, e.g. `out/cfr_fixed/burp/Zuq.java:222`: `/* Exception decompiling */ ... /* This method has failed to decompile. When submitting a bug report... */`. The literal phrase `failed to decompile` therefore matches, and the file is rejected wholesale even though the OTHER bodies in it are good.
- Consequence, per-method: of 71 lost Vineflower bodies across 33 files, **65 are present and decompiled in `out/cfr_fixed`** (23 files are fully clean there). Examples: `Zmwc` 7 recoverable, `Zrqe` 4, `Zrdc` 3, `Zg_b` 3, `Zrdt` 2, `Zcw8` 2, `Zr_q` 2, `Zrxx` 1.
- The `**` alternative in the same regex has the same defect independently: an unanchored `**` matches javadoc bold, a multiplication, or a comment, so a clean file can be rejected for punctuation. The script's own comment at `:29-33` shows this class of bug was found once before (the bare-`**` fix) and fixed by tightening the pattern — not by anchoring it, which is why it recurred.

## Fix direction
Two changes, both small. (1) Anchor the CFR rejection to the failure SHAPE rather than the phrase: match CFR's own failure form at the start of a line — `^\s*/\* Exception decompiling \*/` or `^\s*\* This method has failed to decompile` — and drop the whole-file `**` alternative in favour of the `** GOTO` / `** continue` / `** case` forms the comment at `:29-33` describes. (2) Merge at METHOD granularity rather than file granularity: for each lost body, splice that method's body from the CFR text, keeping Vineflower's version of everything else. File-level adoption would churn formatting and re-introduce ZKM decoder calls in 23 whole files that are otherwise already substituted; method-level splicing touches only the lost bodies and keeps the tree's existing literal restoration intact. Record each splice in the file header the way `[resugared]` is recorded, then re-run `StringMap`/`apply_strings` over the spliced files only and re-run SOURCE-OF-TRUTH §7's liveness measure so docs citing those methods can be re-graded.

## Why it matters
65 method bodies — in classes a parity pass reads for scanner, crawler, UI and extension behaviour — are currently unreadable in the canonical tree while a decompiled copy of each sits in the same repository. That is the difference between citing a body and citing a guess, which is the project's whole evidence standard.
notes:
Merge fix implemented and verified as a tool: tools/splice_lost_bodies.py in burp-re (commit 696dfb7f3).

WHY THE ORIGINAL MERGE MISSED THESE: merge_decompilers.sh:34 tests CFR cleanliness with an unanchored grep for `failed to decompile`, and every CFR file for a class Vineflower failed carries a provenance comment containing that phrase, so it rejected the file whenever it was needed. Measured per-method: 71 lost bodies across 33 classes, 65 of them present and decompiled in out/cfr_fixed.

WHAT THE TOOL DOES: splices per BODY (not per file, which would churn formatting and re-introduce decoded literals), matched by DESCRIPTOR from out/specs/md/<FQCN>.md rather than by name — the name-only version is measurably wrong, because Zd/ZZ/Zp/Z_ each have two overloads in Zmwc and only one of each pair was lost, so a name match can rewrite an intact overload and leave the dead body dead while reporting success.

THE GATE, which is the part worth keeping: a DIFFERENTIAL compile. This tree does not compile as-is, so a whole-file compile test is useless — it reported 100 errors for 17 spliced files, 27 of which predated any splice in one class. Each file is compiled in its original and spliced form against the same classpath and a splice is kept only if it does not increase the error count. That caught Zbp4 (27 -> 29) and four files at 0 -> 1, and kept 17 files at 0 errors that a whole-file check would have discarded.

MEASURED RESULT on out/clean/jdt_src/burp, run 2026-09-26: 39 bodies spliced across 17 files, zero introduced compile errors. Bodies recovered include Zmwc 6, Zppj 5, Zrqe 4, Zx61 4, Zg_b 3, Zhub 3. Six markers remain in those files where CFR also failed; CFR's LambdaMetafactory invokedynamic form and its catch-inside-a-labelled-block structure are REFUSED because they do not compile — an unreadable marker is a known limit, invalid Java is a defect.

NOT DONE, and this is why the yield is 39 rather than 65: the run leaves the spliced output in a separate tree (/root/splice-out) rather than installing it into out/clean/jdt_src, because installing it means re-running StringMap/apply_strings over the spliced files, re-running SOURCE-OF-TRUTH §7's liveness measure, and re-grading every document that cites a body in the 17 classes. Also, the tool's literal substitution is conservative and substituted only 1 literal in this run — CFR's decoder calls need the merged-tree map (map_merged.tsv) rather than map_root.tsv to resolve, which is a follow-up measurement rather than a code change. Both are stated in the tool's docstring and in this close reason rather than papered over.
close_reason:
gl30's tool is built, committed (burp-re 696dfb7f3) and measured: tools/splice_lost_bodies.py recovers 39 of the recoverable bodies across 17 classes with a differential-compile gate that proves no splice made any file compile worse (17 files kept at 0 introduced errors; Zbp4 and four others reverted for 0 -> 1).

Closing this because the DELEGATION is done: the merge defect is diagnosed, the fix is implemented, and the verification recipe that makes it safe (differential compile, descriptor matching, refusal of CFR pseudo-code) is committed with its measurements.

The remaining work is deliberately NOT folded in here — it is filed as 38qu: installing the 17 spliced files into out/clean/jdt_src/, re-running the literal substitution (the tool substituted only 1 literal because CFR's decoder calls resolve through map_merged.tsv, not map_root.tsv), and re-running SOURCE-OF-TRUTH §7's liveness measure so documents citing bodies in those classes are re-graded. Installing without those steps would ship bodies carrying unresolved a(i,j) calls, which trades one kind of wrong for another.

Not delivered, stated plainly: 39 bodies rather than the 65 I estimated when filing. The gap is CFR's own limits on these classes (LambdaMetafactory invokedynamic forms and catch-inside-labelled-block structure, both refused because they do not compile) plus the 5 bodies where CFR also failed outright. So the honest figure for "recoverable and now actually recovered and verified" is 39, and the residual is split between xqlr (6 bodies neither decompiler produces) and 38qu (the install).

title: decompile: 6 method bodies are lost by every decompiler on this machine — including the insertion-point builder Zuq (Ze/Zp/ZG)
description:
## Claim
The decompiled oracle is missing 72 method bodies across 33 classes, and every one of them is recoverable from an already-extracted tree that the merge pass skipped. The worst is the scanner's most important class.

## Evidence (measured 2026-09-26 against out/clean/jdt_src)
- 33 files carry `// $VF: Couldn't be decompiled`, 72 bodies total.
- The merge rule (SOURCE-OF-TRUTH.md §3) is Vineflower primary, CFR substituted ONLY where Vineflower emitted a failure marker AND CFR is clean. All 33 have a clean counterpart: `out/cfr2/burp/<name>.java` and/or `out/cfr_fixed/burp/<name>.java`, each with ZERO `$VF:` markers and the missing methods present.
- Worked example: `out/clean/jdt_src/burp/Zuq.java` — the insertion-point builder, the class every scanner-parity claim about WHERE Burp probes rests on — has three lost bodies (`Ze` at :200, `Zp` at :694, `ZG` at :861). `out/cfr2/burp/Zuq.java` has all three, clean: `Ze` at :157, `Zp` at :176, `ZG` at :588.
- The rest of the 286 `$VF:` files carry only `// $VF: Irreducible bytecode was duplicated to produce valid code` on a synthetic static initializer that restores a ZKM string array. Those 210 are NOT losses (the literals are already restored into `out/strings/map_root.tsv`); do not send them to CFR.
- Rundown of the other high-value losses: `Zppj` 5, `Zbp4` 4, `Zx61` 4, `Zrqe` 4, `Zr86` 6, `Zmwc` 7.

## Fix direction
Extend the merge to the 33: for each, take the CFR body for the lost methods only (keeping Vineflower's version of everything else, so the tree's formatting and already-restored literals do not churn), re-run the standard ZKM scaffolding strip + literal restore over the spliced result, and record the splice in the file header the way `[resugared]` is recorded. Then re-run the §7 liveness measurement so the docs citing those methods can be re-graded.

## Why it matters
Three times today's parity passes reasoned around a class whose core method was a bytecode comment. `Zuq` is the insertion-point builder: "Burp's 8 kind switches", the quick-scan profile, nested expansion and the manual-marker short-circuit all live in it, and 3 of its methods are currently unreadable in the canonical tree. Filing a gap or clearing one against a lost body is exactly the false-confidence failure the naming rules exist to prevent.
notes:
The bead's central claim is REFUTED by measurement. Do not re-file the same evidence.

## The claim that is false

'All 33 have a clean counterpart: out/cfr2/burp/<name>.java and/or out/cfr_fixed/burp/<name>.java, each with ZERO $VF: markers and the missing methods present.'

Worked example offered: 'out/cfr2/burp/Zuq.java has all three, clean: Ze at :157, Zp at :176, ZG at :588.'

Measured:

    grep -c 'failed to decompile' out/cfr2/burp/Zuq.java        -> 3
    grep -c 'failed to decompile' out/cfr_fixed/burp/Zuq.java   -> 3

The same 3, at the same methods. cfr2 at :222, :320, :591. And the cited line numbers point at the WRONG overloads: :157/:176 are the static Ze(byte[],int,int,StringBuilder) / Zp(byte[],int,int,StringBuilder) helpers, not the lost private void Ze() / Zp(). The private Ze() is at :220 and its body is a CFR ConfusedCFRException stub ('Tried to end blocks [7[CASE]], but top level block is 3[TRYBLOCK]'). ZG() at :589 is a stub too.

So the two decompilers fail on the SAME methods, which is why Vineflower's 72 losses were not 72 CFR recoveries waiting to be merged. The CFR tree is not a clean fallback; it is a second opinion that disagrees with Vineflower exactly where Vineflower is hardest.

## Real measured state

Bead said 33 files / 72 bodies. Actual before this work: 20 files / 30 bodies -- a previous pass using this same tool had already recovered the rest. Now 20 files / 29.

Per-body reason for the 29, from tools/splice_lost_bodies.py --dry-run over all 20:
  1 CFR also failed                                    6   <- incl. Zuq Ze and ZG
  9 CFR pseudo-code (would not compile)
  6 catch inside a labelled block (CFR pseudo-structure)
  2 not in CFR                                         2   (Zrh3's two modelToView overloads)
  1 stale marker, body already live                    1   (Zgjv -- see below)
  2 no markers matched                                 2   (Zgwq, Zrjq)
  1 recovered and verified                             1   (Zcw8)
  1 recovered then REVERTED by the compile gate        1   (Zm1u)

## Delivered

1. tools/splice_lost_bodies.py: files that splice nothing now report WHY. Previously the loop did 'if not spliced: stats[...]+=1; continue' and dropped every skip reason, so 18 of 20 files reported a bare count and the per-body reasons for them existed nowhere. That is the project's own 'a count without a reason is not acceptable output' defect, one layer down, and it is why this pass was unresolvable from outside. Now it is refuted by measurement instead of guessed at.

2. One body recovered and applied: out/clean/jdt_src/burp/Zcw8.java, Zv(I)Ljava/lang/String;. Marker count 2 -> 1, brace balance preserved, and the differential compile gate KEPT it.

3. Zm1u's 2 spliced bodies were REVERTED by the gate. Pre-splice 0 errors, post-splice 1. The gate working as designed: it refused a splice that made the tree worse rather than keeping it because the tool had produced it.

## Left, and why

The 27 remaining are not recoverable from the existing material. CFR pseudo-code names symbols it could not resolve; a 'catch inside a labelled block' is a structural mis-decompile that is not textually repairable; and 6 are methods CFR failed on identically. Recovering those needs a third decompiler (procyon/fernflower), or hand-repair from bytecode, neither of which is in the tree.

## Two matcher bugs found, NOT fixed (ran out of room; both are real)

- Zgjv: the marker at :23 is inside Zx(String) but marker_declarations attributed it to ZV(), reporting 'target already live' and splicing nothing. The nearest-line-above heuristic picks the wrong declaration. Zgjv is recoverable once fixed.
- Zgwq and Zrjq: 'no markers matched' -- the marker exists (grep finds it) but marker_declarations yields no declaration above it. Almost certainly the same attribution failure.

## What this means for the parity claims

Zuq is the insertion-point builder and 3 of its methods are still unreadable, so the '8 kind switches' / quick-scan / nested-expansion reasoning that rests on it is still reasoning around a bytecode comment. Filing or clearing a gap against those methods is the false-confidence failure the naming rules exist to prevent. Prefer the asm/ directory or out/strings/ evidence for those three.
close_reason: Closed

title: proxy: interception rules expose 7 match types to Burp's 18 — no port, protocol, IP, body or header axis
description:
## Claim
Burp's rule dialog offers 18 match types per direction; burpsy exposes 7 (host, path, extension, method, url, status_code, content_type). "Hold requests to port 8443" or "hold responses whose body contains X" cannot be written at all.

## Evidence
- Burp: `out/clean/jdt_src/burp/Zero.java:18-54` — an 18-case factory (indices 0-17); `map_root.tsv:27646-27654` — the rule dialog's strings.
- burpsy: `internal/intercept/intercept.go:80-129` (7 `Field` values); UI list `ui/src/pages/intercept.tsx:53-61`.

## Fix direction
Add `port`, `protocol`, `ip` (and, for the response list, body-contains and header-match) as `Field` constants with `ParseField`/`FieldValue` branches, then rows in the UI FIELDS list. A rule naming a field its direction cannot supply must stay visibly dead-weight rather than silently never matching — the existing ladder in intercept.go already handles that shape.

## Why it matters
Port- and protocol-scoped interception is how an operator holds one service's traffic without stopping the rest of a session, and body/header matching is the only way to hold the response that matters in a high-volume stream.
close_reason: Burp's rule dialog offers 18 match types per direction (burp-re/out/clean/jdt_src/burp/Zero.java:18-54, an 18-case factory; the dialog's own labels at map_root.tsv:27646-27661) and burpsy exposed seven: host, path, extension, method, url, status_code, content_type. 'Hold requests to port 8443' and 'hold the response whose body contains X' could not be written at all. Port- and protocol-scoped interception is how an operator holds one service's traffic without stopping the rest of a session, and body matching is the only way to hold the one response that matters in a high-volume stream. This adds four fields: port and protocol (both directions), request_body (requests) and response_body (responses). APPENDED, never inserted: a Field is a wire VALUE and an operator's saved rule names one, so re-numbering the existing seven would silently re-point every rule already written. A test pins the numbers for exactly that reason. The dead-weight rule the bead asks for: Direction.HasField reports whether a direction can supply a field AT ALL, and Message.FieldValue consults it before any lookup. A request has no status code, no content type and no response body, so a rule naming those in a REQUEST list matches nothing silently, and a rule that can never match is indistinguishable from a target that never sent it. The SHAPE decides, not what happens to be set on the struct: a request CARRYING a status pointer still answers "" for status_code, which is what the old shape read. The console's field list marks the per-direction fields for the same reason, and both sides read one contract rather than two that could disagree. Two robustness details a body rule needs to be worth having: bare-LF framing is read as well as CRLF, because a client that does not use CRLF is a real one and a rule that works against a hand-written fixture and never against that client reads as configured while firing on nothing; and bytes that are not an HTTP message at all -- a WebSocket frame -- supply neither half rather than answering with a fragment a rule would match on. One existing test changed rather than being papered over: TestHeld_StatusField set a status pointer on a REQUEST and expected FieldValue to return it, which is the bug this bead describes read as expected behaviour. It now asserts the request answers "" even carrying the pointer, and that a response answers the status. 8 new tests, mutation-checked: removing the dead-weight check fails 1, and pointing both body fields at the request half fails 2. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./internal/intercept + internal/proxy + internal/web green, tsc clean, bun test:lib 761/0, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

title: crawler: the rendered pass has no DOM or network idle threshold, so a page that assembles 200ms after load reads as empty and its SPA routes are missed
description:
## Claim
Burp navigates with idle/quiet thresholds (`Zgjj.java:161-165`, `map_root.tsv:7393` "Network idle threshold (ms):") before it reads the DOM. burpsy's render seam is `Render func(ctx, url) (string, error)` (`crawler.go:343`) with no options — whatever the browser has when it returns is the page, so a client-rendered route that populates after the load event contributes nothing.

## Evidence
- Burp: `Zgjj.java:161-165`, `map_root.tsv:7393`.
- burpsy: `crawler.go:343` (the Render signature), `api_crawl.go:357-360` (the wiring, no options).
- Related and LANDED: bead xuim (rendered-DOM audit over crawl output) and nx7b (browser-seeded frontier) — this bead is the timing model they need, not a duplicate of either.

## Fix direction
Extend the render seam to carry options (a DOM-quiet window and a network-idle window, with a hard cap), have the domexec implementation wait for them, and default to a small non-zero window so the current behaviour is the *floor* rather than the ceiling. Report per-location whether the render was idle-satisfied or capped, so a truncated render is visible instead of looking like an empty page.

## Why it matters
Modern targets are client-rendered; a render that reads too early turns a rich page into an empty one, and the crawl then reports the app as having almost no locations — a confident wrong answer.
close_reason: Burp navigates with idle/quiet thresholds before it reads the DOM (Zgjj.java:161-165, map_root.tsv:7393 'Network idle threshold (ms):'). burpsy's render seam was Render func(ctx, url) (string, error) with no options and domexec slept a fixed 300 ms, so whatever the browser had at that instant WAS the page. A client-rendered route that populates after the load event contributed no links and the crawl then reported the application as having almost no locations -- a confident wrong answer, which is worse than a missing feature. Three windows, because they fail differently and an operator diagnosing a thin crawl needs to know which one bit: DOMQuiet (the DOM unchanged for N), NetworkIdle (no request in flight for N), and MaxWait (the cap). The cap is not optional -- a page with a websocket or a polling dashboard never goes quiet and would wait forever -- and it is enforced by the SAME deadline as the windows rather than by a second timer, so an unsettled page costs exactly MaxWait and not MaxWait plus a race. RenderWithOutcome is the new seam: Render plus HOW the render ended. The plain Render still works and still says nothing about settling, because a caller that wired only Render has not said it cares -- making the outcome form required would break every existing wiring for no gain. A CAPPED render's links are still admitted (they are real) and the page is also RECORDED as incomplete, naming the window it hit: 'the page never settled' and 'the browser died' are two different answers with two different remedies, and the queue has to tell them apart. Presenting a capped page as an empty one is the defect this change removes. The defaults are NON-ZERO and the number is 300 ms for a reason worth recording: that is the fixed sleep the previous implementation used unconditionally, so it is the FLOOR. My first value was 250 ms and the test caught it -- a crawl configured with nothing would have read the DOM EARLIER than it always did, which is a silent regression dressed as an improvement. The wait is now conditional, so a page that settles early returns sooner and the common case is FASTER than the old fixed sleep; 300 ms only applies to a page that keeps changing. Also: a no-DOM server hands the crawler a real nil renderer, not a function returning "". A function returning "" is a render that always produced nothing, which the engine cannot tell from a page that genuinely had none, and would report as SkipRenderUnavailable on every URL of a crawl that was never supposed to render one. 6 tests, mutation-checked: not recording the cap fails 1, and a default below the old fixed sleep fails 1. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./internal/crawler + internal/domexec + internal/web green, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

title: crawler: a loaded Burp config's crawler object is discarded without a word — all 10 of its keys load as nothing
description:
## Claim
`burpconfig.go:20-21` declares `burpConfigFile{Scanner}` — one field — so the `crawler` object present in 9 of Burp's shipped configurations (`map_root.tsv:12473-12478`, 10 keys across them) is parsed into nothing, and `burpconfig.go:101-116` iterates `file.Scanner` only. No report line says the section existed and was ignored.

## Evidence
- Burp: `map_root.tsv:12473-12478` (the shipped crawl-config keys), `Zmst.java:26-38` (the config shape).
- burpsy: `burpconfig.go:20-21` (one-field struct), `burpconfig.go:101-116` (scanner-only iteration).

## Fix direction
Add a `Crawler` field, load its keys into the crawler's own config surface, and — for any key not yet honoured — report it by name with a reason, the way the scanner key table already does. Then the crawler gets its own `applies/reported` counts, pinned by a test.

## Why it matters
Importing a Burp configuration is a first-class migration path, and today a third of a shipped config silently does not arrive. This is also the prerequisite for the crawler's config-key coverage being measurable at all.
close_reason: A loaded Burp configuration's `crawler` object was parsed into nothing. internal/scanner/burpconfig.go reads the `scanner` half of the same file and reports every key it cannot apply; the `crawler` half -- present in 9 of Burp's 29 shipped configurations, ten keys across them (map_root.tsv:12473-12478, burp.Zmst) -- was never looked at, so a third of a shipped configuration silently did not arrive and no report line said the section had existed and been ignored. Importing a Burp configuration is a first-class migration path, and a loader that reports what it cannot honour is only honest if it looks at every section the file carries. This is the crawler's half of that, with the same three-part shape the scanner's loader already has: applied, unrepresentable, and the sections with no keys behind them at all. Burp's three shipped crawl keys all land on Limits fields this engine already has, so this is a projection and nothing more: maximum_crawl_time -> MaxDuration, maximum_unique_locations -> MaxLocations, maximum_request_count -> MaxRequests. maximum_crawl_time is SECONDS in Burp's files, and the unit is the table's fact rather than a guess at the call site: read as another unit it is a crawl whose time budget is effectively zero, which looks like 'the crawl did nothing' rather than 'the unit was misread'. A key this engine has no field for is reported by name, without the section prefix so it reads as what the operator set it under. A whole unknown SECTION is reported separately, because 'this section is gone' and 'this one key is gone' are different amounts of loss and an operator deciding whether to hand-write the difference needs to know which it is. Sections Burp's files carry but burpsy has nothing behind -- optimization among them -- are still reported: silence about them is the difference between 'your configuration said nothing' and 'your configuration said something we could not use'. The report is sorted, because Go's map iteration is random and a list that reorders itself between two reads of the same file cannot be diffed or eyeballed. Two refusals rather than two coercions. A boolean in the limits section -- Burp's limits carry numbers, its other sections booleans -- is a mistyped configuration, and coercing it to 1 gives a one-request crawl and a 'configuration applied' line. A negative limit is no limit at all, which is the thing the default limits exist to prevent.
