POST /api/crawl takes `config` and overlays the crawler half UNDER the explicit per-request limits, so a field the operator typed on this request still wins over the file they also named -- the other order would make a configuration silently override the request that named it. The overlay copies per field for the same reason a struct copy would be wrong: a limit the file never mentioned must not overwrite the caller's value with a zero. The reply carries config_name and config_unapplied_keys, the same not-silent half the audit path reports, because the reason an operator cannot know a third of their configuration is missing is that nothing ever said so. 9 tests, mutation-checked both ways: an unknown key silently dropped fails 2, and a loader whose loop never runs -- the field present and the code not looking at it, which is the pre-fix shape -- fails 4. Worth stating: my first attempt at the second mutation replaced the field with struct{}, which broke the build, and a build failure is not a test result. The mutation that actually models the defect compiles. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./internal/crawler + internal/web green, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

title: crawler: a Sitemap: robots line is fetched, stored, and thrown away — sitemap.xml is never parsed, so a published URL list yields zero locations
description:
## Claim
The crawler admits a `Sitemap:` URL from robots.txt and fetches it, then discards it as non-HTML (`crawler.go:1332-1341`, `SkipNotHTML`) — there is no `encoding/xml` in the package at all. Burp parses it: `Zgkz.java:13,18,22-24` and the `Zb8w.SITEMAP` action kind (`Zb8w.java:15`).

## Evidence
- Burp: `Zgkz.java:13,18,22-24` (sitemap parsing), `map_root.tsv:6161,6185,6193,18373,18387`, `Zb8w.java:15`.
- burpsy: `crawler.go:1544-1546` (the robots `Sitemap:` line is admitted), `crawler.go:1332-1341` (`SkipNotHTML` drops it), no XML decoder in `internal/crawler`.

## Fix direction
Parse sitemap XML (and sitemap-index XML) in the discovery path: emit `<loc>` entries as locations, honour `<lastmod>` for ordering if cheap, and record a distinct crawl action/skip reason for "sitemap parsed, N locations". Leave the `isHTML` gate for HTML extraction and add the XML branch beside it rather than widening the gate.

## Why it matters
A target that publishes its URL list tells the crawler exactly where to go, and burpsy throws the answer away. It is one of the cheapest large coverage wins in the crawler, and it is also a documented Burp behaviour operators will test for.
close_reason: A robots.txt may name its own URL list (`Sitemap: https://x/sitemap.xml`). The crawler admitted that URL and fetched it -- then discarded the response as non-HTML at crawler.go's SkipNotHTML gate, because there was no encoding/xml anywhere in internal/crawler. A target that publishes exactly where to go had its answer fetched, stored, scanned and thrown away, and the crawl mapped only what it linked into: a confident empty result against the sites that volunteer their own structure. Burp parses it (Zgkz.java:13,18,22-24; Zb8w.java:15's SITEMAP action kind is the record of having done so). A SIBLING of the HTML gate, not a relaxation of it. isHTML exists for HTML extraction -- the link walk, form submit, base-href resolution -- and none of that applies to a sitemap; admitting XML through that gate would hand every non-HTML response to the HTML extractor looking for anchors it will never find. A PDF still records SkipNotHTML exactly as before, and a test says so. A <sitemapindex> is a sitemap OF sitemaps, so its entries are marked and re-admitted as sitemaps to fetch. A large site publishes a handful pointing at the rest, and reading only the index finds every one of them empty -- the difference between 'read one file' and 'read the list the operator published', so it is its own counter. <loc> entries enter as DISCOVERED LINKS rather than seeds, for the reason robots.txt paths do: a target-supplied URL passes the destructive-action check, the scope gate and the crawl-scope query like anything else the response contained. A sitemap naming /admin/delete-all must not become a privileged request because the target wrote it down, and a test asserts it was not fetched. The content type is a HINT and not a gate: a great many servers serve a sitemap as octet-stream or text/plain, and requiring the right header would drop the document on exactly the sites that publish one, so the body is sniffed too on the first 512 bytes for the two element names that identify the document. A failed parse is reported rather than treated as a non-sitemap, which is what makes a mislabelled sitemap recoverable instead of silent. SkipSitemapUnparsed is a new reason because the alternative IS the defect: a body that looked like a sitemap and could not be read reported as not-HTML, indistinguishable from a target that published nothing. A gzipped sitemap, a truncated fetch and a document that was never a sitemap are three facts an operator can act on differently and '0 locations' cannot tell them apart. <lastmod> is carried and not interpreted. It is what tells an operator which page changed this morning, and it is deliberately not used to order the frontier: coverage that depends on a date the target may have written wrong is coverage the crawl cannot stand behind. While adding the Skip value: skipLedger.counts was [30]uint64 hand-maintained alongside `var SkipAll = [30]Skip`, and I had the two out of step. The compiler caught SkipAll's length and NOT the counter's -- the array is only indexed at runtime, so the omission surfaced as a panic on the first decline. The counter is now [len(SkipAll)]uint64, which is the shape that cannot drift. 13 tests, mutation-checked both ways: a sitemap parsed and counted but whose locations are never admitted fails 5 (the half-fix that looks complete and finds nothing), and the branch disabled entirely -- the pre-fix shape -- fails 6. The end-to-end test seeds the ORIGIN rather than robots.txt, because the crawler asks for a seed's authority's robots.txt; seeding the file directly asserts on a path no crawl takes, and that mistake produced the one test failure here. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./internal/crawler + internal/web green, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

title: scanner: the skip_all_tests_for_parameters key row says "not applied" while the engine honours the same control under a Go-only name
description:
## Claim
`skip_all_tests_for_parameters` is HONOURED by the engine but the config-key table still reports it unapplied, because the honoured path is a Go-API-only field name. The row is therefore a false statement in the operator-facing settings surface, and the same control has two names.

## Evidence
- Burp: `Zwh1.java:8-13`, `Zs4k.java:199-206` (a per-kind rule engine of 25 booleans).
- burpsy: `audit.go:1174-1179` — row says `applies: false`; `audit.go:622-632` + `insertion.go:396,735` — the same control IS honoured (case-insensitive name-based skip filtering before the per-request cap).
- Related but distinct: bead v9cg (operator skip lists) closed on the mechanism; bead jtmm was a build break. Neither fixed the lying row.

## Fix direction
Point the row's `read`/`apply` at the field the enumerator already consults, so the key and the Go API cannot disagree; keep the reason text only for the parts genuinely not ported (Burp's per-kind rule engine's finer predicates). `audit_config_keys_test.go`'s pinned `wantApplied, wantReported` moves, with a test that fails if the key is accepted and ignored.

## Why it matters
This is the honest-counting defect class the project treats as worse than a missing feature: a settings page that tells an operator a control is unsupported while the engine silently supports it under another name.
close_reason: The config-key table reported skip_all_tests_for_parameters as `applies: false` -- 'not applied' -- while the engine HONOURED it end to end: /api/scanner/config accepts skip_all_tests_for_parameters as a list of parameter names, AuditConfig.SkipAllTestsForParameters carries it, enumerateOptions passes it to the enumerator, and bcheck's skipNamedPoints drops a matching point from every kind as a Declined. The row was false because the honoured path is a LIST-valued field and every row in the table reads through OptUint32, so the key had no shape to land in and the row said nothing. This is the honest-counting defect class the project treats as worse than a missing feature: a settings page that tells an operator their skip list is unsupported while it silently works. v9cg closed on the mechanism and jtmm fixed a build; neither fixed the lying row. But 'applied' would be the mirror-image lie, and the truth is a third thing. Burp's value is a list of MATCH RULES ({enabled, parameter, item, match_type, expression}, e.g. matches_regex over an xml_attribute name); this engine has no matcher over item or expression, so a rule that matched by expression arrives here as a name that matches nothing. So the row is now marked `partial`: BuiltInConfigKey gains Partial bool on the wire and the row struct gains listShaped beside applies, so a consumer filtering on Partial to exclude reduced-support controls from 'unsupported' can. ApplyWithReport skips a partial row rather than letting it fall through to the 'read == nil' arm that builds the unapplied list, and the what text still names exactly what is missing. Three existing tests had to move, and their failure messages are the argument: the shipped-keys test pinned TWO counts (27 applied, 28 not applied) and required every unapplied row's text to start 'not applied: '; it now pins three (27 applied in full, 1 partial, 27 not applied) and checks each bucket's prefix. Test_every_built_in_config_field_has_a_key_row enforced 'no read but claims to apply is a lie' -- which is exactly the partial state -- and now distinguishes the three combinations. The apply-overlay oracle refuses an applying key it cannot check, and skip_all_tests_for_parameters is now NAMED in that switch so the oracle covers it instead of blocking on it. Worth recording because it is silent where a compile error is not: Go accepts two struct fields carrying the SAME json tag. My first attempt gave Partial json:"applies", duplicating the field above it, so the wire carried Partial's value under Applies' name, and the struct-level tests passed because they read the Go value. The fix for that then replaced the wrong occurrence and DROPPED Applies' tag entirely, which would have renamed the field to 'Applies' on the wire. What catches either is a test that decodes the HTTP response into its own struct and asserts on the KEYS: TestEveryConfigKeyFieldReachesTheWireUnderItsOwnName. The lesson generalises -- when a wire shape is contractual, assert on the decoded response, not on the Go value. 9 tests across the two packages, mutation-checked: restoring the row to 'not applied' fails 3, and removing the ApplyWithReport guard passes until the two tests that put a preset naming the key in front of the unapplied list are added -- which is why they exist and why the mutation had to be re-run after they did. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./internal/scanner + internal/web green, tsc clean, bun test:lib 761/0, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

title: scanner: a failed audit item is terminal — Burp's follow-up passes have no loop to run in
description:
## Claim
Burp re-passes a failed item: `number_of_follow_up_passes` (`Zxdx.java:27,36`, shipped default 1 at `Zp0d.java:120-121`) drives a re-pass driver (`Zeeu.java:119,239-241`, `Zfkz.java:57,69-81`). burpsy reports the key unapplied (`audit.go:1072-1077`) and the dispatch loop *breaks* on a failed item (`audit_engine.go:1339`) — so a failure is final.

## Evidence
- Burp: `Zxdx.java:27,36` (key), `Zp0d.java:120-121` (default 1), `Zeeu.java:119,239-241` + `Zfkz.java:57,69-81` (the re-pass).
- burpsy: `audit.go:1072-1077` (row unapplied), `audit_engine.go:1339` (loop breaks).

## Fix direction
Two steps, in order: (1) a re-run narrowing so a follow-up pass does not re-send checks that already failed for a reason the response will not change (`Zwy6.java:138-168` has four prior-failure predicates; burpsy's `audit_engine.go:1256` `Admit` is a single bit with no failure memory); (2) the pass loop itself, bounded by the key with default 1. Step 1 must land first or the loop multiplies traffic on a broken target.

## Why it matters
A transient failure (a timeout, a 502 from a mid-restart backend, a dropped connection) permanently loses that item's coverage and is indistinguishable in the report from "audited and clean". Burp retries it once, once by default.
close_reason: Burp re-passes a FAILED audit item: number_of_follow_up_passes (Zxdx.java:27,36; shipped default 1 at Zp0d.java:120-121) drives a re-pass driver (Zeeu.java:119,239-241, Zfkz.java:57,69-81). burpsy reported the key unapplied and the dispatch loop BROKE on a failed item (audit_engine.go:1339), so a failure was final. A transient failure -- a timeout, a 502 from a backend mid-restart, a dropped connection -- permanently lost that item's coverage and was indistinguishable from a check that found nothing. The ORDER of the two steps is the whole design, and it is why the bead spells it out. A pass REPEATS the dispatch, so the narrowing lands first: without asking which checks already failed, a re-pass re-sends everything the first pass sent -- including the ones whose failure the response cannot change -- and multiplies traffic against a broken target by the number of passes. burpsy's Admit was a single bit with no failure memory, so there was nothing to consult. So the breaker now remembers, per (dispatch unit, check), which probes could not be sent: Burp's predicate asked one level coarser (Zwy6.java's Zz returns 'skip' when failedForEntireInsertionPoint < 1L, per insertion point; the dispatch plan here has (unit, check) as its granularity). Two failure sites feed it -- a check that failed before a verdict, and a check whose probes were all refused -- which are the same fact by different causes and were previously both just a counter. The loop spends a pass only when the item FAILED and some step is still retryable, which after the narrowing means some check in the item has never been tried. A budget-spent item is NOT retried: a second pass would run out of the same budget, and 'retried once' would teach an operator nothing the run's own bounds had not already said. FollowUpPasses is on AuditOutcome because a failed item that was retried and one that was not are different accounts of the same coverage loss. beginPass resets the CONSECUTIVE counters and keeps the memory, and the failed flag survives a pass. That last one is not an oversight: an item that tripped the breaker is still failed after a pass that did not clear it, and clearing the flag would make the engine's verdict depend on whether a retry HAPPENED rather than on whether the work SUCCEEDED -- so a pass that fixed nothing would report the item as merely bounded, a claim this engine does not make. The key row now applies (28 applied in full, 1 partial, 26 not applied -- the counts move, and the test says so in its failure message). Two oracle tests had to learn the new key rather than block on it, which is the guard working as intended: the shipped-keys test pins all three counts, and the apply-overlay oracle refuses an applying key it cannot check, so number_of_follow_up_passes is NAMED in that switch and checked through the resolved followUpPasses() rather than the raw OptUint32. Two of my own test assertions were inverted and said the opposite of what I meant -- that a pass clears the memory, and that it clears the failed flag. The second was a real design question I had answered wrongly before writing the code. 4 tests, mutation-checked: clearing the memory in beginPass fails the narrowing test, and a default of 0 fails the resolution test -- the latter mattering most, because an unset key resolving to 0 reads as 'no retries' and quietly disables the feature the row claims to apply. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./internal/scanner green, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

title: scanner: no mechanism restricts a run to a chosen subset of issue types, so the three selected_issues keys are dead letters
description:
## Claim
Burp's dispatch is a two-stage filter (`Zwy6.java:36-75`, and the per-check predicate at `:170-184` — a synthetic `lambda$isEnabled$1`), so a run can be restricted to an explicit set of issue types. burpsy's `check_contract.go:70` gates on a per-family switch and `audit.go:1044-1061` reports three `selected_issues`-family keys as unapplied, so there is no way to say "audit only for SQL injection and path traversal".

## Evidence
- Burp: `Zwy6.java:36-75` (stage-1 filter), `:170-184` (`lambda$isEnabled$1` per-check predicate), `scan_only_selected_issues` / `select_individual_issues` / `selected_issues` key family.
- burpsy: `check_contract.go:70` (family `Enabled` bool), `audit.go:1044-1061` (three dead keys).

## Fix direction
Add an issue-type allow-list to `AuditConfig`, filter `CheckDescriptor`s on it at registry-aggregation time, and make the three keys read/apply. Also lets `check_coverage.go:19-37` report a row as "runnable but operator-suppressed", which is currently unrepresentable — a coverage number that cannot say that overstates what a run would do.

## Why it matters
Targeted re-audits are the normal operator workflow (confirm one issue class after a fix). Today the only control is a coarse per-family switch, and the three keys that promise selection do nothing.
close_reason: Burp's dispatch is a two-stage filter: the family switches, then a per-check predicate over the selected issue types (Zwy6.java:36-75, and lambda$isEnabled$1 at :170-184). burpsy had the first stage only, so the three selected_issues-family keys were reported unapplied and a run could not be narrowed past its families. Targeted re-audit is the ordinary operator workflow -- fix a bug, confirm the one issue class is gone -- and here it was unreachable. ScanConfig.IssueTypes is a set of catalogue type indexes, empty meaning no restriction. Type indexes rather than names because the catalogue is the identity: a name is a label, and a label an operator typed against Burp's own UI has to mean the same thing here rather than becoming a second vocabulary to keep in step. The filter is applied LAST and to BOTH sources: Burp's own order has the type filter after the family switches, so a run scoped to SQLi and path traversal can still turn the SQLi FAMILY off and select nothing of it; and it is applied to corpus entries as well as the native table, because a selection that filtered one and not the other has a hole exactly where the operator least expects one. A check with NO type index is EXCLUDED whenever a selection is in force: it is not selectable, and a selection that cannot name something must not silently keep it -- the conservative direction, since an operator asked for a set and a check they could not have chosen either way is better reported as unselected than as selected. Two paths, and only one was covered at first. enabledChecks (what a scanner LISTS) and enabledChecksUnder (what a run DISPATCHES, taking the per-run config) are different functions, and a narrowing applied only in the first is computed and discarded for every real audit. The mutation caught it: removing the filter from the audit path passed every test until TestTheSelectionNarrowsTheCheckSetAnAuditWouldDispatch exists. Same trap as nc9s, same lesson -- a test that calls the helper rather than the path a run takes cannot see an unwired seam. hasAuditLevelGate also had to learn about the selection: it answers 'does this configuration narrow the check set at all?', and a configuration that ONLY selects issue types was routed down the path that applies no narrowing -- a gate predicate written before the key existed. CheckCoverageRow gains Suppressed, and NativeCheckCoverageUnder is the selection-aware sibling. A row that is runnable and SUPPRESSED is not covered for a run under this configuration, and a coverage number that cannot say so counts it as covered -- the one thing a coverage number is for. It is distinct from a declined row (never going to run either way) and the two are asserted mutually exclusive, because two explanations for one absence is its own confusion. The three keys now apply as PARTIAL rather than in full, and the distinction is real: Burp's selected_issues value carries a per-issue enabled flag, and here the PRESENCE of a type is the enable, so the two boolean flags carry nothing beyond it. Claiming full support would be the mirror-image lie 86le is about, and the counts move to say so: 28 applied in full, 4 partial, 23 not applied. The wire gained issue_types (absent and empty are told apart by nil, because 'no selection' and 'nothing selected' are different requests) and number_of_follow_up_passes. A type index of 0 is REFUSED rather than accepted: it is not a catalogue entry, and a selection containing it would match no check at all -- an operator auditing nothing while the configuration read as a restriction. Two existing tests were pinned to the old behaviour and had to be retargeted rather than deleted, and one had stopped testing what it was written for. Test_a_parsed_unapplied_key_reaches_the_report used scan_only_selected_issues as its example of a key the parser records and the report drops; that key is honoured now, so the example cannot show the spelling hazard the test exists for (section-qualified name the parser writes vs bare name the listing looks up). It now finds its own example, matches by SUFFIX so a key moving sections cannot make it pass for the wrong reason, and asserts the mirror too: a key the engine DOES honour must not appear under either spelling. 9 tests, mutation-checked: the filter never applied fails 1, never applied on the AUDIT path fails 1, an unset selection narrowing to nothing fails 1. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./internal/scanner + internal/web green, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

title: scanner: the light-audit tier has no per-kind opt-in, and the 8 quick_scan_* key rows are declined for a reason Burp's UI contradicts
description:
## Claim
Burp's `quick_scan_*` keys (`quick_scan_url_params`, `_body_params`, `_cookies`, `_http_headers`, `_param_name`, `_entire_body`, `_url_path_filename`, `_url_path_folders`) gate the **light-audit tier per insertion-point kind** — Burp's own panel text: *"runs a lighter audit ... Select the insertion point types this applies to"* (`Zrdr.java:26`). burpsy's key table declines all eight as "redundant with insertion_point_types" (`internal/scanner/audit.go:1126-1173`), which is factually wrong: `insertion_point_types` chooses WHICH points to enumerate, these choose which of them get the cheap pass.

## Evidence
- Burp: `Zrdr.java:26` (panel text), `Zb1q.java:111-118` (the per-kind gate).
- burpsy: `audit.go:1126-1173` — eight rows, `applies: false`, reason "redundant with insertion_point_types".
- The tier itself EXISTS (`audit_engine.go:509-530`, bead 7bkj): it counts CLEAN same-(kind,host) points and declines the rest from the Nth. What is missing is the operator's per-kind control over it.

## Fix direction
Make the eight keys read/pApply against the light tier's per-kind admission instead of being declined; a kind not ticked runs the full pass for every point of that kind. Each row needs a test that fails if the key is accepted and then ignored (the iueb precedent), and `audit_config_keys_test.go`'s `wantApplied/wantReported` pair moves 27/28 accordingly.

## Why it matters
An operator who wants a light audit of URL parameters but a full audit of body parameters cannot express it, and the settings page currently tells them the keys are redundant — a false statement in the operator-facing surface.
close_reason: The eight quick_scan_* keys now gate the light-audit tier per insertion-point kind. The reason they carried ('redundant with insertion_point_types') was false: insertion_point_types chooses whether a kind is ENUMERATED, quick_scan_* chooses whether an enumerated kind gets the LIGHT pass (Burp's own Zrdr.java:26 panel text and the Zb1q.java:111-118 gate say so). BuiltInConfig/AuditConfig carry the eight OptUint32 fields; AuditConfig.LightAuditKinds is a DERIVED deny list of the kinds excluded, rebuilt once in ApplyWithReport after the key loop. auditItem's shouldSkip consults it, so checks_injection.go:81 honours it unchanged. Wire reports light_audit_kinds_excluded, omitted when empty so the unset case cannot be misread as an empty allow-list. The deny-list polarity is the load-bearing part and I got it backwards first (ticking URL params silently excluded cookies) - caught by TestAKindTickedOffIsOutOfTheLightPass, and the comment on LightApplies now says why. Six mutations checked, all caught; M1 (the engine gate not consulted) and M3 (per-row rebuilds) passed the first suite and shaped the tests - the fix for M1 is a real end-to-end audit run requiring the skip COUNT to differ. Honest counting: 28/4/23 -> 36/4/15 applied/partial/reported, oracle extended to verify all eight through the derived set. Gate: gofmt/build/vet clean, scanner 436s ok, web 45.9s ok, intruder/bcheck/core/tools ok, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

title: history: the parameterized filter cannot see a request body
description:
Split out of burpsy-react-ui-80tg item 3, which shipped the rename instead of the fix.

Burp's SHOW_ONLY_PARAMETERIZED_REQUESTS accepts HttpParameterType.URL OR HttpParameterType.BODY
(burp-re/out/clean/root/Zb2y.java:270-273,450-455). The filter here is path-based only, so every
body-only parameterized request is classified unparameterized and dropped: a JSON API POST with a
body and no query string, a multipart upload, an XML API call. Those are exactly the requests an
operator filters to parameterized traffic in order to find, so the filter does not mean what its
name says.

80tg's fix section offers two options and this is the one not taken: count body parameters the way
the grammar already can, or rename the filter to what it measures. The RENAME shipped (the label
now reads "Requests with query parameters" and the hint says exactly which half is measured), so the
gap is disclosed rather than hidden -- but it is still a gap and the filter is still wrong against
Burp's semantics.

Why the count was not simply added client-side: a history row is an index entry and carries no
request body, and core.Exchange has no request Content-Type either (its Mime is the RESPONSE's).
Computing this per row would mean reading every request body to classify a list entry, which is the
cost the history/message split exists to prevent (internal/web/AGENTS.md: "a list endpoint serves
index rows and never resolves message payloads"). Doing it in the browser would need the body
fetched per visible row, which is worse.

The work is therefore on the ingest side: project a boolean (or a count) onto core.Exchange at the
point its request is already parsed, and carry it on ExchangeView. A BOOLEAN, not a body copy, so
the index-row rule still holds. Then the filter reads the field and the label goes back to
Burp's wording. The rules the count needs, worked out while attempting it:

- urlencoded and multipart bodies enumerate as name/value pairs; a bare flag with no = is a
  parameter, an empty segment between separators is not.
- A body in a format that is not name/value (JSON, XML) must NOT be reported as zero parameters.
  Unexamined is not parameterless, and a filter that hides requests it could not read reports a
  clean answer about a request nobody looked at.
- multipart counts named parts; a file part counts, since filename= names it.
- Content-Length follows any body change, or the correction leaves a request the target rejects
  for a reason the operator cannot see.

The JS side of this was written and then deleted rather than committed unused: a lib module with
a passing test and no caller is dead code in a tree that counts coverage honestly.
close_reason: The correct fix for 80tg item 3, which shipped the rename and filed this. The History 'Parameterized requests' filter counted the query string alone, so every body-only parameterized request was classified unparameterized and dropped: a JSON API POST with a body and no query string, a multipart upload, an XML API call. Those are exactly the requests an operator filters to parameterized traffic in order to find, so the filter did not mean what its name said. The count is computed at the capture seam -- core.RequestParameterCount, called from Capture.Record alongside Mime and RequestFingerprint, for the same reason. A history row is an index entry and carries no request body, so a consumer that wanted this would have to read the bytes back, the cost the history/message split exists to prevent (internal/web/AGENTS.md: 'a list endpoint serves index rows and never resolves message payloads'). A COUNT travels on the row; a body never does. Burp's semantics: SHOW_ONLY_PARAMETERIZED_REQUESTS accepts HttpParameterType.URL OR HttpParameterType.BODY (Zb2y.java:270-273,450-455). So the count is the query string's plus a form body's, and a multipart body's parts are counted by name -- a file part counts, because filename= names it. A bare ?debug with no value is a parameter; an empty segment between separators is not. The load-bearing decision: a body the counter cannot parse -- JSON, XML, anything not name/value -- is counted as ONE, not zero. Reporting zero would tell an operator a request has no parameters when nobody examined it, and a filter that hides requests it could not read reports a clean answer about a request nobody read. It is one and not a guess at how many, because nobody knows and a bigger number would be a claim this function has no basis for. Which makes 0 a weaker claim than it looks, and the column says so: 0 means 'certainly no parameters' and -1 means 'this row predates the count'. That is why the column is NULLABLE rather than NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 like its siblings -- for an unmeasured duration a legacy zero is the honest reading, but for this one it would be a claim no build ever made. A legacy row reads back as -1, the filter KEEPS it, and the hint under the control says how many rows were kept because they were never examined. Dropping a -1 instead would be the filter reporting a verdict on requests it has no information about. The 'Query' table column stays 'Query' and says why: it is the query-string count read off the path, the only half visible without the body. Calling it 'Params' would put a number beside the filter that disagrees with it. The proxy's parity guard required a rule for the new field and was right to: it made explicit what I had left implicit. ruleMayDiffer, for the same reason as RequestFP beside it -- the count comes from the raw request bytes, and the proxy relays them verbatim while the crawler's sender re-renders what it parsed. The parity fixture carries no body so both legs count 0 and ruleIdentical would hold vacuously. 20 tests across four layers, mutation-checked: the pre-fix query-only count fails 6, and reporting an unreadable body as zero fails exactly the JSON, XML and no-Content-Type cases plus the unexamined test -- the overclaim this projection exists to prevent. A legacy row reading as 0 fails the persistence test, and a genuine 0 reading as the unknown sentinel fails its mirror. Verified live twice against a console running this build. Through the real proxy: a urlencoded form post with no query string counts 2, a JSON API post 1, a multipart upload 2, a GET with a query string 2, a GET with neither 0, and a JSON body WITH a query string 1 rather than 2 -- an unreadable body must not add to a query string that already answered. In a browser: the filter keeps all four body- and query-bearing rows and drops the genuine zero, and the hint states the count is computed server-side at capture. Screenshot at the end of the pass. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./internal/core + internal/persist + internal/proxy + internal/web green, bun test:lib 761/0, e2e-go.sh 24/24. The committed bundle is deliberately not rebuilt: HEAD's history.tsx still calls useHistory with three arguments, which only compiles against a data.ts change another session has not committed.

title: network: no DNS address-family preference — a dual-stack host behind one-family routing dials the unreachable address (mr83 part 2)
description:
Split out of burpsy-react-ui-mr83, which bundles three independent dial-path changes. This is the second.

## The gap
Burp: settings/network/dns.html:49-65 — system default, Prefer IPv4, or Prefer IPv6, "because routing restrictions may permit only one family."

burpsy offered system-versus-named-resolver selection plus exact hostname overrides, and returned the resolver addresses unfiltered. Address ordering was entirely the system resolver's.

## The operator loses
Any engagement on a host reachable only over one family. A dual-stack target behind IPv4-only routing can resolve to an AAAA first, and burpsy dials the unreachable address. There was no setting that fixes it; the only workaround was the per-hostname override table, applied one address at a time.

## Fix
Resolution.Family — system (default), ipv4, ipv6. A filter over the resolver answer, not a resolver rewrite: a per-family query (AAAA rather than A) can be answered differently by a split-horizon resolver than a filtered answer to the question the operator actually asked, and the engagement own DNS is the thing that knows. RFC 6555 filtered AAAA exists for deployments that want it; a security tool should not be one by default.

- Applied on BOTH dial paths (the raw sender and the typed transport Repeater uses). Two paths that disagreed here would be a Repeater send that reached an IPv6-only host and a scanner probe that did not.
- An OVERRIDE is never filtered: the operator named an address, and substituting a different one would be worse than the defect being fixed.
- System costs no lookup — the default hands the hostname to the dialer exactly as before, so the ordinary send pays nothing.
- A family with no address in it is a NAMED failure naming the field to change, not a generic "could not resolve" that would send an operator to the DNS settings instead of the family preference.

## Verification, and an honest limit
The preference is proved by a lookup seam answering with BOTH families, IPv6 first, against a real IPv4 listener: the send reaches the listener, and the listener sees the connection. A mutation removing the preference from the typed transport fails it.

The LIVE pass could not demonstrate the defect on this machine, and the reason is recorded in resolution_family_live_test.go: /etc/hosts gave the name both families with the AAAA first, against an IPv4-only listener, and both family=system and family=ipv4 answered 200 in under 10ms. A direct dial to an unroutable AAAA failed in 0.00s — this host has no IPv6 route at all, so an AAAA dial fails instantly rather than timing out. The defect needs a network that DROPs the AAAA rather than rejecting it, which a loopback cannot provide.
close_reason: A dual-stack target behind IPv4-only routing can resolve to an AAAA first, and burpsy dialled the unreachable address, so a request took the connect timeout to fail on a host that was reachable all along; there was no setting that fixed it and the only workaround was the per-hostname override table. Burp's answer is the resolution-address preference (settings/network/dns.html:49-65), 'because routing restrictions may permit only one family'. Resolution.Family is system/ipv4/ipv6, applied on BOTH dial paths -- the raw sender and the typed transport Repeater uses, because two paths that disagreed would be a Repeater send that reached an IPv6-only host and a scanner probe that did not. It is a filter over the resolver's answer rather than a resolver rewrite: a per-family query can be answered differently by a split-horizon resolver than a filtered answer to the question the operator asked, and the engagement's own DNS is what knows. An override is never filtered, because the operator named an address and substituting another is worse than the defect. System costs no lookup, so an ordinary send pays nothing for a preference nobody set. A family with no address is a named failure pointing at the field to change. The live pass could not demonstrate the defect and the reason is recorded in the test: this host has no IPv6 route, so an AAAA dial fails in 0.00s instead of timing out, and both family=system and family=ipv4 answered 200 in under 10ms against an IPv4-only listener. The selection is proved through a Lookup seam answering with both families, IPv6 first, against a real IPv4 listener: the send reaches the listener and the listener sees the connection. Mutation-checked three ways: a no-op filter, system treated as a filter, and removing the preference from the typed transport -- the third survived the first round of tests and is why the two-family seam exists. Split out of mr83, which stays open for the global SOCKS carrier. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./... green with the test cache cleared, tsc clean, bun test:lib 711/0, check:tokens green, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

title: redirect: a followed chain does not replay the cookies each hop set (mr83 part 1)
description:
Split out of burpsy-react-ui-mr83, which bundles three independent dial-path changes. This is the first.

## The gap
Burp: settings/tools/repeater.html:143-145 -- "If you enable this setting, Burp resubmits any cookies set in the redirect response when it follows the redirection target." burpsy built each hop from the previous REQUEST only, so a login or SSO flow that sets a cookie on its 302 arrived at the destination unauthenticated. The redirect was followed, the cookie was not sent, and the destination returned its login page -- which reads as an application failure rather than a missing cookie, and is the single most common redirect shape in an authenticated tool.

internal/web/repeater_options.go stated the absence plainly, so nothing on screen was wrong. This is the capability plus the option Burp exposes alongside it.

## Fix
- RedirectSettings.ReplayCookies, default OFF (unlike a browser: burpsy sends what an operator wrote, and a target-set credential is not one they asked to send; a target that sets throwaway cookies is the other reason a switch is needed).
- The follower absorbs each hop response Set-Cookie into a jar and adds the jar cookies to the NEXT hop, scoped to the hop own authority and Path.
- A hop that already carries a Cookie header keeps it -- the operator typed it.
- The jar is the SESSION coordinator the Session page shows and the other tools already send from, not a second store, so a login performed by a chain is visible everywhere.

## A real bug the unit tests could not see
repeaterSendOptions.redirectPolicy rebuilt RedirectSettings field by field on a per-send mode override, so ReplayCookies silently dropped to false. The console showed the setting ON, the operator sent with "always", and no cookie was replayed. The field-by-field rebuild is replaced with a copy-and-replace-one-field, and a test asserts on the whole struct so a field added later cannot default to false here.

Live through a real console: replay OFF -- the hop request carries no Cookie and the destination answers "LOGIN PAGE"; replay ON -- the hop request carries Cookie: session=real-session-value and the destination answers "DASHBOARD - authenticated".
close_reason: A login or SSO flow that sets a cookie on its 302 arrived at the destination unauthenticated: the redirect was followed, the cookie was not sent, and the destination returned its login page, which reads as an application failure rather than a missing cookie. Burp exposes the fix as a setting; burpsy had the absence documented, so nothing on screen was wrong. ReplayCookies defaults OFF unlike a browser's, because burpsy sends what an operator wrote and a target-set credential is not something they asked to send. Each hop's Set-Cookie is absorbed and the next hop carries it, scoped to that hop's own authority and Path; a hop that already carries a Cookie header keeps it. The jar is the SESSION coordinator rather than a second store, behind a two-method interface because internal/session imports internal/sender, and it takes the Set-Cookie values rather than response bytes. A real bug the unit tests could not see: repeaterSendOptions.redirectPolicy rebuilt RedirectSettings field by field on a per-send mode override, so ReplayCookies dropped to false -- the console showed the setting ON, the operator sent with 'always', and no cookie was replayed, with every sender test green because they attach their own jar. The rebuild is now copy-and-replace-one-field. Live through a real console against a real login flow: replay off, the hop request carries no Cookie and the destination answers LOGIN PAGE; replay on, the same request carries Cookie: session=real-session-value and the destination answers DASHBOARD. Mutation-checked six ways including removing the absorb, removing the apply, letting the jar replace the operator's own header, never attaching the session jar, and dropping the hop's Path. Split out of mr83, which stays open for the DNS family preference and the global SOCKS carrier. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./... green, tsc clean, bun test:lib 711/0, check:tokens green, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

title: history: the Search box searches five columns of loaded rows, and the default message reading is hard-coded to edited
description:
QA PASS 2026-09-25 — history's Search box searches five columns of the rows already loaded, and the default message reading is hard-coded.

## 1. Search covers five fields, not the data (P2)

**Burp:** tools/proxy/http-history/index.html:136-140 — *"Enter a search term in the Search box to find matching items across all columns. The search applies to the underlying data, regardless of any filters you have applied."* The second sentence is the load-bearing one: the search is over the **capture**, not over the visible page.

**burpsy:** the dedicated search runs over method, host, path, MIME and comment of the rows already fetched (`pages/history.tsx:645-650`), and the page loads at most the newest 2,000 / 5,000 / 10,000 / 50,000 rows (`:423,1284-1295`). The code says so plainly at `:1493-1497`: the search operates over already-loaded rows.

**What the operator loses:** anything outside those five columns and outside the loaded window. A page title, a response header, a request body fragment, a comment on a row older than the cap, or a listener port — none is findable from the Search box, and each has to be reconstructed as a separate DSL filter. The box is labelled Search, sitting next to a Filter button, and the two are documented as different in Burp; here the Search box quietly behaves like a filter over the current page.

**Fix:** make the Search box a server-side query over the store, with the existing DSL as its grammar and the current client-side path kept for the instant narrow case. The API already takes `q` (`api_capture.go`), so this is a UI routing change, not a new search engine. The help text under the box should say which of the two it is.

## 2. The default message reading is not configurable (P3)

**Burp:** `map_root.tsv:20253` — *"Use this setting to choose whether the Proxy history message editor displays auto-modified, manually edited, or original messages by default"*; the neighbouring rows name the persisted key `user_options.proxy.default_display_message`.

**burpsy:** `pages/history.tsx:685-701` hard-codes both `requestVariant` and `responseVariant` to `"edited"`, and resets them to `"edited"` on every selection. No store field, no setting, no API path changes that default.

**What the operator loses:** the ability to make Original or Auto-modified the standing reading. On an engagement where auto-modification is routinely involved, every inspected exchange needs the picker re-clicked, and — worse — the default silently differs from Burp's, so a migrated operator sees a different message than the one their habits expect.

**Fix:** a three-way setting in the editor's own settings, persisted in the workspace store beside the other editor preferences (`editorTabs`, `urlEncodeAsYouType`), defaulting to Burp's own default so the out-of-box reading matches. Small, self-contained, and it removes a difference an operator cannot currently see or change.
