title: history/intercept: rules cannot AND/OR, no listener filter, parameterized counts query only, no newline correction on an edited forward
description:
QA PASS 2026-09-25 — four interception/history behaviours Burp has that burpsy does not. Grouped because each is a control the operator is shown or promised, and none of them is a large engine change.

## 1. Interception rules cannot combine with AND or OR (P2)

**Burp:** settings/tools/proxy.html:246-268 — each rule picks AND or OR to combine it with the rules above, and *"Each rule is combined to the rules above in order, using the selected boolean operator."*

**burpsy:** `internal/intercept/intercept.go:722-778` evaluates the enabled list as **first matching rule wins**, and the rule editor (`internal/web/ui/src/pages/intercept.tsx:261-384`) offers field, match, action, comment, enable and ordering — no operator column.

**The operator loses:** any hold condition that is a conjunction. "Hold requests to host A **and** path /admin" is two rules that today behave as an OR (the first that matches decides), so the operator either over-holds or writes a single brittle rule that has to enumerate both facts in one matcher. This is the reason Burp has the boolean column, and it is the most commonly written interception rule after "hold on this host".

**Fix:** an operator field per rule and a left-to-right fold over the enabled list, with the current first-match behaviour as the default when every rule says OR. A test that two-rule conjunction holds only when both facts match, and that the default ordering is unchanged.

## 2. No listener-port filter in HTTP history (P2)

**Burp:** tools/proxy/http-history/filter-settings.html:109-116 — *"Filter by listener - You can show items received on a specific listener port. This can be useful when testing access controls."*

**burpsy:** the Listener port column is rendered (`pages/history.tsx:984-996`) but the complete More-filters surface (`:1499-1555`) has no listener control and no listener query field.

**The operator loses:** isolating one listener's traffic when several receive it. The port is captured and displayed but not filterable, and a column cannot be filtered without reconstructing the predicate as DSL. `tyeo` was closed as a duplicate of `mr4p`, whose close reason implemented only the IP column — so the listener filter was closed without ever being built.

**Fix:** a `listener` filter beside the existing port/protocol axes, a query field for it, and a `tyeo` follow-up note so the duplicate closure is recorded rather than repeated.

## 3. "Parameterized requests" counts only query parameters (P2)

**Burp:** `out/clean/root/Zb2y.java:270-273,450-455` — Burp's SHOW_ONLY_PARAMETERIZED_REQUESTS predicate explicitly accepts `HttpParameterType.URL` **or** `HttpParameterType.BODY`.

**burpsy:** `pages/history.tsx:326-338` deliberately counts query parameters only, applies that as the onlyParameterized filter (`:638-640`), and discloses the limitation in the filter's own help (`:1502-1507`).

**The operator loses:** every body-only parameterized request. A JSON API POST with a body and no query string, a multipart upload, an XML API call — all classified as unparameterized and all dropped when the operator filters to parameterized traffic, which is the filter you use to find attack surface. The disclosure is honest, and the answer is still "the filter does not mean what its name says".

**Fix:** count body parameters the way the grammar already can (`queryParamCount` is path-based; the request body is available in the same projection), or rename the filter to what it measures. The first is correct, because Burp's own semantics are the first.

## 4. No newline correction on a forwarded interception edit (P2)

**Burp:** settings/tools/proxy.html:273-292 — Burp can add a missing blank line after headers and remove trailing newlines from URL-encoded bodies when an **edited** intercepted request is forwarded.

**burpsy:** the interception editor offers only "Fix Content-Length when forwarding" (`pages/intercept.tsx:1155-1160`); `internal/intercept/intercept.go:886-899` applies only `rewriteContentLength`, which changes no newline bytes.

**The operator loses:** a reliable forward after editing. An edit that drops the blank line after headers, or leaves a trailing newline in a form body, produces a request the target may reject — and the failure looks like the application's, not the operator's. Content-Length is fixed automatically; framing is not.

**Fix:** the two corrections Burp names, applied on the release path when the request was edited, each with its own toggle in the interception settings. Both are local byte edits on a message the operator already chose to edit, so neither widens what the proxy can send.

## Why together

Each is a control an operator either cannot find or cannot express, and each is a bounded change: a rule field and a fold, a filter and a query field, a count, two byte-level corrections. They are filed together because they are all "the last mile of an existing surface" rather than missing subsystems — the same shape as the last QA batch, and the same reason an operator would rather have them than not.
close_reason: All four items addressed; two shipped as fixes and two shipped as the honest option each was given. 1. Rules combine with AND (75ff80d). Burp's proxy.html:246-268 gives every rule a boolean operator and folds left to right; the enabled list was first-matching-rule-wins, so a conjunction could not be written at all -- 'hold host A AND path /admin' is two rules behaving as a disjunction, which means over-holding or one brittle rule enumerating both facts in one matcher, and it is the most-written interception rule after 'hold on this host'. The default is OR, which is what every pre-existing list evaluates as, so the fold reproduces the old behaviour exactly and adding the column changes nothing until an operator opts in; an unrecognised operator reads as OR for the same reason the action parser does. Two semantics the tests pin because a fold gets them wrong: an AND cannot be rescued by an OR below it, and AND on the FIRST rule is ignored rather than refused (nothing above it to combine with, and the rest of the list must keep working). A near-miss worth recording: SetRules rebuilds every rule field by field and the first version forgot Op on the literal branch -- the field existed, decoded, stored, and was dropped on the way in, the same shape as the Params field whose own comment says the wire shape silently dropped it. 2. Listener filter, same commit. Burp's filter-settings.html:109-116; the column rendered and could not be filtered, and tyeo was closed as a duplicate of mr4p whose close reason implemented only the IP column, so it was closed without ever being built. A comma-separated field normalised like the extension lists. The one rule extracted because it fails quietly: a non-numeric segment is DROPPED, not coerced to 0 -- 0 is what a Repeater/Intruder/crawl row carries, so coercing 'abc' to 0 would show exactly the traffic the operator did not ask for. 0 is not offered as a choice because it is not a port. 3. Parameterized renamed, NOT fixed, and that is the bead's own second option. The label now reads 'Requests with query parameters' and the hint says which half is measured, why a history row cannot see the other, and that the Search box does read bytes. The count -- the correct fix -- is filed as 7py5 because it cannot be done where the filter runs: a history row is an index entry with no request body and core.Exchange has no request Content-Type (its Mime is the RESPONSE's), so per-row computation means reading every request body to classify a list entry, the exact cost the history/message split exists to prevent. The JS half was written, tested, and DELETED rather than committed unused; 7py5 records the rules, the unexamined-is-not-parameterless case being what decides whether the eventual fix is honest or merely wider. 4. Newline corrections on an edited forward, same commit as 1. Burp can add a missing blank line after the headers and strip trailing newlines from a urlencoded body on an EDITED request (proxy.html:273-292); neither existed and Content-Length was already fixed, which changes no newline bytes. Two switches because they are two defects with two symptoms and fixing one does not fix the other; both apply only to an edited message, since untouched traffic came off the wire and is well-formed by construction. The trailing-newline fix is scoped to urlencoded/multipart because a trailing newline in JSON is meaningful inside a string. Content-Length is recomputed after every body change. Restoring the blank line needed a header-block scan because both obvious guesses are wrong in a way that matters -- 'last CRLF' truncates the body by two bytes and 'first CRLF' throws the headers away -- so it walks the lines and asks what each one is, and refuses a message with no CRLF rather than inventing a boundary. A bodiless header block does get its terminator, because that is what makes it forwardable. The setting is an engine setting with its own GET/PUT rather than a per-forward argument, for the reason fixContentLength is not on the route: an operator sets it once, and threading it through Forward would put a setting on every call site that could forget it; GET reads back what is in force because a checkbox showing the defaults while a plugin has set one is a control lying about what it is doing. 27 tests across the three shipped items, mutation-checked: dropping the operator from the fold fails 4, dropping Op in SetRules fails 3, not applying the correction fails the wiring test, trimming non-urlencoded bodies fails the JSON case, and coercing a bad listener segment to 0 fails the coercion case. That last group includes a test added only after a mutation exposed the gap -- every other newline test called Apply directly, so removing the call from Forward passed all of them until one exercised Forward's own bytes through held.Wait. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./internal/intercept + internal/proxy + internal/web green, tsc clean, bun test:lib 761/0, e2e-go.sh 24/24. One caveat: the committed dist/app.js is deliberately not rebuilt, because HEAD's history.tsx carries a three-argument useHistory that only compiles against a data.ts change another session has not committed; a bundle built now would either fail or absorb their uncommitted work.

title: scanner: an audit item cannot be cancelled, issues carry no time/source, and a single finding cannot be reported with its HTTP evidence
description:
QA PASS 2026-09-25 — the audit queue cannot cancel one item, and the Issues table cannot say where an issue came from or when it was found. Filed together: both are "the data exists, the operator cannot act on it".

## 1. No per-item cancel (P2)

**Burp:** running-scans/results/audit-items/index.html:102-115 — the audit-item context menu provides **Cancel** to stop auditing one item.

**burpsy:** the only accepted audit-item action is `POST /api/scanner/audit-items/{id}/again` (`internal/web/api_scanner_audit_items.go:301-308`), and the row menu offers only "Audit again" (`internal/web/ui/src/pages/auditqueue.tsx:149-162`).

**The operator loses:** the ability to stop one long-running or unwanted item. The options are to wait for it or to disable the enclosing live task, which stops everything including the items that are fine. A crawler that reached a slow or heavily-guarded URL holds a slot and a thread until its own bounds expire, and the queue offers no way to reclaim just that one.

**Fix:** `POST .../{id}/cancel`, wired to the same `Control` the pause/stop path already uses (`internal/intruder/control.go` is the model), with the item's terminal state recorded as cancelled — a distinct state from skipped or errored, because "we stopped this" and "this could not run" are different facts about coverage.

## 2. Issues carry no time, source, or check-kind (P2)

**Burp:** running-scans/results/issues.html:89-118,132-165 lists **Time** and **Source** on every issue and filters by BCheck / Scan check / Extension / manually generated provenance. map_root.tsv:10282-10295 carries the same literals.

**burpsy:** the issue view has `task_id` but omits the finding's timestamp and has no source or check-kind field (`internal/web/api_capture.go:804-851`); the Issues page filters on severity, confidence, false-positive state and free text only, and displays no time, task or check kind (`internal/web/ui/src/pages/scanner.tsx:190-259, 830-872`).

**The operator loses:** the ability to separate a manual finding from a scan's, to tell which of three tasks raised an issue, to filter by check provenance, or to order by when something was found. On a long engagement the issue list is an unordered set of rows from every producer in the project.

**Fix:** project `core.Finding.Timestamp` and the existing task attribution into the issue view, add a source facet (scan check / BCheck / manual, all of which the finding already knows), and render Time and Source as columns. This is a projection and a filter, not a schema change.

## 3. A single finding cannot be reported with its HTTP evidence (P2)

**Burp:** issues.html:195-228 offers **Report selected issues**; report-settings.html:98-111 lets a report include the relevant request/response extract or the full HTTP messages.

**burpsy:** the per-issue Report menu opens whole-scan HTML/JSON/SARIF exports (`internal/web/ui/src/pages/scanner.tsx:455-463`), and report Evidence holds only method, host, path and status — no bytes (`internal/report/report.go:67-73`).

**The operator loses:** a self-contained handoff for one finding. The deliverable an assessor needs is the request that produced it and the response that came back; the available export is scan-wide and metadata-only, so a single-issue report has to be assembled by hand.

**Fix:** a selected-issue report that carries the evidence rows the project already stores — the finding's occurrence already names request and response message ids, and `store.Raw` can read the bytes at export time, so no new storage is required.

## Why together

Each is the same shape: the data is retained (audit-item evidence, finding timestamps, occurrence message ids) and the operator-facing layer drops it. One rendering/projection change per item, and together they are the difference between a queue an operator can steer and one they can only watch.
notes: PARTIAL: item 2 of 3 done and committed (f44e46e, 2f2fc27, f54ca57). Items 1 (per-item cancel) and 3 (single-finding report carrying request/response bytes) remain open.
close_reason: All three items, and all three were the same shape: the data is retained and the operator-facing layer drops it. 1. Per-item cancel (a0e4122's sibling commit): Burp's audit-item context menu has offered Cancel since running-scans/results/audit-items/index.html:102-115 and the queue had no way to stop one item. The alternatives were waiting for a slow or heavily-guarded URL to exhaust its own bounds (holding a slot and a thread throughout) or disabling the enclosing live task, which stops every item including the ones that were fine. POST /api/scanner/audit-items/{id}/cancel stops one queued item and nothing else, and is NOT routed through runAudit because it sends nothing -- the route manifest records it as riskLocal where its sibling {id}/again is riskAttack, so an unattended caller is not asked to confirm the one queue action that cannot touch the target. ItemStateCancelled is a NINTH state rather than a flavour of ItemStateBounded, and that is the point: bounded says the target was too expensive, cancelled says a person stopped it, and folding one into the other reports a decision as a budget. Burp has CANCELLED for exactly this reason. It is terminal and NOT a completed audit, so 'how much of this queue finished' keeps counting only work that finished. The cancel is recorded and read at the engine's gate inside auditItem (so both AuditWithin and AuditMultiple get it) rather than applied to work in flight, because there is no per-item context to abandon a dispatched probe with and a half-sent request counted as complete is worse than a late cancel. A refused cancel changes NOTHING, which is asserted rather than assumed -- my first test asserted the opposite, which would have made the gate stop an audit already in flight. 2. Issues carry time and source (f44e46e, 2f2fc27, f54ca57): the view had task_id but not the finding's timestamp, and no source. Both were knowable -- FindingStore.Add has stamped Timestamp since the beginning and TaskID distinguishes a run from a person -- so the wire shape was the only thing missing, which is the same defect the Params field's own comment records ('the store kept the set, the console rendered it, the test asserted it, and the wire shape in between silently dropped it'). Source is derived rather than stored and deliberately has TWO values: there is no provenance field on core.Finding, and guessing BCheck-vs-native from the check name would put an unverifiable claim in a column an operator filters on. The console gains a scan/manual label and a relative age per row, plus a source facet whose empty value means all, and a finding with no timestamp renders as an em dash rather than a date -- new Date(0) is a perfectly good date, which is exactly the problem. 3. A single finding reports with its evidence (a0e4122): GET /api/report/finding/{id} carries the same row the scan-wide export produces plus the request and response behind each evidence entry. Nothing new is stored. Three decisions, each the wrong answer first: JSON only (a second HTML renderer for one finding, and a SARIF rendering of a single result is a shape no tool consumes, is decoration not evidence); the scan-wide exports keep carrying no bytes (thousands of rows and their bodies would make the document unusable, and that constraint is why this path exists, so a test pins it); and ONE row builder extracted so the two exports cannot describe a finding differently, which the old inline comment records having already got wrong once. The zero-id bug this surfaced would have made the FIRST message's evidence vanish: request_msg_id had omitempty and these ids count from zero, so 0 is the first message the project ever captured. Explicit has_request/has_response flags now exist because a zero cannot say whether a message exists. A second honesty fix came from the same work: findingEvidence skipped an entire entry when the exchange could not resolve, so an evicted capture produced a report claiming the finding had been seen nowhere -- the convenience took the evidence with it. Unreadable bytes are counted in messages_omitted rather than dropped, because a report that silently omits half its evidence reads as 'there was no request', which is a claim about the target rather than about the capture. 31 tests across the three items, mutation-checked throughout. Verified live in headless Chromium on a ui-live.sh console: a task's pane shows none of three other-run findings and reads 'This task recorded no issues'; issue rows read 'scan just now', 'manual --' and 'scan 3h ago' with no 1970 anywhere and the Manual facet narrowing 9 items to 3; the single-finding document for a real finding carries 2 messages whose first is the actual captured request, while the scan-wide export carries none. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./internal/scanner + internal/web + internal/report green, tsc clean, bun test:lib 755/0, e2e-go.sh 24/24. One full-suite note: internal/blindxss's TestCaptureThroughRealBrowser timed out on its 15s browser-callback deadline in the run where eight packages competed for CPU; it passes at HEAD in a pristine worktree under the same eight-way load and twice in isolation, so it is a real-browser timing flake in an untouched package, not a regression.

title: scanner: the audit-queue parity table denies the light-audit pass the same package implemented
description:
QA PASS 2026-09-25 — the audit-queue's own parity table says a light-audit pass does not exist, in the same package that implemented it.

## The contradiction

`burpsy-go/internal/scanner/audit_items.go:145-151` — the table of Burp statuses this engine does not model — says, three times, that there is no light-active pass:

- `LIGHT_AUDITING` — *"there is no light-active pass: every admitted check runs its full probe set or is refused"*
- `LIGHT_AUDITED` — *"there is no light-active pass, so no item can finish having had only one"*
- `NOT_LIGHT_AUDITED` — *"there is no light-active pass to have been eligible for and skipped"*

`burpsy-go/internal/scanner/audit_engine.go:443` — *"lightAudit is the light-audit tier's per-run state (burpsy-react-ui-7bkj)"* — implements it, with the decision path at `:443-509`.

So the engine has a light tier, the parity table says it does not exist, and both live in `internal/scanner`. This is the third finding in this QA pass with the same shape: a bead closed on the mechanism, a stale claim left behind for the operator to read.

## Why it matters more than a stale comment

This table is the project's own **disclosure** of what it cannot do. Its whole purpose is to let a reader — or a reviewer comparing against Burp — see precisely which Burp behaviours are absent, so an absent capability is never discovered by surprise. A table that denies a capability the engine has is worse than no table: it makes every OTHER row in the table untrustworthy, because a reader who has just been wrong about light-auditing has no reason to believe the parameter-type or selection rows either.

## What the operator loses

- **Directly:** nothing yet — the engine is ahead of the disclosure.
- **Indirectly, and this is the real cost:** an operator reviewing the queue's parity panel concludes burpsy cannot do light audits and either does not configure them, or believes the light tier they selected is not happening. Both are wrong, and both change what they run against a live target.
- For a reviewer: `7bkj`'s close reason is contradicted by the file it claims to have completed.

## Fix

- Update the three rows against what the engine now does: `LIGHT_AUDITED` is reachable, `LIGHT_AUDITING` is a real transient, `NOT_LIGHT_AUDITED` is the repetitive-skip disposition. Each row's `Why` should name the actual behaviour, and a row that is now modelled belongs in the **modelled** list, not the not-modelled one.
- Then check every other row in the same table against the current engine — this pass found three stale rows in one table, which is enough to say the table was edited once and not re-audited.
- The audit-queue UI (`pages/auditqueue.tsx:79-119`) reduces the retained per-item evidence (Checks, Steps, Outcome, Breakers, point records, timestamps — all present in the API at `api_scanner_audit_items.go:133-150`) to six state totals, so even a corrected table has nothing to show. Burp's audit-item page exposes phase, requests, errors, insertion points scanned, and start/end time precisely so a partial audit can be diagnosed; the data is already retained, so surfacing it is a rendering change.
- A test that asserts the not-modelled list and the engine agree — for each row, that the named Burp status is genuinely unreachable. A stale row is then a failing test, not a comment someone has to re-read.
close_reason: BurpStatusesNotModelled said 'there is no light-active pass' three times while audit_engine.go had implemented one since 7bkj, both in internal/scanner. The three rows are now true, and the truth is narrower than either old sentence: the light tier IS here (auditRun.lightAudit counts CLEAN same-(kind, host) points across a run and, from the Nth, declines the rest of that type on that host), but what does not exist is a light PASS an item is dispatched into. So LIGHT_AUDITING has no window (an item is auditing and the tier takes a skip decision inside it), LIGHT_AUDITED has no state (a declined point is counted in the item's skipped total and the item still finishes in the ordinary audited state), and NOT_LIGHT_AUDITED describes no disposition (a point either runs or is declined for repetition, both visible on the item that raised it). SKIPPED_DUE_TO_REPETITIVE_BEHAVIOUR moves OUT of the not-modelled list entirely -- it claimed 'there is no repetitive-response detector' while the engine skips points as repetitive. It is the one row whose status genuinely changed, and the modelled count is derived (BurpAuditItemStatusCount - len(NotModelled)), so it rises from 6 to 7 with no arithmetic to keep in step. The table's doc comment now says what the engine DOES with the repetitive rule, so a reader who came for that row finds an explanation rather than an absence. Why this was worth more than a stale comment: the table is the project's own disclosure of what it cannot do, so that an absent capability is never discovered by surprise. A table that denies a capability the engine has is worse than no table -- a reader just wronged about light auditing has no reason to believe the rows about selection or parameter types either. That is why every other row was re-checked rather than the three patched. The table can no longer go stale quietly: four tests check it against the engine -- the doc comment's stated count must equal the row count (the prose is what a reader believes, and a count disagreeing with the rows beneath it is the same defect as a row disagreeing with the engine); every row must give a reason and a stub-length one fails; the three light rows must not claim the tier is absent; and the repetitive row must not be listed while the engine skips for it. The third item: the audit-queue page reduced the retained per-item evidence to six state totals. All of it was already on the wire -- the endpoint hands out scanner.AuditItem wholesale, carrying StepsPlanned, StepsDone, UnitsPlanned, Checks, the three point counts, PointKinds and both timestamps -- but AuditItemRow in the client declared almost none of it, so the page could not render what it was being sent. Those fields are declared now, and Progress / Points / Timing are columns, because a partial audit is diagnosed FROM THE TABLE: the question is which items stopped early and how far they got, which needs every row's number visible at once. Two distinctions the engine's comments insist on are kept and tested: a zero plan reads 'not planned' not 0% (StepsPlanned is zero for an item refused BEFORE planning, a different fact from a plan of length zero that ran), and the percentage is not clamped (a plan grows when a breaker opens, and a clamped 100% hides the denominator moving). Enumerated points and points dropped at the per-request ceiling stay two numbers. Verified live on a console from ui-live.sh with a queue holding one item stopped after 2 of 5 steps, one refused before planning and one complete: the rows read '2/5 steps (40%)' with '9 +3 at limit' points, 'not planned', and '8/8 steps (100%)'. 14 tests across both halves, mutation-checked: folding the empty plan into 0% fails 2, clamping to 100% fails the over-planned case. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./... green with the cache cleared, tsc clean, bun test:lib 748/0, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

title: proxy: upstream TLS is never verified and has no policy — an invalid certificate is indistinguishable from a good one
description:
QA PASS 2026-09-25 — the proxy never verifies upstream TLS certificates, and offers no policy: no verify toggle, no custom CA, no protocol/cipher bounds.

## What is hardcoded

`burpsy-go/internal/proxy/tls_dial.go:95-100` — every intercepted TLS leg opens with `alpn.Dialer{InsecureSkipVerify: true, ...}`. The file's own comment explains why client certificates are configured there; it says nothing about verification, because verification is simply off. `internal/alpn/alpn.go:136-185` — the production TLS config — carries only `ServerName`, `InsecureSkipVerify`, `NextProtos` and the client-cert callback: no root pool, no `MinVersion`/`CipherSuites`, no renegotiation policy, no `ClientSessionCache` control, no SNI-off switch.

## What Burp offers (settings/network/tls.html:60-85, 138-155)

- verify upstream TLS (on by default, per **Burp**);
- select allowed protocols and cipher suites;
- allow unsafe renegotiation;
- disable session resumption;
- supply a custom CA;
- disable Java SNI for misconfigured servers;
- client certificates (burpsy HAS this one — `ClientCerts` is wired on the same dialer).

## Why this is filed as a P2 gap, not a security finding

A MITM proxy that verifies the upstream certificate would break the common case of an operator intercepting a site with a certificate burpsy's CA is not related to — but the certificate is still VALID, and a correctly chained one should verify. The current setting makes an invalid, expired, or hostname-mismatched upstream certificate indistinguishable from a good one: burpsy will proxy to a server presenting a certificate for a different name, and the operator sees a normal-looking exchange. That is a real fidelity loss for a tool whose job is to show what is really on the wire.

It is not filed as a security vulnerability because skipping verification on an interception leg is a recognized, deliberate MITM behavior and burpsy's own setting defaults to verifying. The gap is that burpsy has **no way to turn verification on**, and so cannot match Burp's default or reproduce a target that only presents a valid chain.

## The operator loses

- A target presenting an invalid, expired, self-signed-without-the-private-CA, or hostname-mismatched certificate: burpsy cannot detect or refuse it. An operator comparing two builds of the same app cannot tell from burpsy whether the certificate changed.
- Any policy requirement to constrain TLS versions or ciphers, or to forbid renegotiation.
- A private CA the target's issuer is not in the system pool, other than the certificate burpsy itself minted.

## Fix

- One setting, matching Burp's: verify upstream TLS, defaulting to ON. The interception leg then verifies against the system pool, with an escape hatch (a custom CA, or the existing "do not verify" switch) for the self-signed targets every assessor meets.
- Carry `MinVersion`/`CipherSuites` and a renegotiation policy through the same `alpn.Dialer` the sender already uses, so the proxy and the sender cannot drift.
- The custom-CA field is the same client-cert store shape burpsy already persists; one more entry in the network settings bundle.
close_reason: Every intercepted TLS leg opened with InsecureSkipVerify: true and nothing anywhere could turn it off, so an operator comparing two builds of the same app could not tell from burpsy whether the certificate had changed -- a swapped, expired, self-signed or hostname-mismatched certificate was indistinguishable from a good one. Verification now defaults to ON (Burp's default, and the only safe reading of a field whose absence would mean accept anything), with two escape hatches replacing the unconditional skip: a custom CA bundle that keeps verification on while trusting one more issuer, and verify:false as the deliberate opt-out for a self-signed lab target. Both live in NetworkSettings, so the setting is live, persisted and API-edited and the SAME edit reaches the sender and the proxy; the sender's TLSVerify is the fallback for a sender built without network settings applied. alpn.Dialer gained RootCAs and MinVersion, which is where the two legs would otherwise have drifted. A protocol floor below TLS 1.0 is refused rather than clamped, and a CA bundle that will not parse is reported when it is configured rather than at a later handshake. Eleven existing tests drive self-signed origins and began failing; that is the change working, and the fix was a named permissiveTLS() helper so each test declares it needs an unverified origin instead of relying on a skip that no longer exists. Verified live through a real console against a real self-signed origin: REFUSED with verification on, 200 after the operator's own CA was added with verification still on, 200 with verification explicitly off, each set through the console's API -- before the change the first case returned 200 silently. Mutation-checked three ways: restoring the hardcoded skip, dropping the custom CA from the dialer, and replacing the attached policy at restore. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./... green, tsc clean, bun test:lib 711/0, check:tokens green, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

title: network: redirects do not replay Set-Cookie, DNS has no address-family preference, and SOCKS cannot carry an upstream HTTP proxy
description:
QA PASS 2026-09-25 — three network settings Burp has that burpsy either lacks or applies too narrowly, filed together because each is one dial-path change in the sender or upstream package.

These are capability gaps with honest current behaviour. None of them is a lie on screen: the sender's open-ended declaration, the platform-auth setting's own help, and the upstream rule editor each say what they cover. What is missing is Burp's coverage, and in two cases the missing coverage is what makes a configured setting stop working on part of the traffic.

## 1. Followed redirects do not replay Set-Cookie (P2)

**Burp:** settings/tools/repeater.html:143-145 — *"If you enable this setting, Burp resubmits any cookies set in the redirect response when it follows the redirection target."*

**burpsy:** `internal/sender/redirect.go` builds each hop from the previous request only; `grep -n 'Set-Cookie'` finds one occurrence and it is a comment. `internal/web/repeater_options.go:18-22` states the absence plainly: redirect hops do not replay cookies.

**The operator loses:** login, SSO and consent flows that set a cookie during a redirect. The redirect is followed, the cookie is not sent, the destination returns the login page, and Repeater shows a page that looks like an application failure rather than a missing cookie. This is the single most common shape of a redirect in an authenticated tool.

**Fix:** ingest Set-Cookie from each hop's response into the jar the next hop is built from, and add the option Burp exposes so an operator can turn replay off for a target that sets throwaway cookies.

## 2. No DNS address-family preference (P2)

**Burp:** settings/network/dns.html:49-65 — system default, **Prefer IPv4**, or **Prefer IPv6**, *"because routing restrictions may permit only one family."*

**burpsy:** `internal/sender/network.go` offers system versus named-resolver selection plus exact hostname overrides, and returns the resolver's addresses unfiltered (`:485-518`). Address ordering is entirely the system resolver's.

**The operator loses:** any engagement on a host reachable only over one family. A dual-stack target behind IPv4-only routing can resolve to an AAAA first, and burpsy dials the unreachable address; the operator has no setting that fixes it and must override the hostname one address at a time.

**Fix:** a resolution-order option that filters or prefers an address family after the resolver answers, applied in the same place the existing hostname overrides are. It is a filter over an existing answer set, not a resolver rewrite.

## 3. SOCKS is a per-destination kind, not a global carrier (P2)

**Burp:** settings/network/connections.html:177-199 — SOCKS is a **global TCP layer**: *"every outbound connection, including requests to upstream HTTP proxies, goes through the SOCKS proxy"*, with per-host bypasses and a remote-DNS choice.

**burpsy:** `internal/web/api_network_proxy.go:15-21` makes proxy KIND part of each destination rule, and `internal/upstream/upstream.go` first-match selection returns exactly one proxy per destination. There is no layer beneath an HTTP upstream proxy.

**The operator loses:** the common corporate shape — burpsy reaches the internet through an HTTP proxy, and that HTTP proxy is itself only reachable through a SOCKS hop. With a single-layer rule the operator must choose one and lose the other. Global SOCKS bypasses are likewise inexpressible.

**Fix:** a global SOCKS carrier applied beneath whichever upstream proxy (or direct dial) a destination rule selects, with the same bypass list the destination rules use. The layering is a dial concern, so it belongs in `internal/upstream` rather than in the rule editor's model.

## Why these three together

Each is a small, well-understood change in code that already has the surrounding concept (the open-ended declaration, the hostname override table, the upstream policy). Filed together because they share a test surface — one target that redirects and sets a cookie, one dual-stack resolution, one nested proxy — and because they are the settings half of a gap the transport pass found alongside the two P1s already filed.
notes: Parts: 1) burpsy-react-ui-6wq7 (redirect cookie replay, done). 2) DNS address-family preference. 3) global SOCKS carrier beneath an upstream HTTP proxy. This bead stays open for 2 and 3.
close_reason: Burp's SOCKS setting is a global TCP layer (settings/network/connections.html:177-199): every outbound connection, including requests to upstream HTTP proxies, goes through the SOCKS proxy, with per-host bypasses and a remote-DNS choice. burpsy's model makes proxy KIND part of each destination rule and the policy returns exactly one proxy per address, so there was no layer beneath an HTTP upstream proxy -- an operator had to choose one and lose the other. The layering is a dial concern rather than a rule-editor one: a rule answers which proxy carries this host and a carrier answers what opens the socket to reach that proxy. A carrier carries a DIRECT destination (Burp says every connection), a proxied one, and a SOCKS-rule one, and exempts its own authority host AND port so the hop cannot dial itself; a host-only exemption made the layer silently do nothing for a dev-box operator, which the tests now pin. net.Dialer has no overridable dial field, so a dialer 'carrying' a carrier silently ignores it -- which is why the carrier is a dial FUNCTION applied at the one seam every connection opens through. A live pass found the routing bug the whole unit suite missed: every dial site read the carrier, the panel reported it configured, and the connection still went out direct, because Proxy.DialContext's KindDirect arm opened a bare net.Dialer and an operator who sets a SOCKS layer with no HTTP proxy has a policy resolving everything to Direct. One line in that arm is the feature, and TestADirectPolicyStillCarries is the regression that names it. The carrier is one instance shared by the sender, the proxy listener and the console, carried on SenderConfig at construction because the transport's client captures it then. An HTTPS upstream proxy is NOT carried -- crypto/tls has no dialer field to replace -- and the server reports that in the carrier's limits so the panel says 'Not carried' rather than the setting looking complete. Persisted beside the policy in its own settings row, restored FATAL on refusal. Verified live through a real console: with a carrier configured the SOCKS hop saw the connection and the origin saw none. Mutation-checked three ways plus the Direct arm. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./... green with the test cache cleared, tsc clean, bun test:lib 715/0, check:tokens green, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

title: intruder: Copy other payload is refused outside Pitchfork, which is the combination attack Burp documents it for
description:
QA PASS 2026-09-25 — Copy other payload is refused outside Pitchfork, which is the one combination attack Burp documents it for.

## What Burp's control is for

tools/intruder/configure-attack/payload-types.html:709-722 — *Copy other payload* copies the current payload to another position, and Burp gives the motivating case explicitly: two parameters that must always match, **with the Cluster bomb attack type used to manipulate the other parameters**. That is the entire reason a "copy another position" generator exists: hold two fields identical while the attack varies everything else.

## What burpsy does

- `burpsy-go/internal/web/api_tools.go:1007-1012` refuses every attack kind except pitchfork, with the message `copy_other: only supported in pitchfork, where every position advances in lockstep; <kind> does not guarantee the two positions match on every request`.
- `burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:2426-2432` labels the option Pitchfork-only in the UI, so the capability is visibly absent rather than broken.

## What the operator loses

The password / password-confirmation case, and every other "these two must match, vary the rest" shape. Pitchfork is a strict subset: it varies the copied pair TOGETHER, not the rest of the attack independently. A combination attack over a form whose confirmation field must track the password cannot be expressed.

## Already-tracked correction

`burpsy-react-ui-2g13` is CLOSED. Its reason is candid that copy_other is "refused outside pitchfork with a named reason (cluster bomb's mixed-radix Fill cannot guarantee the two positions match every request without a larger engine change)". The refusal is real and named, so nothing is misreported — but the bead's own title lists the payload type as delivered, and the documented use case is the one refused. This is the same class as the 03z parallel-send finding: a bounded, honest subset shipped under a bead that reads as full delivery.

## Fix

- Implement Copy other for cluster bomb: the copied positions are filled from their source's processed set by ordinal while the varied positions run their own mixed-radix enumeration, so the two tracks are independent.
- The engine change the close reason names is real but smaller than "larger engine": cluster bomb's Fill already walks a mixed-radix counter, so the copied positions need to consume their source set by the same counter value rather than being excluded from the enumeration.
- If that lands later, the option's help text should name the refused case rather than saying "Pitchfork only", so an operator knows what they are missing.
close_reason: Burp's Copy other payload exists so two parameters can be held identical while the Cluster bomb varies the rest -- the password and its confirmation case Burp names explicitly. burpsy refused it outside pitchfork, and the refusal was correct: cluster bomb's mixed-radix Fill advances each position's set at a rate that depends on that position's place in the radix system, so a copy stepped by its own ordinal coincided with its source on some requests and diverged on the rest. The test added here measures it -- 60 of 75 requests mismatched, which is 'right most of the time', the worst possible disguise for a correctness bug. The fix is small and exact: Fill already decodes each position's digit as (i/weight_j) % len_j, so a copied position takes the SOURCE's digit at the same ordinal, with the weights computed once per Fill so twenty positions decode twenty digits rather than four hundred. The engine needed no change -- Slot already carries Set and Payload and engine.go reads setBytes[Set][Payload], so a copy is a slot naming its source's set with the source's own ordinal. Pitchfork takes the same path and stays exact for a different reason (one ordinal, not one per radix digit). Sniper and battering ram remain refused, and the message now says why -- they advance ONE set across every position, so 'another position's payload' has no per-position meaning to copy from; the old message blamed cluster bomb, which is no longer true and would have been a lie in the refusal itself. A copy naming a forward, self or out-of-range position is still refused rather than clamped, because a copy that silently resolved elsewhere produces requests whose two 'identical' fields differ. The UI hint no longer says 'Pitchfork only'. Mutation-checked: restoring the own-ordinal copy fails both copy tests. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./... green with the test cache cleared, tsc clean, bun test:lib 715/0, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

title: dashboard: a task's Issue activity, traffic and coverage panes show project-wide data, so a clean run reports other runs' findings
description:
QA PASS 2026-09-25 — a task's detail pane shows project-wide issues, traffic and coverage, so a finished run reports what it found and the operator cannot tell.

## What the pane claims and what it shows

`burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/pages/dashboard.tsx` renders, inside the detail pane of ONE task:
- **Issue activity** (`:1130-1174`) — `activityFindings` is `[...issuesDetailed.data.findings].sort(by id desc).slice(0, 20)` (`:1080-1094` region). That is the project's finding feed with the task discarded, sorted and capped. The tab sits beside a specific task and the heading says "Findings as they were raised" with no qualifying word.
- **Traffic sources** (`:1339`) and **Recent traffic** (`:1407`) — the project-wide task-window counters, not this task's.
- **Coverage** — the project's coverage roll-up.

The findings are attributed to tasks internally; the API projects by `task_id` (burpy-go/internal/web/api_capture.go:849-851) and the audit report carries per-task counts. The pane simply does not ask.

## Burp's shape

running-scans/results/index.html:39-62 — select a task, then its tabs: **Issues** *"Provides details of all security vulnerabilities that the task has found"*, **Logger** *"Provides a list of all HTTP traffic generated by the task"*, **Event log**. Every one is scoped to the selected task, and the Summary tab (running-scans/results/summary.html) is likewise that task's.

## Why this is filed as an honesty defect, not a feature gap

A finished task's pane is how an operator answers "what did that scan actually find?". Here it answers with whatever the last 20 project findings were — another scan's findings, a collaborator's, or a manual recording — with the task's name in the header. Two concrete failures:
1. **A clean task shows findings.** A scan that found nothing displays other tasks' findings under its own name.
2. **A busy task is under-reported.** With more than 20 project findings, older findings this task raised are dropped by the slice while newer ones it never raised are shown.

Either way the pane attributes work to the wrong run, which is the failure mode this project treats as worse than an absent panel.

## Already-tracked correction

`burpsy-react-ui-i18` is CLOSED and its reason describes a project-wide reverse-chronological feed with the finding id as the ordering key — which is what the code does. The gap is the task scoping; the close did not claim it and should have, because the audit the bead came from treated "Issue activity" as the task's issues tab.

## Fix

- Filter `activityFindings` by the selected task's id, and say so when the task has none ("This task recorded no issues") rather than falling back to the project feed. A task-scoped empty state is a fact; a project feed under a task's name is not.
- Scope Traffic sources / Recent traffic / Coverage to the task, or label them "Project-wide" where that is what they are — the honest option is available and costs a heading.
- The projection already exists server-side; this is a query parameter, not a new endpoint.
close_reason: A task's detail pane answers 'what did that scan actually find?', and it was answering with the last 20 project findings -- another scan's, a collaborator's, a manual recording -- with the task's name in the header. Burp scopes every one of these tabs to the selected task (running-scans/results/index.html:39-62). Two failure modes, bad in opposite directions: (1) a clean task shows findings, because a scan that found nothing displayed other runs' findings under its own name; (2) a busy task is under-reported, because past 20 project findings this task's own older ones were dropped by the slice while newer ones it never raised were shown. Either way the pane attributes work to the wrong run, which this project treats as worse than an absent panel. The data was already there and the console could not see it: api_capture.go sends task_id on every FindingDetail ('the run that produced this finding'), but types.attack.ts's FindingDetail did not declare it, so the pane could not have asked even if it wanted to. It is declared now, and the scoping lives in a tested module rather than a filter inline in the component -- a filter that returns its input unchanged looks exactly like one that scopes it, which is why this survived a close. Scoping happens BEFORE the 20-cap, and that ordering is the second failure mode's whole defence: capping first lets a busy neighbouring task consume the budget and push this task's older findings out of its own pane. The pane now also says how many it left out, because a cap that reads as a total is the same defect one level up. A finding with no task_id -- a manual recording, an imported collaborator result -- belongs to no run and is excluded from every task's pane; that is a real loss and the right one, since attributing an untracked finding to the scan the operator is looking at is the failure this fixes, and the Issues page still carries every finding including those. The other three panels in the same pane are labelled 'Project-wide' rather than scoped, the honest option this bead names, and it costs a heading. They cannot be scoped without server work that does not exist: Sources is a dashboard-level histogram with no task dimension (api_dashboard.go), CoverageSummary is {label,unit,work_unit,breakdown} with no task id, and ToolLogRow carries no task_id either -- so an Intruder payload's row in a crawl's pane is a misattribution the operator cannot see through. Labelling says what they are; per-task accounting is a different change and is not smuggled in here. Verified live on a console started by ui-live.sh with the project feed forced to hold three findings belonging to OTHER tasks: the pane shows none of them and reads 'This task recorded no issues -- Nothing was raised against this run. The Issues page carries every finding in the project, including the ones this task did not raise.' The previous bundle at HEAD has no such state, so the same fixture would have listed all three. 8 tests, mutation-checked both ways: removing the filter fails 4, capping before scoping fails 2 (the ordering test is the only defence of the ordering). go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./internal/web green, tsc clean, bun test:lib 738/0, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

title: settings: the export confirmation says three sections were affected and never shows the bundle's own eleven omissions
description:
QA PASS 2026-09-25 — a configuration export that carries 4 of 15 settings says "these 3 are affected", and the bundle's own coverage report is never shown.

## What is true

`burpsy-go/internal/web/api_config.go` is honest in the API: `configIncludedSections` holds 4 entries, `configOmittedSections` holds 11 (client_certificates, match_replace_rules, network_settings, platform_authentication, proxy_options, resource_pools, scanner_config, scheduled_tasks, tls_passthrough, upstream_proxy), and the bundle carries a `configCoverage{Partial, Included, Omitted}` that "travels inside the bundle so the file is self-describing". `Partial` is derived from `Omitted` so it cannot claim completeness while omissions exist. That is the right design.

## What the operator is told

`burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/app.tsx:1248-1252` — the success modal says, in full: **"Scope, intercept rules and session handling rules are affected."** It does not render the bundle's `omitted` list, does not say the export is partial, and does not mention `uninteresting_headers`, which IS included. An operator who exports a project to another burpsy, migrates, or keeps a configuration record is told their scope, intercept and session rules moved and nothing else was said either way.

## Why this is filed as a defect rather than a gap

The capability gap (which settings are in the bundle) is a deliberate, documented decision and is not what this bead is about. The defect is that **the honest answer already computed by the server is discarded at the UI**, so a partial transfer reads as a complete one. This project treats that as its worst outcome. The fix is small and does not require deciding what belongs in the bundle: render the returned `coverage.omitted` in the import/export confirmation, label the transfer partial when `partial` is true, and name the included sections from the response rather than from a hand-written sentence that has already drifted (it omits `uninteresting_headers`).
close_reason: api_config.go was honest and the UI discarded the answer. configIncludedSections holds 4 entries, configOmittedSections holds 10, and the bundle carries a configCoverage that travels inside the bundle so the file is self-describing, with Partial derived from Omitted so it cannot claim completeness while omissions exist. The modal said, in full, 'Scope, intercept rules and session handling rules are affected' -- three of the four carried sections, omitting uninteresting_headers which IS carried, and saying nothing about the ten settings the export never carried. An operator migrating a project or keeping a configuration record read a partial transfer as a complete one. Two defects, and the second is why the first was not merely untidy. The sentence was a hand-written list, and a hand-written list drifts -- it had already drifted from the server. The fix derives the applied sections from what the server reports applying, so there is nothing left to drift, including the section the old text got wrong in the OTHER direction (a bundle carrying only header lists was described as affecting scope, intercept and session rules while the one thing that moved went unmentioned). And the coverage is read out of the FILE, not the import response, because that split is deliberate on the server: 'a bundle's own account of what it carries is evidence about the file, not an instruction to the importer' (configBundle.Coverage's doc). The distinction the modal now turns on: a bundle with no coverage block has told us nothing about its coverage, which is NOT the same as having told us it carries everything. readBundleCoverage therefore returns undefined rather than {partial:false, omitted:[]}, and the modal says the file does not say what it can carry. A failed import leaves it undefined for the same reason -- nothing applied is a fact, coverage never read is an absence of information -- and collapsing those two is the bug this bead exists to fix, so it is collapsed nowhere. A hand-edited file with a non-string in omitted renders only the strings rather than showing '42' as a setting name. Verified live on both branches against a console started by ui-live.sh: importing a real export reports all 10 omitted settings by name, labels the transfer partial, and lists 'uninteresting headers' among the applied; importing a hand-written bundle with no coverage block gives the unknown-coverage wording, no invented omissions, and no claim of a known-partial transfer it cannot justify. 12 tests, mutation-checked both directions (collapsing unknown to empty fails one case; dropping uninteresting_headers fails two). go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./internal/web green, tsc clean, bun test:lib 730/0, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

title: intruder: character_blocks is not Burp's character frobber — the per-character incrementing generator is absent
description:
QA PASS 2026-09-25 — `2g13` closed "character blocks/frobber" as one generator. They are different generators, and the one Burp documents is absent.

## The two are not the same thing

`CharacterBlocks` (`burpsy-go/internal/intruder/payload.go`, the `type CharacterBlocks struct` block) cycles a fixed alphabet to fill repeated blocks of a chosen length — `MinLen`/`MaxLen`/`Step`, all about block LENGTH. Burp's **Character frobber** (tools/intruder/configure-attack/payload-types.html:590-595) *"modif[ies] the value of each character position of an input"* and increments one character at a time, so a token's characters can be walked through their values to find which one tracks session state.

A repeated-block generator cannot do that. It has no input value to increment; it only has an alphabet and a length range. The close reason's "character_blocks/frobber" naming is what made this look delivered.

## What an operator loses

Character-by-character mutation of a session token or a parameter is how you find which position an authorization check or a parser actually depends on. Without it the operator can only mutate the token wholesale.

## Fix

- A `character_frobber` source: for each position in a base value, emit the characters of an alphabet in order at that position with the rest held fixed. The base is the operator's current value, which is the mode's defining input and the reason it cannot be expressed as blocks.
- A per-position total the operator can see before launch, like every other generator's.
- Rename the existing type's UI label to "Character blocks" and stop calling it a frobber, so the two stop sharing a name in the close reasons as well as in the UI.
close_reason: Burp's Character frobber and burpsy's CharacterBlocks are two generators, and the close reason that named them together ('character blocks/frobber') is what made the absence look delivered. CharacterBlocks cycles an alphabet to fill repeated blocks of a chosen LENGTH -- alphabet, MinLen/MaxLen/Step, and no input value to vary. Burp's Character frobber 'modifies the value of each character position of an input' and increments one character at a time, and its input is the operator's CURRENT value. Character-by-character mutation of a session token is how an operator finds which position an authorization check or a parser depends on; without it the token can only be mutated wholesale, which cannot separate 'the signature covers all of it' from 'the signature covers the first ten characters'. Three decisions are named in the code. Position-major, so one position is walked across the whole alphabet before moving on and the first divergence from the valid token surfaces in the first few payloads. Characters rather than bytes, so a multi-byte character is one position -- the mutation that delegates the frobber to the blocks generator reports FIVE positions for the two-character base 'e-acute snowman' and splits the snowman in half, which is the conflation made concrete. And the base's own character is emitted first where the alphabet contains it, so an operator can tell whether a position matters; where the alphabet lacks that character, no payload is the base and none is manufactured, because claiming an unperturbed position that was perturbed is the same overclaim as a copy that matches most requests. An empty alphabet defaults to printable ASCII rather than refusing (that is what a token's characters are); an empty base is refused and names the base, because there is nothing to increment. The console label read 'Character blocks (frobber)' on a menu item that WAS the blocks generator; it now reads 'Character blocks' with 'Character frobber' as its own entry and its own fields. The two stale doc claims are corrected so the generators stop sharing a name in the close reasons as well as on screen. Mutation-checked both directions: delegating to the blocks generator fails 3 of 8 tests, and the character-major swap passes every test except the ordering assertion -- which is therefore the only defence of the order. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test ./internal/intruder + internal/web green, tsc clean, bun test:lib 715/0, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

title: intruder: auto-pause shipped the predicate and the wire field but has no control, so the capability is unreachable
description:
QA PASS 2026-09-25 — auto-pause has an engine and a wire field, and no control anywhere in the UI.

## What shipped and what did not

`burpsy-react-ui-8f2` is CLOSED with a reason that describes a complete mechanism: the `AutoPause` predicate, appears/missing mode, simple-vs-regex, case sensitivity, a 400 for an uncompilable expression, an in-flight response collected whole, an attack-level `auto_paused` counter, and the `intruderRunReq.auto_pause` wire field. Every claim about the *engine* is true. The close reason never says whether an operator can turn it on.

They cannot. `grep auto_pause burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx` → no match, and the launch body at `intruder.tsx:1523-1572` is built without the field. The Settings tab (`intruder.tsx:2788-2894`) has no auto-pause controls.

## Why this is worse than absent

An operator who knows the feature exists — the API takes it, the report counts it — has no way to use it, and the only way to halt a spray is the manual pause, which requires watching the attack. The bead's own acceptance criteria required the operator-facing controls (Enable auto-pause, appears/missing, expression list, Simple/Regex, Case-sensitive); the close reason verified only the predicate. A capability the operator cannot reach is the same gap as a capability that does not exist, and the close reason reads as though it were delivered.

## What a fix needs

- The four controls in the Settings tab, in the same draft-state shape as every other attack setting: an enable switch, an appears/missing radio, a textarea of expressions, a Simple/Regex radio, and a Case-sensitive switch.
- The launch body sends `auto_pause` only when enabled, for the same reason the other settings are omitted rather than sent empty: an absent field and an empty expression list must not be two wire shapes for "I did not choose".
- A round-trip test through `intruder-config-file.ts`, so a saved attack resumes with auto-pause configured rather than silently dropping it — the same failure fmxv's settings had.
- The uncompilable-expression refusal already exists server-side and should be surfaced as a field error, not a toast after launch.
close_reason: The auto-pause ENGINE shipped complete with 8f2 -- the predicate, appears/missing mode, simple-vs-regex, case sensitivity, a 400 for an uncompilable expression, an in-flight response collected whole, an attack-level auto_paused counter, and the auto_pause wire field. Every claim about the engine was true. The close reason never said whether an operator could turn it on, and they could not: grep auto_pause in intruder.tsx matched nothing and the launch body was built without the field, so the only way to halt a spray was the manual pause, which requires watching the attack. A capability an operator cannot reach is the same gap as one that does not exist, and the 8f2 reason reads as though it were delivered. This change is only the four controls that reach the engine. The block is sent only when the switch is on AND at least one expression is typed, the same omission rule every other optional field follows, because an absent field and an empty expression list must not be two wire shapes for 'I did not choose'. The server reads an empty list as unconfigured (NewAutoPause returns nil, nil), which is what makes the omission honest, and a test pins the two by running both and comparing. The switch decides only whether the block is SENT; the expressions and mode are the attack's own settings, so toggling off and on must find the list intact. An uncompilable expression is surfaced NEXT TO THE EXPRESSIONS rather than only as a toast: the server answers 400, and a toast after a launch that visibly did nothing is the wrong place when the operator's next action is to edit the expression. The re-homing is narrow on purpose -- only a 400 whose body names auto-pause or an expression, because every other 400 belongs to something else in the form. Five config-file tests now carry the block with NON-default values, since defaults survive almost any bug; the round-trip that failed is the one fmxv's settings had. Two notes learned from writing the tests wrong first: the missing-mode test originally used a reflecting target and expected a mid-run pause, which CANNOT work because Control.Pause blocks until resumed, so a mid-run fire leaves the handler waiting and the assertions never run -- it now fires on the last request. And the mode inversion is pinned by a PAIR, because either test alone passes against a server treating missing as always-true; the mutation check confirms it is caught. Verified live in headless Chromium: checkbox present, off by default, expressions hidden while off, all four controls appearing when enabled, mode offering exactly appears/missing, field reporting its count, plus a screenshot and zero axe-core violations in the enabled state. The only console errors are a missing proxy CA file and a crawler endpoint, neither touched here. go build/vet/gofmt clean, go test green, tsc clean, bun test:lib 715/0, e2e-go.sh 24/24.

title: repeater: the ws tab cannot send — its own ws:// target spelling is refused before the dial
description:
## Claim

burpsy-react-ui-6ex landed a WebSocket Repeater tab whose Target field is seeded with the
`ws://host:port` spelling ("ws://127.0.0.1:8080" is the literal default in
internal/web/ui/src/pages/repeater.tsx at HEAD). The send endpoint refuses that spelling
before it dials, so **every send from the ws tab fails** and the reply pane shows its idle
placeholder — which reads as "nothing happened" rather than "the send was refused".

## Evidence (measured at HEAD ec9ad84, in a detached worktree whose porcelain was clean)

    POST /api/repeater/ws-send {"target":"ws://127.0.0.1:1", ...}
      -> 400  unknown scheme "ws"

Cause: internal/web/api_repeater_ws.go's prepareWsSend hands req.Target to targetParts
(internal/web/api_types.go), which accepts only http/https/bare host:port:

    switch strings.ToLower(scheme) {
    case "https": tls = true
    case "http", "": tls = false
    default: return "", 0, false, fmt.Errorf("unknown scheme %q", scheme)
    }

The UI offers `ws://` (and `wss://` for TLS), the wire understands neither. My own live pass
hit this: four UI sends produced no tool-log row and no pane update until the target was
changed to a bare host:port, at which point the same tab sent fine and rendered the echo.

## Fix direction

Translate the ws spellings on the ONE path where ws:// is what the operator meant
(prepareWsSend), rather than widening targetParts — widening the shared helper would let an
HTTP send be given a ws:// target and silently dial plaintext. A `ws://` naming no host must
be refused, not guessed at ("unknown scheme" and "no host" are different facts).

## Acceptance criteria

A ws:// and a wss:// target both reach the dial (wss asks for TLS), a bare host:port still
works, `ws://` with no host is refused with a reason naming the target, and a test asserts
all four.
close_reason: ROOT CAUSE FOUND AND FIXED, measured at HEAD ec9ad84 in a detached worktree with clean porcelain: POST /api/repeater/ws-send {"target":"ws://127.0.0.1:1"} -> 400 unknown scheme "ws". prepareWsSend handed req.Target to targetParts, which accepts http/https/bare host:port only, while the ws tab's own Target field is seeded with ws://host:port (literal default "ws://127.0.0.1:8080" at HEAD). So every send from the ws tab was refused before the dial and the reply pane kept its idle placeholder, which read as "nothing happened". FIX: wsSchemeTarget translates ws:// / wss:// on the ws-send path only (widening the shared targetParts would let an HTTP send be given a ws:// target and silently dial plaintext); wss asks for TLS; "ws://" with no host is refused with a reason naming the target. Also restored Burp's DIRECTION CHOICE, which the landed work dropped (its code comment said "the direction choice is to-server here" with no control for it): the tab now offers To server / To client, and the wire's existing 400 + reason for to-client is surfaced in the reply pane (new `failure` prop) instead of being invisible. The HTTP response editor no longer renders under the ws panes (two panes answering different questions was what hid the bug). VERIFIED: two new Go tests, mutation-checked (removing the translation fails them with exactly unknown scheme "ws"/"wss"); live on a console built from the commit against a local echo origin — ws tab sent "live wire" and rendered "Reply 1 · text · 14 B  echo:live wire", To client showed the wire's refusal verbatim, switching back sent again and rendered "echo:direction probe". tsc clean, test:lib 710/0, gofmt clean. Commit 098017f.

title: tests: TestASkippedExchangeWhoseResponseLaterLandsIsAuditedOnceAsRetried races the next tick for the retry slot — ~40% flake
description:
## Claim

`TestASkippedExchangeWhoseResponseLaterLandsIsAuditedOnceAsRetried` (internal/web/liveaudit_retry_test.go:68) fails intermittently with "pending retry slot is empty: the give-up must file the id it skipped", measured 5/12 single-run failures at pristine HEAD in a detached worktree (1109eb1). Not related to any change under test — reproduced identically on a gofmt-only tree (1/12; same test, noise in the rate).

## Root cause (measured)

The test waits for `Skipped() != 0`, then immediately reads `pendingRetryID()` and requires `pending == true`. But the sweep is entitled to consume that slot on its very next tick: `takePendingRetry` (liveaudit.go:444-458) clears the slot "whether or not it landed" — the retry is ONCE by design (iyqg), and a tick 5ms after the give-up clears the slot before the test's read. The test observes a transient the product deliberately does not hold:

    give-up tick T0:   recordSkipped(1, id) -> skipped=1, pendingRetry=id+1
    test poll (≤5ms):  sees skipped==1, reads pendingRetryID()
    tick T0+5ms:       takePendingRetry -> pendingRetry=0 (response still nil)

The give-up loop's own condition is only `Skipped() == 0`, so the test can lose the race between the give-up and the next tick.

## Fix direction

Poll for the pair of facts the test actually depends on — skipped==1 AND the slot holding OUR id — within the existing 15s budget, and only then fail. Alternatively land the response before the give-up and assert the retry consumption instead of the slot's existence, which is the fact the rest of the test already waits on (`Retried() == 1`). The former is the smaller change; the latter removes the transient entirely.

## Do not

Do not widen `takePendingRetry`'s clearing rule or add any hold to the product state — the once-only retry is iyqg's contract and the flake is in the test's observation window, not the sweep.

Surfaced while landing dp8p (the liveaudit.go gofmt fix): the web package suite this test sits in must be green to trust that gate.
close_reason: Test-side fix, no product change. The flake was the test's: it polled Skipped() then read the pending-retry slot as if held, but takePendingRetry clears the slot on the first tick after the give-up whether or not the response landed (iyqg's once-only contract), so a background 5ms tick was entitled to empty it first - measured 5/12 failures at pristine HEAD, 1/12 on an unrelated tree. Rewritten to drive liveAuditTick by hand (the liveaudit_coverage_test.go pattern): the give-up is asserted tick by tick, the filed id is checked to be the test's own /late exchange, the response lands between two driven ticks, the next tick takes the retry (retried==1, slot cleared), and one more tick proves no third chance. The tick arithmetic is now explicit: tick 0 admits the two seeded exchanges before it first waits, so the give-up is the liveAuditStallTicks-th no-progress tick, the (ticks+1)-th in all. Measured in a worktree at HEAD with only this file changed: 0/40 failures in isolation (was 5/12), the retry family green, the whole internal/web package green (28.9s), gofmt and vet clean. Commit e0397a5.

title: scanner: the stored-XSS row misses /st/note while the fixture declares itself vulnerable there
description:
## Claim

The `internal/scanner` runtime coverage suite fails at HEAD: 159 of 160 rows demonstrated, missing `Cross-site scripting (stored)` at `/st/note?text=seed`.

## Evidence

Measured 2026-09-22 against HEAD 629740a, twice, in detached worktrees whose `git status --porcelain` was empty. `/tmp/verify-s9ma` at 9cd2424 and `/tmp/verify-7suo` at 629740a both reproduce it:

```
--- FAIL: .../rows/Cross-site_scripting_(stored)_via_/st/note?text=seed
    runtime_coverage_test.go:846: the target is vulnerable here (a note submitted here is inlined unescaped
    into a <script> literal by /st/notes on a later request) but "Cross-site scripting (stored)" was not reported.
    rows reported instead: ASP.NET debugging enabled, ... Input returned in response (stored), ...
    runtime detection: 159 distinct catalog rows demonstrated across 162 endpoints, 1 missed
```

Note what IS reported for that exchange: `Input returned in response (stored)` and `Suspicious input transformation (stored)`. So the stored family runs and the capture path works; it is specifically the XSS-stored row that does not fire.

## What is NOT yet established

Whether this is a detector regression or a fixture/environment artefact. Two candidates worth ruling out before touching a detector:

1. The deferred render phase. `vulnapp_stored.go:159` declares the case as `{Path: "/st/note?text=seed", Row: "Cross-site scripting (stored)", Stored: true, Note: "a note submitted here is inlined unescaped into a <script> literal by /st/notes on a later request"}`. The row depends on `/st/notes` being re-fetched by the deferred phase. Commit 0714504 ("run the stored-DOM deferred phase once, not once per endpoint") changed exactly that sequencing, taking the suite from 1115s to 478s. Check first whether the deferred phase still covers this endpoint after that change.
2. Headless-Chrome / DISPLAY. The project already knows autofocus and onfocus payloads never fire headless, and that `cmd/xsschallenge` refuses to score without a DISPLAY. This suite reported the other 159 rows, so Chrome is present, but the stored XSS row may still be the one needing a real window.

## Do not

Do NOT fix this by relaxing the pin to 159 or by marking the row skipped. The suite exists to prove detection; a pin lowered to match a regression is the exact defect this codebase treats as worse than the failure. If it turns out to be environmental, the honest outcome is a bead stating the precondition, not a lowered number.

## Fix direction

Bisect between 0714504 and HEAD on this one endpoint first. If the deferred phase lost coverage, restore it. If it is a detector regression, fix the detector and confirm the row returns WITHOUT changing any other row verdict.
notes: SCOPE FINDING 2026-09-22 (Main): this miss is being fixed by a peer in the uncommitted WIP at internal/vulnapp/vulnapp_stored.go, which rewrites storedRenderNotes from `var note = "<value>"` to a bare-expression assignment with a comment explaining that a quoted literal correctly contains the value, so a scanner refusing to call it a breakout is RIGHT and such a fixture cannot demonstrate stored XSS at all. Do NOT implement independently — coordinate with the owner of that file. Still binding: never lower the runtime-coverage pin to 159.
close_reason: Fixture bug, not a detector regression, and not the deferred phase or headless Chrome either. The old storedRenderNotes wrote the stored note inside a quoted JS string literal (var note = '<value>'), and jsBreakoutConfirmed is RIGHT to refuse that shape - a canary still enclosed by a literal did not break out (xss_jscontext.go:210), the exact anti-false-positive direction. A fixture whose canary can only ever be contained cannot demonstrate the row. Proven at the predicate level with a temporary in-package probe: jsBreakoutConfirmed=false for the old shape, true for the bare-expression shape (note = <value>). The fix is the fixture only: the render now assigns the stored note as its own expression (var note = 'sticky'; note = <value>), the shape an app concatenating user input into a script body actually produces. Measured in a worktree at HEAD with ONLY this file changed: go test ./internal/scanner/ -run TestTheScannerDetectsWhatTheTargetDeclaresItIsVulnerableTo now reports 160 distinct catalog rows demonstrated across 163 endpoints, 0 missed (was 159, 1 missed); wantDemonstrated stays 160 and no other row verdict changed (single-row and full-suite runs both green; /st/note row PASS in 4.29s). Commit 9a21f11.
