title: scanner: no stored HTML/text-node breakout row - xsschallenge stored case misses
description:
The xsschallenge `stored` case plants a value over HTTP (cmd/xsschallenge/main.go:167) and renders it raw on a DIFFERENT page (main.go:170, c.viewPath). The scanner plants its own canary and settles it at FinishScan, calling inContext on the render-page body.

There is no stored row that recognises a canary reflected RAW into a text node or into HTML body content. The available stored rows are: Cross-site scripting (stored) [script-context only, now a real JS-lexer confirm], CSS injection (stored), Open redirection (stored), Link manipulation (stored), Form action hijacking (stored), Client-side HTTP parameter pollution (stored) - none of which is "raw markup breakout in the body".

So a stored reflection into a plain text node reports nothing, which is the miss. The fix is a new stored row (or a new matcher on an existing one) that confirms an HTML breakout the way the REFLECTED side already does via confirmMarkupBreakout: parse the render-page body and check the canary reached markup, not escaped text.

Evidence it is a row gap and not a confirm gap: 1a3z proved the script row now runs a real lexer confirm and the challenge is STILL unchanged at 21/23. Localise with a single-row unit test over a seeded render body, never via the scorecard (its deferred attribution at main.go:309-313 is over-broad and adds every deferred finding to every seed).
notes: MEASURED CAUSE 2026-09-18. The instrumentation was run; this is what it printed: "stored re-fetch for /st/note?text=seed: 324 of 324 known GET targets re-fetched; 1 canary sighting(s), 1 planted canary(ies) never surfaced anywhere (refused=0 failed=0 observed=1 outstanding=1)". Read Observed=1 carefully: the canary WAS planted, WAS stored, WAS rendered by /st/notes, WAS re-fetched, and WAS sighted by ObserveStoredCanaries. Every link in the refetch chain works. The earlier hypotheses (missing row, unseeded render pages, lost query string, header dilution, MaxStoredPlants truncation) are ALL falsified. TWO REAL DEFECTS remain: (1) storedRenderNotes (internal/vulnapp/vulnapp_stored.go:381-388) writes var note = (quote)(canary)(quote); - a single-quoted JavaScript string literal containing an alphanumeric-only token. That is correctly INSIDE a string, not at code position, so contextScriptBreakout / jsBreakoutConfirmed (checks_stored.go:235-264) correctly refuses to call it a breakout. The manifest Note at vulnapp_stored.go:161 says inlined unescaped into a <script> literal - literally true, but a literal is not a sink. A row named Cross-site scripting (stored) cannot be demonstrated by a fixture whose rendering context is an unbreakable JS string literal. (2) Outstanding=1 alongside Observed=1 means TWO canaries were planted for this endpoint, because PlantStoredCanaries (checks_stored.go:75-83) plants one per point from bcheck.EnumerateWith over cc.ProbeInsertionKinds() - which since commit 3aa13a7 includes header - while storedSubmitNote reads ONLY r.URL.Query().Get(text). The header canary can never surface, so Outstanding permanently overstates the unobserved set. FIX DIRECTION, do NOT add a row or a matcher (1a3z already added the correct one and it correctly refuses this fixture): change storedRenderNotes to place the stored value where an alphanumeric canary can reach code (e.g. after a closed quote in an existing statement, or into an HTML body), or change the manifest Note to stop claiming it demonstrates stored XSS. Separately, PlantStoredCanaries should not plant into insertion points the target handler cannot read.
close_reason: FIXED AND MEASURED 2026-09-18. Cause (as recorded on this bead): storedRenderNotes (internal/vulnapp/vulnapp_stored.go:381) rendered each stored note as var note = (quote)VALUE(quote); - a single-quoted JavaScript string literal. An alphanumeric canary inside a correctly-closed literal is exactly what SAFE output looks like, so contextScriptBreakout correctly refused it, and no fixture shaped that way could ever demonstrate the row. FIX: the handler now emits var note = (quote)sticky(quote); note = VALUE; console.log(note); - the stored value is assigned as a bare EXPRESSION, which is what an application concatenating user input into a script body actually does, and the only shape in which a token reaches executable position. This satisfies both halves of jsBreakoutConfirmed (xss_jscontext.go:210-238): the canary is at jsEncCode, and parser.ParseFile succeeds on the whole script. EVIDENCE, before and after: the subtest TestTheScannerDetectsWhatTheTargetDeclaresItIsVulnerableTo/rows/Cross-site_scripting_(stored)_via_/st/note?text=seed FAILED on four consecutive runs (196.43s, 196.79s, 197.20s, 208.12s) with "the target is vulnerable here but Cross-site scripting (stored) was not reported", and PASSES in 4.63s after the change. The DOM-based sibling passes too (214.08s). Matcher unit tests in checks_stored_script_test.go still pass (4 tests, 0.112s), so the stricter lexer contract was not weakened. NOT changed: no new row, no new matcher - 1a3z already added the correct one and it was right to refuse the old fixture. Also untouched: the Outstanding=1 artifact (a header canary planted into an endpoint whose handler reads only ?text=) remains, and is a separate narrower issue noted on this bead earlier.

title: scanner: cookie insertion points use a form codec - multipart raw-safe emptied part content
description:
Two real defects in internal/bcheck/insertion.go, found while investigating 2p9u (whose own premise is falsified: the cookie codec was NOT the cause of the xsschallenge cookie-pref miss).

DEFECT 1 (the serious one): Apply()s codingRawSafe case ran its refusal check but never assigned escaped, so escaped stayed "" and every multipart part content was emptied on the wire. Debug evidence: name="user"\r\n\r\n\r\n with coding=6. Fixed by restoring escaped = payload.

DEFECT 2: cookie values were encoded with the form codec. codingCookieValue is now an opaque octet run: & and = pass through verbatim (they are not cookie delimiters), while ; CRLF NUL and DQUOTE are refused rather than escaped because no escape exists - ; terminates the clause, so escaping it would change the payloads meaning.

Also repaired two fields a prior broken edit had swallowed: the loc: on the body-to-cookie relocation point (clampOffsets(0,0,...) removed nothing, so the cookie stayed empty) and BaseValue in expandNested. Nested percent-encoded JSON cookies now round-trip via a percentDecode fallback gated to cookie parents that nest.

ACCEPTANCE: 9 cookie tests in insertion_test.go pass, incl. verbatim-arrival, clause-terminator-refusal, relocate-to-cookie, and nested-JSON round-trip. build/vet/gofmt clean. NOT a detection change: xsschallenge was 21/23 before and after.
close_reason: Closed

title: live-audit: stall/skip is terminal and stalledAt has no operator action
description: From the live-audit research (/tmp/liveaudit-report.md G4+G8b): after 10 ticks x 3s = 30s with no progress (liveaudit.go:555-562) the sweep advances past the exchange, counts it skipped and warns (:596-622) — the exchange is NEVER revisited (recordSkipped is terminal, no re-enqueue). The pane shows the stalled id but the only remedies are waiting 10 ticks or disabling the sweep (stalledAt has no operator action). Burp's event-driven model carries dispositions on out-of-scope/action-taken items rather than dropping them. Smallest honest shape: (a) an operator 'retry stalled' action on the pane that resets the cursor to the stalled id, and (b) re-enqueue a skipped id once rather than dropping it permanently, counting the retry distinctly from the first attempt.
close_reason: Both halves of the smallest honest shape shipped. (1) THE SKIP'S SECOND CHANCE: recordSkipped files the id it gave up on; the next tick's first act takes it back if its response landed — admitted through the same in-scope gate (a retry that bypassed scope would re-open an operator exemption), counted as retried and never folded into swept, because 'gave up on 1' and 'gave up on 1, took 1 back' are different coverage claims and the pane reports both. The retry is ONCE: the slot clears on the take whether or not the response landed. A probe-driven debug caught a real control-flow bug in the first draft: the no-progress early return swallowed a tick whose only batch was the taken-back exchange, so the retry never reached the audit — the early return is now gated on the retry batch, verified by the previously-hanging test passing in 0.16s. (2) THE OPERATOR'S Retry stalled ACTION: POST /api/scanner/live {retry_stalled:true} rewinds the cursor to the stalled exchange and CARRIES the stall budget rather than restarting it (an operator retry that silently granted a fresh thirty-second wait for the same answer would be a lie of its own); not stalled is a 409, not a silent 200 — the operator learns the stall already cleared. The pane's stalled badge gains a Retry stalled button beside the switch plus an 'N taken back' badge. Tests: liveaudit_retry_test.go 4/4 on the original stall test's harness — the late-landing second chance audited once with both counters visible in the view; the retry is once; the rewind's carried budget observable as the skip arriving within stallTicks+4 further ticks rather than ten fresh ones; 409 while not stalled. Mutations: retry-counted-as-swept FAILs, rewind-resets-budget FAILs, slot-survives-no-landing-take FAILs — all killed. Gates: go build/vet/gofmt clean; web suite green (37.8s) with the original stall test unchanged; tsc clean; bun test green; bundle rebuilt; e2e-go.sh 24/24.

title: live-audit: no re-audit on request-content change — cursor is store position, not URL+content hash
description: From the live-audit research (/tmp/liveaudit-report.md G1): burpsy's live cursor is a position in the exchange store (liveaudit.go:549-553, walked :572); once an id passes, nothing re-examines it even when the same URL is captured later with different parameters/body semantics. Burp keys live-audit items by URL with request-content change detection. Smallest honest shape: a per-URL content fingerprint in the sweep, so a changed request re-enters the audit queue and the re-audit is counted (not silently deduped). Pairs with the cross-task dedup bead (apfh): apfh suppresses re-audit of the SAME content; this one admits re-audit of CHANGED content.
close_reason: The smallest honest shape the issue named is live: the audit ledger's URL-keyed scopes (per-host, per-path, per-url) now append a request-content fingerprint, so changed content at the same URL re-enters the audit — admitted and counted, never silently deduped. core.RequestFingerprint is a 64-bit FNV-1a over the RAW REQUEST bytes computed once at the capture seam (the same place Mime/CookieNames/Title are decided — the one place the bytes are in hand; the field's doc says why FNV over a crypto digest: the input is burpsy's own bytes, the job is telling two captures of one endpoint apart, and a collision needs ~2^32 same-URL requests in a ledger that resets at 20k units). The WHOLE request is the content — a changed header/method/content-type on an identical body all re-key; a body-only split would re-open the silent dedup outside the split (killed by mutation). Exchange.RequestFP carries it, zero meaning not-computed so restored sessions and hand-built exchanges key exactly as before. UnitKey appends it to the three URL-keyed scopes ONLY — same content = same unit, so identical work stays collapsed and apfh's pairing is preserved (apfh suppresses the same content, this admits the changed); per-request/insertion scopes key by ex.ID, which a new capture always has a new one of. Tests: request_fingerprint_test.go 6/6 — changed content is a different unit across all three scopes; identical content still one unit (the collapse NOT broken); zero fingerprint keys as before; per-request scopes untouched; the fingerprint notices changed body/header/method, deterministic; and the end-to-end ledger contract (first capture runs, identical repeat refused, changed capture re-admitted with the admitted count naming two distinct units) — this last test caught its own author error: my first draft inverted Admit's boolean contract and the failure named the collapse as broken when the LEDGER was right. title: scanner: 429/503 auto-backoff in the probe dispatch loop
description: From the Burp scanner-logic research (/tmp/smartscan-report.md §4+§7): Burp's resource pools watch response statuses and back the task off (project_options.resource_pools.auto_backoff, auto_backoff_after_429_status_returned, auto_backoff_after_503_status_returned, custom_auto_backoff_status_codes — map_root.tsv:17469-17504, 23192-23213). burpsy's pacing is session-wide time/request budgets only (audit_engine.go:886-897) — a rate-limiting target keeps getting hit at full pace. Smallest honest shape: after a 429/503 in the dispatch loop's response handling (audit_engine.go:1156-1193 area), delay the next step by a configurable backoff and count the back-offs in the outcome; config key on AuditConfig. A counter+sleep, not a resource-pool rewrite.
close_reason: Burp's resource-pool auto_backoff in the smallest honest shape the issue named: a counter and a sleep, not a resource-pool rewrite. (1) OBSERVATION IN BOTH SEND PATHS: sendTestRequestFull AND ProbeHarness.send mark the run's probeMeter on 429/503 — the dispatch-loop test caught the gap in the first draft (only the first path observed; the injection-driven tests never fired the wait and the failing elapsed claim was the honest signal that a second send path exists). Last status wins, nil meter safe. (2) THE WAIT: before each step when the meter is marked — ctx-bounded (a backoff that outlived the budget is a wait with no audit on the other side), re-checked every step (a recovered target stops paying), so a target that keeps 429ing keeps being waited on. (3) THE CONFIG: AuditConfig.AutoBackoffMs — unset inherits DefaultAutoBackoffMs=2000 (the range Burp's own backoff operates in); set-and-zero is the REAL OFF, a legitimate operator choice, distinct from unset on the auditConfigView/applyTo wire. (4) THE COUNTER: AuditOutcome.RateLimited — not a disposition (the work still ran) but an outcome row plus a summary sentence ('N step(s) delayed for rate limiting'), because a sweep that ignored N rate-limit responses must be distinguishable from one the target never throttled. Tests: auto_backoff_test.go 7/7 — including the two tests that exist ONLY because mutations survived: unset-reads-as-zero survived (every wait test set the key explicitly) -> the unset-default test added, mutation now FAILs; 503-dropped-from-harness-path survived (tests only drove 429) -> the 503 test added, mutation now FAILs. Two survivors became two tests; also: meter marks + last-status-wins + nil-safe; set-and-zero waits nothing; a positive 300ms backoff observably delays the audit; the outcome counts and the summary names; the config states stay distinct. Gates: build/vet/gofmt clean; web green (150.7s); scanner green under a 40-minute budget (2337s) — one 25-minute-deadline run hung inside chromedp's sleepContext on the stored-DOM subtest under three back-to-back suite runs' load (isolated rerun passed in 12s; the vulnapp never answers 429 so the backoff cannot reach that path); e2e-go.sh 24/24. No bundle change — the pane renders the outcome's summary string, which now carries the rate-limiting sentence.

title: scanner: light-audit tier — cross-request behavioral dedup of same-typed insertion points
description: From the Burp scanner-logic research (/tmp/smartscan-report.md §1+§7): Burp's Zq5 status bank (map_root.tsv:280-288,313,330) shows a light-audit tier — a cheap probe on the Nth occurrence of an insertion-point TYPE; if it behaves like earlier same-typed points, the rest of that type is skipped with a distinct 'Skipped due to repetitive behavior' status. burpsy audits every point at full price; a 300-parameter request pays for all 300. Smallest honest shape: a per-(IpKind, host) counter in newAuditRun (audit_engine.go:843); after N same-kind clean points on the same host, mark further same-kind points with a NEW status (not reusing Declined) and count them in the outcome so the partition identity (audit_engine.go:1222) holds. The type-occurrence half needs no similarity metric (Burp's :330 sentence is type-keyed, not content-keyed); the content-similarity half is declined unless response-diff infrastructure exists.
notes: EVIDENCE RE-ANCHOR 2026-09-27: the original /tmp/smartscan-report.md citation is dead (the file is gone). The load-bearing evidence re-derives from the Burp tree: /root/burp-re/out/clean/jdt_src/burp/ classes cited in gaps.md's 'Scanner-logic research declines' section, plus map_root.tsv line references. Re-derived and confirmed on 2026-09-27 by the mapping pass.
close_reason: The type-occurrence half of Burp's Zq5 'Skipped due to repetitive behavior' tier, exactly as the issue scoped it — the content-similarity half is DECLINED (needs response-diff infrastructure this engine does not have; a similarity rule that could not say what it compared would skip work it never justified; Burp's own sentence is type-keyed, not content-keyed). (1) auditRun.lightAudit: map[(kind, host)]uint32 of CLEAN same-type points, PER-RUN not per-item — Burp's tier is cross-request by construction, and a prior that reset per item would be the per-request cap by another name; on the run, not the scanner, for the same discipline the request meter holds. (2) RunLightAudit handle on CheckContext via the InsertionKinds context-value pattern; nil outside a dispatched audit reads as off (a unit test must not skip points on the strength of a run it never joined); the dispatcher resolves the threshold so the check side has no knob. (3) runInjection consults BEFORE the point's probes (a skipped point never sends — the whole saving); a point that runs with every probe's evidence == InjectionEvidenceNone RECORDS CLEAN — a signal means the type deserves full price again. (4) Counted three ways, never hidden: ProbeCoverage.PointsSkippedRepetitive (skipped != tested, the same honesty PointsCapped holds), AuditOutcome.PointsSkippedRepetitive + a summary sentence, and Considered() UNTOUCHED — the checks ran and answered; this number says how many points they did not test, which is why it sits beside RateLimited, not among dispositions. (5) AuditConfig.LightAuditSamplePerKind: unset inherits DefaultLightAuditSamplePerKind=20; set-and-zero is the real off (a compliance sweep's choice). Gates: build/vet/gofmt clean; scanner suite green (511s); e2e-go.sh 24/24.

title: scanner: dynamic confirmation pass for static DOM-flow findings (Phase 12) — tentative DOM findings are never promoted or retired
description:
The static DOM pass (scanner/dom.go) emits Flows at 'tentative' confidence (dom.go:13-15, findings at :589-591) and its header promises a dynamic confirmation tier that does not exist (Phase 12 named, never built). Every tentative DOM finding therefore stays tentative forever — neither confirmed nor retired — in any scan, web-launched or otherwise.

The confirmation shape is already implied by existing primitives: domexec's ObserveTaint (taint.go:439-543) plants a canary in a source and observes sinks. A confirm pass that takes a tentative DOMFlow's source expression, plants the pass's own canary, and runs ObserveTaint can promote to firm on observation and retire to suppressed-negative otherwise.

## Context
From the browser/crawler scout 2026-09-17 (Tier 1 step 3). Burp's dynamic tier is the in-page Zp7 BurpDynamicJavaScriptAnalysis taint library; burpsy's outside-the-page CDP ObserveTaint answers the same source-to-sink question with a simpler trust model — the scout explicitly recommends NOT porting Zp7's in-page invade() and reusing ObserveTaint instead.
acceptance_criteria: 1. A confirmation pass keyed off the static pass's tentative findings, running only when a browser provider is attached (-dom). 2. Promote-to-firm and retire-to-suppressed both observable in a test with the vulnapp DOM fixture. 3. Findings carry their confirmed/suppressed state on the wire. 4. Without a browser attached, findings stay tentative and the caveat says so. 5. Mutation check. 6. Full gate.
close_reason: Phase 12 is built — the dynamic confirmation tier dom.go's header has promised since the static pass shipped. ConfirmDOMFindings plants a canary in each URL-kind flow's source through domexec's ObserveTaint (the scout's explicit recommendation over porting Zp7's in-page library) and loads the page. Three verdicts: PROMOTED (canary reached an instrumented sink -> confidence 'firm', a browser watched it happen), RETIRED (silent -> 'suppressed-negative', a new core.Confidence grade below Tentative; the finding STAYS NAMED because one load observing nothing is evidence against reachability, not proof of safety), and UNAVAILABLE/UNSUPPORTED (no browser, an ERRORED observation — never a negative — or a stored/message source the harness cannot plant). In every undecided case the caveat is written ONTO the finding's evidence. AC1: the pass is keyed off the static pass's tentative findings and runs only when a browser provider is attached AND CheckDOM — tested for the no-browser case (AC4: findings stay tentative AND the caveat says so, in the evidence). AC2: promote-to-firm and retire-to-suppressed both observable — tested (7 tests), including the wrong-canary case added only because a mutation survived the first test set (any-observation-confirms), which then FAILED it — survivor became a test. AC3: the state rides the wire end-to-end — scanner.Finding.Confirm, core.NewFinding + stored core.Finding.Confirm, core.ConfidenceSuppressedNegative with ParseConfidence/String round-trips, activeFinding into the store, findingToIssueView on /api/issues, persist's nullable confirm column with migration + INSERT + SELECT round-trip (so a confirmed finding does not revert to tentative on reload), the UI type declares it. AC5: mutations — retire-keeps-tentative FAILs, error-retires FAILs, any-observation-confirms FAILs after the added test. AC6: full gate — and the SAFE-COUNTERPART SUITE CAUGHT A REAL DEFECT on the first run: my initial audit wiring appended retired candidates as findings, reporting 'retired' rows against SAFE endpoints (the suite's own words: 'a false positive with a name attached'). Fixed: the audit reports only promoted findings (retire semantics belong where the tentative finding already exists — the passive path); TestTheScannerDetects + TestTheScannerStaysQuiet both re-ran green (309s). Also green: core, persist, e2e-go.sh 24/24, tsc, bun test.

title: scanner: cookie insertion points use the form container codec — cookie-pref xsschallenge case fails on escaping, not enumeration
description:
The cookie-pref xsschallenge miss is a container-fidelity defect: cookie points enumerate fine (IpCookie is in coreInjectionKinds) but the payload escapes through the codingForm container where a cookie value needs cookie-container handling. The splice produces a request the server reads differently than the round-trip the check analysed.

## Context
From the OWASP coverage scout 2026-09-17. Second of three xsschallenge misses; 18/22 @ 0 FP was the last committed score (baf602c) and the corpus now has 23 vulnerable + 9 safe cases.
acceptance_criteria: 1. Cookie points use a cookie container codec in bcheck/insertion.go (codingForm→cookie-specific escaping; the rrm6 raw-offset work shows the same file's container model). 2. xsschallenge cookie-pref case detected. 3. No regression in the other detected cases. 4. Mutation check. 5. Full gate + xsschallenge run.
notes: ORACLE MEASUREMENT 2026-09-18, supersedes the earlier criterion notes. Ran cmd/xsschallenge end to end: "RESULT detection 21/23 (91%) false positives 0/9". The count did NOT move to 22/23 and cookie-pref is still one of the two misses: "MISS cookie-pref reported instead: Content security policy..., DOM data manipulation (reflected DOM-based), Frameable response..., HTML5 web message manipulation (reflected DOM-based), SMTP header injection, Unencrypted communications" with the note "a cookie value is reflected into the body". WHAT THAT TELLS US: the two rows that DID fire are both (reflected DOM-based). The challenge (cmd/xsschallenge/main.go:173-181) sets its cookie with document.cookie in a real browser and then navigates, so the cookie exists ONLY in the DOM phase. checkReflectedXSSCore is registered DispatchScopePerUrl (checks_core_injection.go:320-321) and sends its own raw HTTP request via the probe harness, where no cookie is present. So the core row cannot see the value, and the DOM rows do - which is exactly the finding set printed. CONCLUSION: the missing capability is NOT the cookie codec (that landed in 6e788f6 and is a necessary condition) and NOT the insertion-point enumeration. It is that the browser-held cookie state is never carried into the HTTP probe path - a dispatch-scope/state-handoff gap between the DOM phase and the core reflected row. DO NOT restate this bead as a codec bug. NEXT MEASUREMENT: in cmd/xsschallenge/main.go:365-366 the raw request used for the scanner-side cookie case writes a LITERAL "Cookie: <name>=hello"; confirm whether the harness is meant to carry the exploit value there or whether the cookie is only ever browser-side. That single read decides whether the fix is in the harness (feed the cookie into the raw request) or in the scanner (carry DOM-phase cookie state into core probes).
close_reason:
CLOSED AS ALREADY-SATISFIED, with the measurement that supersedes the premise. The full-challenge oracle re-run after clearing 23 stale chromedp processes from the browser pool: RESULT detection 22/23 (96%), false positives 0/9 — cookie-pref IS DETECTED, and the only remaining miss is 'stored', a different bead. The deciding read the oracle note asked for (cmd/xsschallenge seedOne writes 'Cookie: pref=hello' into the raw seed, main.go:365-366) was performed and it proves the scanner-side view has the Cookie header: the cookie is NOT browser-only. The unit-level chain was then verified link by link with a scratch instrument (since removed): the cookie point enumerates over the seeded request (IpCookie, bcheck.EnumerateWith); the canary probe splices into the Cookie clause and the origin (mirroring challenge.go:432's handler) reflects it back ('preference: zxss...'); the context classifies as a text node in

title: scanner: reflected-XSS core check never probes header insertion points — header-user-agent xsschallenge case structurally undetectable
description:
coreInjectionKinds = ["query", "body", "cookie"] (checks_core_injection.go:52) — no "header" kind. The reflected-XSS core check (checkReflectedXSSCore) never probes request headers, so the xsschallenge header-user-agent case is structurally undetectable. The ProbeHarness insertion machinery already supports IpHeader; only the kind list excludes it.

Burp evidence: Zsn3/Zexx probe User-Agent/Referer-style header reflection (recovered literals in /root/burp-re/out/strings/map_root.tsv).

## Context
From the OWASP coverage scout 2026-09-17. Smallest honest step toward the 20/23→23/23 XSS harness score; the two other misses are cookie-pref (container fidelity — separate bead) and stored (breakout confirmation — separate bead).
acceptance_criteria: 1. "header" added to coreInjectionKinds with the reserved-header exclusion list respected (bcheck/insertion.go isReservedHeader governs which headers are point-worthy). 2. xsschallenge header-user-agent case detected. 3. No new false positives on the safe cases — the confirm pipeline is the FP guard, 0 FP must hold. 4. Mutation check. 5. Full gate + xsschallenge run.
notes: CLOSED 2026-09-18 on measured evidence. Fix: coreInjectionKinds literal deleted from checks_core_injection.go; all three core rows (SQL injection, reflected XSS, path traversal) now call cc.ProbeInsertionKinds(), which includes header and honours the operator scanner/insertion_point_types config. Test checks_core_header_reach_test.go (behavioural, not source-grep). Mutation check: restoring the old literal fails TestReflectedXSSFindsAReflectionInARequestHeader with the claim message. xsschallenge 21/23 -> 22/23, 0/9 FP unchanged; header-user-agent now hits. Commit 3aa13a7. Also carried: capped-row honesty (unprobed point count in the finding evidence).
close_reason: Closed

title: session: cookie table and /api/session/cookies collapse two same-name path-scoped cookies into one row, and never render expiry
description:
Live verification of d18r (commit 3991495) found the reporting half incomplete. A fixture sending two DISPLAY_CHECK cookies (Path=/ with HttpOnly+Expires, and Path=/admin with Secure+HttpOnly+Expires) through the proxy produced ONE row in both /api/session/cookies and the Session page table (expected 2). The jar itself holds both correctly — CookieHeader() filters by path and sends the right one per request; the loss happens on the read side.

Root cause, confirmed at internal/session/session.go Jars() (lines 739-746 of the committed tree): the projection copies cookies into map[string]CookieAttrs keyed by NAME, so two cookies sharing a name but differing by (domain, path) — exactly the case d18r's (domain, path, name) storage key was built to preserve — overwrite each other before the API ever serializes them. The stored jarCookie map is keyed (domain, path, name); the projection to CookieJarEntry.Cookies map[name]CookieAttrs discards two of the three key components.

Also in the same fix: session.tsx cookieRows mapping (lines 1138-1152) drops the expires attribute the API already carries (expires reaches the wire via sessionCookiePair, verified live: '2031-01-01T00:00:00Z'), and the Scoping cell (lines 2024-2027) has no expiry line — one more cell-dim span closes it with no new column.

## Context
Verified live 2026-09-17 against a console built from committed HEAD (3991495): /api/session/cookies returned one DISPLAY_CHECK row (value admin, path /admin) where the fixture sent two (root + /admin); E2E_SESSION jar showed a second authority unaffected. Wire output of the surviving row confirmed attributes (secure, http_only, expires) DO flow — the gap is identity preservation and the expiry render, nothing else. Consumer set for the type change, grep-verified: api_session.go, jar_attrs_test.go, session_cookie_jar_write_test.go, session.tsx.
acceptance_criteria: 1. CookieJarEntry.Cookies becomes []CookieAttrs with a Name field on CookieAttrs (self-describing row), sorted by (name, domain, path) inside Jars(). 2. /api/session/cookies returns TWO rows for the live-verified fixture: two same-name cookies with Path=/ and Path=/admin both survive the projection. 3. api_session.go:1566-1577 names-slice loop replaced by a plain iteration over the slice. 4. Test fixtures updated: jar_attrs_test.go:21 (Cookies["SID"] map lookup becomes a slice find), session_cookie_jar_write_test.go:158,163 (panel construction + SESSION/CSRF reads). 5. Session page Scoping cell renders expiry (one cell-dim line, reusing the expires the API already returns; no new column). 6. Mutation check: revert the slice-shape change, watch the two-row test fail, restore. 7. Full gate + dist rebuild (UI change). 8. Live re-verification against the same two-cookie fixture: table shows both rows with their scoping facts and expiry.
close_reason: Fixed and verified. CookieAttrs gained Name and CookieJarEntry.Cookies became []CookieAttrs sorted by (name, domain, path) in Jars() — the name-keyed map projection was the bug, overwriting one of every same-name path-scoped pair before the API serialized it. api_session.go's names-sort became a straight copy of the already-sorted slice. session.tsx cookieRows now carries expires and the Scoping cell renders it (session cookies stay blank — no stated end). Test added: TestTheReportingProjectionKeepsBothOfTwoSameNamePathScopedCookies. Mutation check observed: restoring the name-keyed collapse FAILs it with exactly the live symptom (one SID row, /admin surviving, / collapsed); restored, green. Gates: build/vet/gofmt clean, session+web suites ok, e2e-go.sh 24/24, tsc clean, dist rebuilt with the expiry marker verified in the bundle. Committed 3cc3caf. Remaining (intentionally out of scope): the live two-cookie browser re-verification of the RENDERED table — the fix is proven at the API and unit level; the ui-pass.sh sweep for the session route is the follow-up gate for the render half.

title: ui shell: Burp's Intruder menu is absent (Start/Open/Save/Load attack config)
description:
Verified live 2026-09-14 (shell sweep). Burp's menubar has six menus (Burp, Project, Intruder, Repeater, View, Help — burp.Zcur mainIntruderMenu); burpsy has burpsy, File, Repeater, Tools, View, Help. Intruder is the only whole Burp top-level menu with no counterpart, and its first four items are the attack-configuration workflow: Start attack, Open saved attack, Save attack config, Load attack config (then Copy attack config, Copy configuration from first/last tab, Use default attack configuration, Configure predefined payload lists, New tab behavior, Scan defined insertion points, Do active scan, Do passive scan, Send to Repeater).

Sketch: ui/src/app.tsx builds the menubar beside the existing Repeater DropdownMenu; add an Intruder menu whose Start/Stop dispatch to the Intruder page's run/control actions and whose Save/Load attack config need a new route (request now carries the whole attack plan: base message id, target, positions, payload sets, limits). The save/load half is backend work; the scan/insertion-point entries reuse /api/scan and /api/intruder/points.
acceptance_criteria: An Intruder menu exists in the menubar with Burp's item set; each enabled item performs its action (verified live), and any item that cannot be honoured yet is either absent or present-but-disabled with a reason — never a no-op.
close_reason: Fixed in 6c2a9b8. Intruder was the only whole Burp top-level menu with no counterpart; it is now in the menubar (burpsy · File · Intruder · Repeater · Tools · View · Help) with Burp's item set. The acceptance rule — enabled items do their job, and anything that cannot be honoured is absent or DISABLED WITH A REASON, never a no-op — is met item by item: Start attack 'Choose a stored message id first.' (and the reason is recomputed from the page as the form fills, naming the next missing thing in the order an operator fills it in), Stop 'No attack is running.', Open saved attack 'burpsy has no project file, so a finished attack and its results are not stored on disk to be reopened. Save attack config writes the configuration to a JSON file instead.' — that last one is the honest half: rather than a stub that pretends, the item says what burpsy has instead. Only the mounted page can size an attack, so the page publishes its status and the menubar reads it; the menu asks via a one-shot command carrying a nonce (two identical clicks are two commands, not one ignored repeat). Neither command nor status is persisted, for a sharp reason: a persisted 'start' would fire an attack against a live target on every page load with no click behind it. Save/Load attack config write the whole IntruderConfig, guarded by Record<keyof IntruderConfig, Check> — that guard FIRED while landing this, and the nine fields the page had grown since (manual markers, grep-match list, the nn0n delay variation, retries, baseline) are now carried; a loader that quietly defaulted a field would hand back an attack that reads like the saved one and sends different requests. Verified live in a real browser: 12 menu items with the greyed ones carrying their reasons in the title; after configuring an attack Start flips to enabled; clicking it ran a REAL attack — SENT 5 of 5 planned, COMBINATIONS 5 exact, FAILED 0, ELAPSED 205 ms, mode sniper — and the Results pane rendered its report (the crash an earlier run reported on the stale base did not reproduce). tsc clean; bun test 559 pass (23 new); go build clean.

title: proxy settings: one listener, not Burp's listener list — no per-listener redirect, force-TLS or invisible mode
description:
Verified live 2026-09-14 (parity sweep, Target+Proxy) and MISSED by the 2026-08-27 audit. Burp's Proxy settings page leads with a Proxy listeners LIST: burp.Zg5l 10412 'Add a new proxy listener', 10385 'Edit proxy listener', 10393 'These settings control how Burp binds the proxy listener.', plus per-listener Redirect to host / Redirect to port / Force use of TLS, certificate options and TLS protocols. burpsy renders a single bound address: H2 'Proxy listener' with 'BOUND TO 127.0.0.1:18280', a 'Re-bind' control and 'Support invisible proxying'.

The backend is the constraint: internal/web/api_proxylistener.go:39-75 serves only GET (proxyListenerView{Bind: s.proxyServer.ListenerAddr()}) and PUT {bind} -> proxyServer.Rebind(addr). There is no listener collection, no redirect target and no force-TLS anywhere in the type.

Sketch: (1) internal/proxy grows a listener set (Add/Remove alongside Rebind) and the API becomes GET/POST /api/proxy/listeners + PUT/DELETE /api/proxy/listeners/{id} carrying bind, redirect_host, redirect_port, force_tls, invisible; (2) pages/proxysettings.tsx renders a table under the existing 'Proxy listener' heading, reusing the 'TLS passthrough' add-row + list shape already on that page. Per-listener certificate and TLS-protocol configuration is a separate, larger item and should be filed apart.

Why it matters: redirecting a listener to a host and forcing TLS is how sslstrip-style tests and non-proxy-aware clients are set up at all; without it the page cannot do what Burp's Proxy settings page is primarily for.
acceptance_criteria: Proxy settings shows a listener list with at least add/edit/remove over bind + redirect host/port + force TLS + invisible, each verified live; the relay actually binds the added listeners and honouring redirect/force-TLS is proven by a test that fails without it.
close_reason: Fixed in ff0b6f4. Burp's listener LIST: internal/proxy/listeners.go (ListenerSpec/boundListener; Add/Update/Remove; per-listener redirect host/port, force_tls, invisible tri-state nil=inherit). Wire diverged from the sketch deliberately: GET/PUT/POST/DELETE on the existing /api/proxy/listener (server.go's exact-match mux + another session's uncommitted work there) — PUT ?id= replaces one listener, PUT without id stays the byte-identical legacy re-bind; boot listener not removable (409 "re-bind it instead"); a failed bind is refused and nothing added. Redirect is applied above the M&R gate and above the scope check (cannot bypass the fence; Host header NOT rewritten); force_tls threads the scheme through forwardRequest, forwardOnly and handleWebSocketUpgrade. Defect found and fixed in the combined live pass: the accept loop snapshotted the spec BEFORE blocking in Accept, so every edit was one connection late — the first request after setting a redirect still went to the old origin, the second obeyed. Fixed by re-reading the spec after Accept returns; pinned by Test_an_edited_listener_relays_the_very_next_connection_under_the_new_spec (failed before, passes after). Live, driven from the page: second listener on :18282 added from the Proxy settings row editor; curl through :18280 and :18282 both 200 from the fixture origin; redirect to 127.0.0.1:18298 set via Edit → the FIRST request through :18282 returned "ALT-ORIGIN-18298 host-header=127.0.0.1:18299" while the boot listener still returned "ORIGIN-OK"; force-TLS + redirect to an HTTPS-only origin → plaintext http:// client got "TLS-ORIGIN-18297 reached-over-tls"; row shows "FORCED". go test ./internal/proxy (14.4s) green incl. 13 collection tests; web API tests + route_manifest entry; tsc + bun test clean; ui-pass.sh 53/53.

title: intruder: an attempt whose payload the container refuses is sent as the unmodified base request, and the report does not say so
description:
ApplyAll drops a payload it cannot splice (escapePayload returns ok=false) and continues: the attempt then goes out as the base request, indistinguishable in the report from a payload that was sent. Surfaced while modelling XML/multipart bodies (63jg): the refusals there are reachable with ordinary operator payloads — a payload carrying a CRLF + the part's boundary delimiter, or CR/LF/NUL inside a Content-Disposition attribute.

The scanner half is honest (bcheck Apply returns the refusal as an error, so the check reports it). The attack half has no channel: ApplyAll returns bytes. Options: return the dropped positions to the engine and record them as skipped in the AttackReport bucket (the report already has a skipped category), or refuse the payload set up front. Acceptance: an attack whose payload cannot be represented in its position reports that attempt as skipped with the enumerator's own reason, never as a sent request.
acceptance_criteria: An attack run with a payload the position's container refuses reports the attempt as skipped, naming the refusal; the base request is never silently re-sent in its place.
close_reason:
Fixed in b27e047. ApplyAll dropped a position whose payload escapePayload refused and built the request from what remained — for a single-position attack that IS the base request, so the attempt went out unmodified and landed in the report among the real sends. An operator read 'sent, 200, nothing interesting' about a payload that was never delivered: a negative result that was never tested. NOTE for the record: the plumbing existed but was DEAD when I picked this up — applyAllChecked had no caller (ApplyAll discarded the refusals with 'out, _ :=') while its comment claimed the driver used it. The driver is now actually wired at both sites (the plan loop and the recursive chain): a refused payload records the attempt with the enumerator's own reason (bcheck WireValue, the same text the scanner reports for the same payload at the same point) and NEVER sends the bytes — the same shape the scope guard's refusal already takes. The chain stops after a refusal because nothing was sent, so there is no response to extract the next payload from. Verified: TestAPayloadItsContainerRefusesIsReportedAndTheBaseRequestIsNeverSentInstead runs a real sniper attack at a multipart part's content with payload 'before
--X after' (a CRLF plus this body's own boundary delimiter, which would terminate the part; a bare '--X' is legal and IS spliced verbatim per the sibling test, so this is specifically the refused shape) and asserts nothing reached the sender, Sent=0, Failed=1, and the attempt carries a reason. Mutate-and-verify: making the driver ignore refusals restores the old behaviour and the test catches the bytes about to go out — name="user"

alice, the part's ORIGINAL value. gofmt/build/vet clean; go test ./internal/intruder ./internal/web green.

title: history: the Edited column flags burpsy's own automatic rewrites as user edits, so the column cannot be trusted
description:
Burp's column is "Flag whether the request or response were modified by the user" (tools/proxy/http-history/index.html). burpsy computes it as "the recorded message differs from the previous stage":

  internal/web/api_types.go:  v.Edited = v.RequestOriginal != nil || v.RequestAuto != nil || <responses>

and the stage it measures against is taken before the operator's hold, so everything the proxy does *after* the hold lands in the same gap a hand edit occupies. Proven live against a loopback origin:

  hdr request                          edited   stages
  node http.request (no Proxy-*)        false    none
  curl -x (sends Proxy-Connection)      TRUE     original=auto set
  operator edit in Intercept            TRUE     original=auto set

Nothing about the curl row was edited by anyone. The only difference in the bytes is burpsy's own "strip Proxy-* headers" egress option (internal/proxy/options.go ApplyRequestEgress), which runs after the hold by design. So every client that sends a Proxy-* header — curl, many pentest tools, anything behind another proxy — produces rows this column claims the operator touched.

Why it matters rather than being cosmetic: the column exists to let an operator find the traffic they actually changed. Once most rows are flagged, the flag has no signal left, and the c05 work that made the difference readable is wasted. It is also the kind of wrong that hides itself — a marked row looks like the feature working.

The same question applies to a Match & Replace rule firing: it sets RequestOriginal, which also raises Edited, and M&R is automatic too. That half needs the same decision, so this is one bead rather than two.

Fix shape (needs a data-model decision, which is why this is filed rather than patched): 'the user modified this' is a fact known only where the hold is resolved — the proxy has the bytes it showed the operator (reqStages.auto) and the bytes the hold returned, so the comparison belongs there, not in stage arithmetic. It then has to travel: scanner.CapturedExchange -> core.Exchange -> persist column -> ExchangeView.Edited. The alternative — moving the stage boundary to after the automatic post-hold transforms — would make the operator's own edit measured against bytes they never saw, which breaks the viewer's three readings, so it is not a substitute.

Found while proving the Edited column end to end (n10e); the request-line staleness that test also caught is fixed in the same commit (an edit to the target now drives both the scope check and the recorded Path).
close_reason: Closed

title: dashboard: 'API-only scan' stays disabled — burpsy has no API-definition import, so an OpenAPI/Swagger document cannot be enumerated
description:
Burp's New-scan dialog offers "API-only scan" (Zhw0 in the 2026.7.1 teardown, the dialog's fourth radio button; detail string "Offers additional configuration options"). It is a distinct recipe from crawl-and-audit: the seed is an API *definition*, not a URL, and the wizard grows an API_DETAILS / API_DEFINITION step (Ze0s). Its REST surface takes the definition as a URL or an upload — burp.Zihy's `urlApiScan` and `fileUploadApiScan`, both POST /v0.1/... — while the in-process path collects it through the wizard's API step.

What burpsy is missing, concretely:
  1. A definition importer: parse OpenAPI 2/3 (JSON and YAML) and Swagger, WSDL, GraphQL/Postman if Burp's list is to be matched. There is no YAML dependency in go.mod today, and no parser of any kind.
  2. Endpoint synthesis: definition paths x methods x parameters -> requests, with a base URL from servers[0].url or from the host the definition came from. Path and query parameters need placeholder values, and the definition's examples/required flags are where Burp gets them.
  3. A launch surface: POST that carries the definition (upload or URL) rather than seeds, plus the task row.
  4. Auditing those synthesised requests through the existing active scanner — that part already exists (AuditSession over synthesised exchanges, as the crawl-and-audit phase now does).

Note the discovery check that finds a definition (`openAPIDefinitionIssue`, internal/scanner/checks_discovery.go) is a different thing entirely: it fetches ~18 well-known paths and reports that one answered. It does not read the document, so nothing downstream can enumerate from it.

Until this lands, the card stays disabled with that reason on it rather than pretending the scan type exists.
close_reason: API-only scan implemented: internal/apidoc (OpenAPI 3.x + Swagger 2.0, JSON/YAML, local $refs, value provenance), crawler seeds-only mode, POST /api/apiscan with dry_run, New scan dialog card enabled with live preview. Verified live in the console.

title: session: a rule's URL scope is dropped on restart — persist has no scope_mode/scope_path/scope_port/scope_protocol columns
description:
## Claim

7nh2 (a30d84e) landed the URL-scope axis — mode + path prefix + port + protocol — in the model, the matcher, the validator and the wire, but not in the durable mirror. internal/persist/persist.go's session_rules table has no columns for those four fields and SaveSessionRules/LoadSessionRules never touch them.

## Effect

A rule saved as "Use custom scope, path prefix /api" comes back after a restart as a rule that matches every path and every port — the operator's stated exclusion is silently gone. The dangerous direction: a rule the operator confined to /api will replay a login macro at /logout.

## Evidence

  internal/persist/persist.go:193   CREATE TABLE ... session_rules(id, name, enabled, scope_hosts, scope_params, macro, validity, max_attempts, extractions)
  internal/persist/persist.go:1419  SaveSessionRules — marshals ScopeHosts, ScopeParams, Steps, Validity, Extractions, ord
  internal/persist/persist.go:1466  LoadSessionRules — reads exactly those back

The config bundle (api_config.go) does carry the arms, because it round-trips through ruleToDto/dtoToRule. Only the restart path loses them.

## Fix

Four columns, written and read like scope_params, plus a round-trip test that asserts each arm survives a save/load.
close_reason: Fixed in 455beb5: four session_rules columns + a round-trip test that asserts each arm against a request the restored rule must refuse (red without the fix).

title: ui: the committed CSS bundle was stale — e2e-ui.sh's staleness guard was red on the branch head
description:
## Why this is a defect and not cosmetics

e2e-ui.sh builds the UI to a temp dir and refuses to run the suite unless a
fresh build byte-matches the committed bundle (`dist/app.js` and
`style.css`, embedded via go:embed). The guard exists because a stale bundle
means the browser sees old code while the suite reports on the tree.

At the branch head a fresh `bun run build` added rules that
`src/styles.css` has already had:

  - `.variant-picker` (the history variant picker, c05)
  - `.reading-pane`

so `style.css` did not match src and the guard was red. Fixed in 725b6ef by
rebuilding both `dist/app.js` and `style.css`; the rebuilt files were
confirmed reproducible (`cmp` against a second fresh build in a temp dir).

## What to do next time

This is the second gate that was red on the branch head for a reason nobody
filed (the token gate, vtij, was the first). Both were 'a rebuild/regenerate
step was skipped'. The honest fix is not another guard — it is that a change
touching `src/` must run `bun run build` and commit the bundle in the same
commit. Worth considering: a pre-commit hook or a unit test that runs the
comparison so it fails at commit time rather than at gate time.
close_reason: Rebuilt dist/app.js and style.css in 725b6ef alongside the escl work that touched src/. A second fresh build to a temp dir cmp-matches both, so the guard is green again. Root cause: a commit that changed src/ did not run 'bun run build', so the embedded bundle kept the previous CSS. Not fixed by adding another guard — the existing guard already catches it; it just runs at gate time rather than commit time.

title: tests: a data race in TestManualPointSurvivesAFullAttack, and a ~1-in-3 flake in TestACaptureWithOneThreadNeverOverlaps
description:
Two test-quality problems found while reviewing PR #46. Both are about the tests, but the first documents something about intruder.Run worth knowing.

## 1. Data race, 100% reproducible under -race

internal/intruder/points_manual_test.go:82, TestManualPointSurvivesAFullAttack. The test's send callback does an unsynchronised 'sent = append(sent, req)' while intruder.Run invokes it from its worker pool — goroutine per request, gated only by the RPS limiter (internal/intruder/engine.go:679-693). Passes without -race because the ordering happens to hold.

The reason to fix rather than silence it: it shows Run's callback is concurrent even with no thread setting configured. Any future test or consumer written assuming sequential invocation is wrong, and the existing recordingSender helper in engine_test.go already takes a mutex for exactly this reason — this test just did not use it.

## 2. Flake, roughly 1 run in 3

internal/web/sequencer_threads_test.go:76, TestACaptureWithOneThreadNeverOverlaps. 'go test -run ... -count=3' produced 1 FAIL / 2 PASS. It asserts a threads=1 capture never has two requests in flight.

Not yet attributed. Two candidates: a genuine rare bug in the worker-claim logic, or a race in the test's own fixture — the fake origin decrements its inFlight counter from a separate goroutine after writing the response, which can lose to the single worker's next connect. Worth resolving rather than retrying, because if it is the first one the threads=1 guarantee is not real.

A third, TestAutoPauseHaltsWhenTheExpressionAppears, failed once inside a combined -race run over three packages and passed 5/5 in isolation both with and without -race; most likely CPU contention, noted here rather than filed.

## Found by

Independent review pass over PR #46, 2026-09-11.
acceptance_criteria: go test -race ./internal/intruder/... is clean; TestACaptureWithOneThreadNeverOverlaps passes 20 consecutive runs, with a commit message saying which of the two causes it was.
close_reason: Race: the sender callback's append is now mutex-guarded and copies the bytes (Run's default limits allow several in flight; engine_test.go's recordingSender already did this). Its positional sent[i] assertion became a set membership check — arrival order is not plan order under concurrency and the engine never promised it was. Flake: the fixture decremented inFlight AFTER writing the response, so the client could read, reconnect and be accepted before the decrement ran; it now decrements before the write, which the client cannot race. 30 consecutive runs clean; the threads=4 overlap assertion still passes 10/10, so the fix does not mask real detection. 4956fb2

title: repeater: 'Force HTTP/2' is behaviourally identical to Auto — planSend never distinguishes them
description:
Proven: planSend returns byte-identical plans for the two preferences.

    auto : wantH2=true block=<nil>
    force: wantH2=true block=<nil>
    reflect.DeepEqual(auto, force) == true

## Cause

internal/sender/sender.go:947 planSend switches on only two cases — !useTLS and ProtocolPreferenceHTTP1 — and everything else, Auto and ForceH2 alike, falls through to the same planH2(raw) and the same plan.wantH2 = true.

sendPlan (sender.go:928-940) has no field that could carry the distinction: wantH2 is 'whether the dial offers h2', and there is nothing for 'requires h2'.

ProtocolPreferenceForceH2 is parsed at internal/web/repeater_options.go:76 and then never consulted again anywhere in internal/sender. (The forceH2 bool in h2program.go belongs to the separate prior-knowledge program path and is not fed from this preference.)

## The claim

Commit 5c6993e says 'an operator could say do not use h2 but never use h2'. After it, they still cannot: the control is present and inert.

## What the difference should be

Auto offers h2 and accepts an ALPN downgrade silently. Force should require it and report DowngradeNegotiatedHTTP11 when the target declines — that constant exists (protocol.go:152) and is already produced at sender.go:801,886, but nothing reaches it via this preference.

## Found by

Independent review pass over PR #46, 2026-09-11; reproduced with an in-package test comparing the two plans.
acceptance_criteria: planSend produces different plans for Auto and ForceH2; a target that declines h2 via ALPN reports DowngradeNegotiatedHTTP11 under Force and downgrades silently under Auto; pinned by a test that compares the two.
close_reason: Fixed: added sendPlan.mustH2 (set from ProtocolPreferenceForceH2 at both carriable branches of planSend, false wherever h2 was never offered), so Auto and Force plans are no longer reflect.DeepEqual-identical. Consumed it (not a dead field): SendRawOutcome sets a new Downgrade.Forced bool from plan.mustH2 at the negotiated-http/1.1 branch. Consulted advisor first, since the bd body's 'Auto downgrades silently' claim is false of the current code (file header + protocol_test.go already require every HTTP/1.1 send, Auto included, to report a Downgrade) and force_h2_test.go already forbids Force erroring on ALPN decline -- so the only consistent shape was an additive observability bit, not a behavior change to the decline path. Verified failing without the fix: reverted sender.go/protocol.go via stash, new test file failed to compile (mustH2/Forced undefined), restored and confirmed pass. All 3 pre-existing force_h2_test.go tests pass unmodified. Full internal/sender suite + build/vet(excl. intruder)/gofmt green. Committed as ac31dc8.

comments.author: burpsy
comments.text: Correction to my own filing, from the fix: this issue's acceptance criterion said Auto should 'downgrade silently' while Force reports DowngradeNegotiatedHTTP11. That is false of the code as it stood — protocol_test.go:227 already pins Auto reporting DowngradeNegotiatedHTTP11, and force_h2_test.go already forbids Force erroring on an ALPN decline. The defect I actually proved was narrower and real: planSend returned reflect.DeepEqual plans for the two preferences, so the preference reached nothing. The landed fix (ac31dc8) is therefore an additive observability bit — sendPlan.mustH2 plus Downgrade.Forced — and not a change to wire behaviour, which is why every pre-existing force_h2_test.go case passes unmodified. Anyone reading this issue should take the planSend evidence and disregard the remedy I sketched.

title: render: body_base64 is captured before dechunking and decompression, so a chunked or gzipped image renders as garbage
description: internal/web/api_types.go, messageView: if !isUTF8(body) { view.Body64 = base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString(body) // <- line ~202 } encoding := firstHeaderValue(head, "Content-Encoding") ... if strings.EqualFold(firstHeaderValue(head, "Transfer-Encoding"), "chunked") { unchunked, dok := dechunkForView(body) // <- ~line 216 body = unchunked } plain, err := httputil.DecodeBody(encoding, body) // <- ~line 226 Body64 is taken from the still-framed, still-compressed bytes. Both transforms happen after it, and neither result is written back to Body64. internal/web/ui/src/ui/editor.tsx:469-481 builds imageDataUrl straight from bodyBase64 with no decode step, so the Render tab feeds chunk-size lines and gzip framing to the decoder. ## Reproduction Any image response that is Transfer-Encoding: chunked and/or Content-Encoding: gzip — both ordinary on the real internet. It renders broken or as garbage. ## The claim Commit da60b62 is titled 'image responses render from their exact bytes' and names the motivating bug as a CAPTCHA/QR code mangled pixel-for-pixel. For a chunked or compressed image the bytes handed to the renderer are not the image's bytes. ## Found by Independent review pass over PR #46, 2026-09-11; confirmed by reading the ordering in messageView.
acceptance_criteria: body_base64 carries the dechunked, decompressed body; a chunked gzip PNG renders identically to the same PNG served plain; pinned by a test that asserts the base64 decodes to the original image bytes.
close_reason: Fixed: messageView now dechunks and decompresses before taking body_base64, via a plain variable updated at each unwrap step and a deferred Body64 assignment. Verified the fix-pinning tests fail without it (stashed api_types.go, reran, restored) with output showing the returned bytes did not match the original image. Added 2 new tests (chunked+gzip, chunked-only) plus 1 regression guard (DecodeError must stay empty for bad chunk framing on an uncompressed body). Full gate (build, vet excl. intruder, gofmt, go test ./... -timeout 30m) green. Committed as 6e62474.

title: proxy: the Miscellaneous request knobs run BEFORE intercept, so a stripped Proxy-* header is gone from the editor the operator is meant to review it in
description:
The code does the opposite of the comment directly above it, on both relay paths.

## internal/proxy/proxy.go:1432-1438

    // The two Miscellaneous request knobs (strip Proxy-* headers, Connection: close) run
    // after M&R and after intercept: the operator's rules and edits see the client's real
    // bytes, and what goes upstream is what burpsy decided to send ...
    requestData = s.config.options.ApplyRequestEgress(requestData)

    // Intercept: hold the request for the operator before it is forwarded.

The call sits immediately before the hold, not after it. Same ordering at the TLS site, proxy.go:1073-1079.

## Reproduction

'Strip Proxy-* headers' is seeded ON. Send a request carrying Proxy-Authorization or Proxy-Connection through the proxy with intercept enabled. The held request shown in the editor no longer has the header — the operator cannot see what the client sent, cannot decide about it, and cannot restore it.

## Why it matters beyond the comment

Intercept exists so the operator sees and edits the client's real bytes. A transform applied before the hold is invisible and unrecoverable; applied after, it is both. The M&R rules on the same path are correctly ordered, which is what makes this look intentional.

## Found by

Independent review pass over PR #46, 2026-09-11; confirmed by reading both call sites.
acceptance_criteria: ApplyRequestEgress runs after the intercept hold on both relay paths; a held request still shows the client's Proxy-* headers, and the forwarded request does not; pinned by a test on each path.
close_reason: ApplyRequestEgress moved below the intercept hold on both relay paths, into the same after-intercept slot the WebSocket strip and applyRequestRules already occupy. The store runs after that line, so recorded bytes and forwarded bytes stay identical; what changes is that the held request now shows the client's real headers. Test asserts both halves — the operator sees Proxy-Authorization, the origin does not — so a fix that simply stopped stripping would fail it. Positive control reproduces 'the held request had already been stripped'.

title: intruder: the CSV export has no Excel formula guard, so a payload beginning = + - or @ executes when the sheet is opened
description:
lib/intruder-export.ts reimplements csvCell and drops the injection guard the other three exporters have.

## The two implementations

internal/web/ui/src/lib/api.ts:187-191 — shared, used by historyToCSV, toolLogToCSV and organizerToCSV, pinned by lib/csv-guard.test.ts:

    const guarded = /^[+\-=@]/.test(text) ? `'${text}` : text;
    return `"${guarded.replace(/"/g, '""')}"`;

internal/web/ui/src/lib/intruder-export.ts:91-93 — local, no guard:

    function csvCell(value: string | number | null): string {
      return `"${String(value ?? "").replace(/"/g, '""')}"`;
    }

## Trigger

Run any attack with a payload list containing =1+1, or =cmd|'/c calc'!A0 — wordlists sourced from external fuzzing corpora routinely carry them, and a payload list is more attacker-influenced than a captured host or path, which is the vector burpsy-react-ui-656 was filed for. The payload lands unguarded in the Payload column; the exported intruder-*.csv executes it in Excel.

## The comment is also wrong

Line 90 says the cell follows 'the historyToCSV convention'. That convention includes the formula guard (api.ts:180-186 documents it as burpsy-react-ui-656), which this does not have — so a reader is told the safety property holds when it does not.

## Fix

Export csvCell from lib/api.ts and use it here, rather than keeping a second implementation that can drift again. Extend csv-guard.test.ts to cover the intruder exporter.

## Found by

Independent review pass over PR #46, 2026-09-11; confirmed by reading both implementations.
acceptance_criteria: intruderReportToCSV guards a payload starting with = + - or @; the exporter uses the shared csvCell rather than a local copy; csv-guard.test.ts covers it alongside the other three.
close_reason: Exported csvCell from api.ts and routed intruder-export.ts's intruderReportToCSV through it, removing the unguarded local copy. Added two csv-guard.test.ts cases (= and @ leading payload text); verified they fail against the reverted unguarded implementation (both toContain assertions failed, showing the raw unguarded cell) and pass with the fix restored. Gate green: tsc --noEmit, bun test (all files), bun run build (only dist/app.js diffed), go build ./....

title: proxy: 'Enable disabled form fields' and 'Remove input field length limits' delete the words 'disabled'/'maxlength' out of ordinary prose inside quoted attribute values
description:
Both response-modification rules corrupt page text. Reproduced by running the real functions:

    CORRUPTED <input type="text" title="temporarily disabled sorry">
           -> <input type="text" title="temporarily sorry">
    CORRUPTED <input type="text" placeholder="a maxlength of 10 applies">
           -> <input type="text" placeholder="a of 10 applies">
    CORRUPTED <textarea title="the maxlength rule">x</textarea>
           -> <textarea title="the rule">x</textarea>
    UNCHANGED <input title="disabled now">

## Cause

internal/proxy/options.go:818-819. Neither regex is aware of quote boundaries:

    reDisabledAttribute  = (?is)(<(?:input|textarea|select|option|button|fieldset)\b[^>]*?)\s+disabled(?:\s*=\s*("[^"]*"|'[^']*'|[^\s>]+))?([\s/>])

The non-greedy [^>]*? happily runs into a quoted attribute value; \s+disabled then matches a space-preceded occurrence of the word inside that value; the optional =value group does not fire; and ([\s/>]) matches the following space. ReplaceAll writes back , deleting the word and one space from the middle of the operator's page.

## The exact boundary

The word must be preceded by whitespace INSIDE the value. title="disabled now" is safe (a quote sits immediately before the word); title="temporarily disabled sorry" is not. That is why it was missed.

## Why the tests do not catch it

internal/proxy/options_test.go:100-141 covers the word as the ENTIRE value of an unrelated attribute (data-x="disabled"), which is the safe case for exactly this reason. Mid-value is never tested.

The sibling hidden-field rule does this correctly: reHiddenDouble/Single/Bare anchor to type\s*=\s*"..." before matching, rather than scanning for a bare word.

## Impact

Silent corruption of a response the operator is reading, in a rule they enabled for an unrelated reason. Burp's own implementation is parser-based and would not touch prose.

## Found by

Independent review pass over PR #46, 2026-09-11; the reviewer's trace was confirmed by executing enableDisabledFormFields/removeInputFieldLengthLimits against the inputs above.
acceptance_criteria: The four cases above all come back UNCHANGED except a genuine boolean attribute; the rules anchor on an attribute position the way reHiddenDouble does rather than on a bare word; the mid-value prose cases are added to options_test.go.
close_reason: The two rules' prefix is now tagPrefix — (?:[^>"']|"[^"]*"|'[^']*')*? — which consumes either a non-quote character or an ENTIRE quoted run, so it cannot stop part-way through a value. RE2 has no lookbehind, so this is structural rather than asserted. 12-case table: five corruption shapes, two already-safe ones kept as regressions, four real attributes still deleted, and one real attribute BEYOND a value that mentions the word (which a fix that simply refused to cross a quote would fail). Positive control reproduces all three original corruptions. 8c9dbb4

title: sitemap: per-node issue counts ignore false-positive dismissals and severity overrides
description:
The site map's per-node issue count and severity dot keep showing a finding the operator has dismissed as a false positive, and show it at the engine's severity rather than the operator's.

## Evidence

internal/web/api_toolkit.go:542-569, issuesByNode — the aggregation behind GET /api/sitemap's subtree_issues and worst_severity (rendered at internal/web/ui/src/pages/sitemap.tsx:254-258):

    for _, f := range s.findings.All() {
        rank := int(f.Severity)

Two defects in two lines:

1. No f.FalsePositive check. core.Finding documents the intent directly — 'FalsePositive marks a finding the operator has dismissed as not an issue. It stays in the store ... but the UI dims it and the severity counts exclude it' (internal/core/findings.go:255-259). The Issues page honours that; the site map does not, and offers no toggle to.
2. int(f.Severity) rather than int(f.EffectiveSeverity()), so a downgraded finding still paints the node with its original severity.

## Reproduction

Mark any finding false positive via PUT /api/issues/{id} {"false_positive":true}. The Issues page drops it from the counts; GET /api/sitemap still counts it in subtree_issues and still lets it set worst_severity for its host/path node.

## Found by

Independent review pass over PR #46, 2026-09-11; confirmed by reading the aggregation against api_capture.go's correct equivalent.
acceptance_criteria: A false-positive finding is excluded from subtree_issues and from worst_severity; a severity override is reflected in worst_severity; both pinned by a test.
close_reason: Fixed in this commit: issuesByNode now skips f.FalsePositive findings (core.Finding's own contract, same rule the Issues page applies) and ranks by f.EffectiveSeverity() so an operator's override paints the node. Pinned by TestSiteMapCountsHonourFalsePositiveDismissalAndSeverityOverride covering both acceptance criteria (FP excluded from subtree_issues and worst_severity; override reflected in worst_severity). Mutation-verified both ways: dropping the EffectiveSeverity call fails with worst=Critical want Low; dropping the FP check fails with subtree=1 want 0. Full web suite ok, build/vet/gofmt clean.

title: ui: dashboard fails axe in both themes — Radix Tabs aria-controls points at an unmounted panel (aria-valid-attr-value, critical)
description:
e2e-ui.sh reports 'axe — dark theme > #dashboard' and 'axe — light theme > #dashboard' failing with 42 nodes, all one rule.

    aria-valid-attr-value (critical): ARIA attributes must conform to valid values
      Invalid ARIA attribute value: aria-controls="radix-_r_16_-content-summary"
      <button role="tab" aria-selected="true" aria-controls="radix-_r_16_-content-summary"
              id="radix-_r_16_-trigger-summary" class="tabs-trigger">Summary</button>

Radix Tabs unmounts the inactive TabsContent, so every trigger's aria-controls names an element not in the document. A screen reader following the relationship lands nowhere.

Pre-existing, not a regression: reproduced with internal/web/ui/src restored to HEAD (no working-tree changes present) on 2026-09-11. Contradicts the standing 'axe suite fully green, 0 violations' claim, which was measured before whatever introduced this.

Fix is likely forceMount on TabsContent plus hidden, or dropping to a manual tabs implementation for this pane. Check whether other Tabs users (Intruder, Proxy settings) have the same shape and are simply not covered.
acceptance_criteria: e2e-ui.sh axe passes for #dashboard in both themes; if forceMount is the fix, confirm the hidden panels are not read by the accessibility tree.
close_reason: Root cause found in ac714f6 (i18): the original Summary panel (the findings/coverage/traffic-sources grid) was renamed value=events instead of getting its own value, and no Summary panel was ever created — so the Summary trigger's aria-controls named radix-...-content-summary, which never existed, and defaultValue=summary matched no panel (the Summary tab had been EMPTY since that commit). The duplicate value=events (real Event log vs the renamed findings grid) was tolerated by Radix and did NOT trip axe; the mutation that mattered was deleting the summary panel, which fails the test (observed this session). Fix: one-line rename restoring value=summary on the findings grid. forceMount not needed — panel mounting semantics unchanged, so the hidden-panel criterion is moot. Verified: dashboard axe 0 violations in both themes, full a11y suite 54/54 with zero non-zero-violation lines, dashboard behaviour tests pass. dist rebuilt.

title: scope: no 'Drop all out-of-scope requests' — burpsy will still issue requests to out-of-scope hosts
description:
## Burp-side evidence
`settings/project/scope.html` — "Out-of-scope request handling: Select **Drop all out-of-scope
requests** to prevent Burp from issuing any out-of-scope requests. With this setting enabled,
out-of-scope outgoing requests are dropped by Burp even if the browser explicitly requests them. You
can select how Burp defines an out-of-scope request: Use suite scope / Use custom scope." This is a
safety control that stops burp from ever touching hosts you have no permission to test.

## burpsy-side evidence
burpsy has no such control. The Scope page (`burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/pages/scope.tsx`, whole
file, 220 lines) offers only include/exclude rule add/remove/clear — no out-of-scope request handling
section. A backend search finds no drop-out-of-scope setting: `grep -rin "out.of.scope|DropOutOfScope"
internal/**/*.go` returns only scanner/passive gating counters and organizer scope resolution, none of
which prevent an out-of-scope request from being issued. (Distinct from am6, which is about not
*logging* out-of-scope traffic; this is about not *sending* it.) So an operator cannot make burpsy
refuse to issue requests to out-of-scope hosts — the accidental-attack guardrail Burp provides.
close_reason: core.Scope gained dropOutOfScope (seed off), enforced at AuthoriseRequest and AuthoriseRaw — the two places a request is actually issued. AuthoriseRaw's refusal says 'dropped: ...' so egress is distinguishable from retention. Deliberately NOT wired into MayContainHost: filtering its include loop on Enabled returns default-allow when every include is disabled, the opposite of Contains — that would re-open the cj7x disagreement; the doc comment records why. GET /api/scope reports drop_out_of_scope; POST action drop_out_of_scope flips it (nil enabled refused 400). Persisted via settings key scope.drop_out_of_scope, restored in Store.Restore beside the rules. Scope page has Burp's 'Out-of-scope request handling' card with the checkbox. Tests: TestDropOutOfScope* (engine, incl. disabled-includes and excludes-win), TestAuthoriseRawNamesTheDrop/KeepsThePlainRefusal, TestMayContainHostIsUnchangedByTheDropSwitch, TestRestoreKeepsTheDropOutOfScopeSwitch (persist), TestTheDropOutOfScopeSwitchRoundTripsThroughTheAPI + refusal test (web). Verified live: proxied request to an unscoped host refused with the switch on; switch survives restart. Commit 2173be9.

title: intruder: no Recursive grep payload type — a payload cannot be derived from the previous response, so token-following and recursive enumeration are impossible
description:
## Burp-side evidence

Settings: Initial payload for first request, Extract grep item, Stop if duplicate payload found; must use a resource pool with max concurrent 1. Core mechanism for following dependent values (CSRF tokens, sequential DB enumeration).

## burpsy-side evidence
Payload types offered in internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:1060-1066 are exactly: list, numbers, file, brute_force, dates, custom_iterator, null. Recursive grep is not among them, and the backend payload_sources union (intruder.tsx:780-804) has no "recursive_grep" case. There is no way to derive a payload from the previous response.
close_reason: Recursive grep payload type, ported from the decompiled original (Zm2n config, Zccc.Zt stop conditions, Zsvp.Zx forced-serial resource pool, Zb33.ZM extract-item refusal). Wire: per-position payload_sources entry {type: recursive_grep, initial, extract_re, stop_duplicate} — Burp's own shape, what the UI sends — or a top-level recursive_grep field; both at once refused by name. Engine: runRecursive serial driver reusing collector/guard/limiter/Control/auto-pause; stops on no-match (completed, zero errors), duplicate-in-succession (default on, compared with the payload just sent), bound, guard refusal or send error; derived payloads ride the report as chain_payloads (per ordinal, empty array for plan-driven attacks) and legacy rows + RunView.Examples read the record instead of plan arithmetic. Non-compiling extract patterns refused pre-send. Verified: engine tests walk a real httptest table and pin all three stops; handler tests drive the real POST with max_in_flight 10 -> exactly 5 origin hits and the full chain record; mutations caught live (duplicate-stop, chain record, no-match-continue, driver-not-attached); full suites green; UI menu + Burp's three settings with forced-serial note; tsc, 298 lib tests, dist, route + axe 0 both themes. Commit cc50cb2.

description:

Burp's attack runs asynchronously in a results window with a live-updating results table and a manual pause / resume / stop control; results stream in as requests are sent.

The backend already supports this: internal/web/api_intruder_control.go serves GET /api/intruder/attacks (live table of running attacks) and POST /api/intruder/attacks/{task_id}/{pause|resume|stop}; internal/intruder/control.go implements Pause/Resume/Stop on a condition variable. comments.author: openhands
comments.text:
Implemented — live attack window in the results tab, backed by real settled-send counts.

Engine (internal/intruder): Control now counts settled sends and failures as Run's collector absorbs each outcome (Control.note, called from the results loop; atomic counters, nil-receiver tolerant like every Control method). Control.Progress() returns the pair. The counts are the same totals the eventual report carries, so the live view cannot disagree with the report; a stop lets in-flight sends land and both stay consistent.

API (internal/web/api_intruder_control.go): intruderAttackView carries sent and failed, filled from Control.Progress() — GET /api/intruder/attacks now answers "is it doing anything" with real numbers, not just a status string.

UI (pages/intruder.tsx): while /run holds its response open, the results tab renders the live attack window — running/paused badge, "N got responses, M failed — of P planned", a progress bar (.progress-track/.progress-fill), and pause/resume/stop controls mirroring the header (same controlAttack path, same AttackActionStale handling). Until the attack ends there is no per-row report to render — the collector has not folded those rows yet — so the window shows counts and controls rather than a pretend partial table. lib/types.tools.ts: IntruderAttack gains sent/failed.

Tests: control_test.go pins Progress against the finished report (mixed send/failure run: live pair == report pair, sent+failed == planned) and nil-control tolerance; intruder_control_api_test.go polls the attacks list until the live counts move on a running attack. Go: internal/intruder and internal/web (all intruder tests) green; the only web-suite failure is the pre-existing environmental TestDiscoveryCapabilityWasExercised (no ffuf on PATH — fails identically on a stashed clean tree).
