Fixed: strip '}' only when the token carries an unclosed '{' before it. Mutation-checked - reverting the fix fails TestTheSpeculativePhaseFindsTheStraightQuotedRoutes with exactly that string.

JSLUICE NOT ADDED, and the reason is worth keeping in the record: jsluice's go.mod requires github.com/smacker/go-tree-sitter, which is CGO bindings to a C parser. This tree verifies 'CGO_ENABLED=0 go build ./...' as clean (docs/HANDOFF-2026-08-13.md:191) and ships a single static binary with no C toolchain requirement. Whether burpsy becomes cgo-dependent is a release decision, not a coding one, so I measured what exists instead of reaching for the dependency.

WHAT ALREADY WORKS, which makes the gap narrower than the bead assumes: the speculative phase reads script BODIES (discover.go:167-170), so quoted route literals, path-valued constants and comment-borne URLs reach the frontier through the same gates as every other link. The bundle's own filename is correctly not extracted.

WHAT IS STILL MISSING, recorded as tests that assert the misses so the day one closes it says so: a CONCATENATED path (fetch(BASE + n) where BASE is never a complete literal - the case that decides whether cgo is warranted), a TEMPLATE-LITERAL path assembled at runtime, and the SOURCE MAP (//# sourceMappingURL is visible in the body but not extracted, because the phase mines root-shaped tokens and this is scheme-relative; criterion 2 needs a deliberate fetch, which would be the only new request this bead introduces).

Criteria 1 and 2 are NOT met and are not claimed. Criterion 3 (passive, no new requests) is preserved. What landed is the bug fix plus the baseline measurement the next change is measured against.

Separately, and with some irony: this very commit swept four internal/web files in from a stale index - the exact failure recorded in d70004a and 32af2d9, which I had written up minutes earlier. Caught it because the summary said 6 files where I added 2, reverted in 47e5895, and verified.
CRITERION 2 LANDED in 95268c1, after 7dd8a5e fixed the /orders/{id} bug. Still partial overall.

WHAT LANDED: a script's //# sourceMappingURL is read and the map is FETCHED through perform() — the same path every other request takes — so it is scope-authorised, rate-limited, captured and counted. Report.SourceMapsFetched reports it, because a .map is a build artifact rather than a page and would otherwise be invisible in the location counts. Criterion 3 (passive: no requests beyond the map) is preserved and asserted: one test names every request the pass made and fails on any path beyond the page's own and the map.

THE CONSTRAINT THAT SHAPED IT, and it is not obvious: an EXTERNAL script src is a subresource the crawler never fetches (discover.go:24), so a map named by one is unreachable without fetching the bundle first, which criterion 3 forbids. What is reachable is a script whose body the crawl already holds — an inline script, and an external bundle already captured as live traffic. So the reference is read from the script TEXT.

A BUG THAT FALLS OUT OF THAT, worth recording because the tests are how it was found: the reference was read from the element's own Data, which is empty for an element — a script's text is in its CHILD nodes, and a minified bundle with an inline map parses into several text nodes. scriptBody concatenates them. It is a separate walk from nodeText on purpose: nodeText deliberately EXCLUDES script contents (discover.go:554), which is right for a link label and exactly wrong here. Reverting to n.Data fails two named tests.

STILL NOT DONE, and the reason is a judgement rather than an oversight: the map's sources array is not turned into locations. "/src/routes/dashboard.ts" is a FILE PATH, not a URL, and admitting it would flood the frontier with TypeScript filenames that 404. The fetch happens and is counted; the paths inside sourcesContent are not yet mined. That is the remaining piece of this bead.

Criterion 1 is still not met in full either: quoted route literals and path-valued constants already reach the frontier through the speculative phase (t5m0), and the /orders/{id} truncation is fixed, but a CONCATENATED path (fetch(BASE + n)) and a TEMPLATE-LITERAL path are still not recoverable from source text alone. Those are the cases that would decide whether cgo is warranted, and they are recorded as tests that assert the misses so the day one closes it says so.

TOOLING NOTE for whoever works here next: the shell used for heredoc commands in this environment injects a `__omp_shell(...)` wrapper into Go string literals. It silently corrupted a test fixture and cost two rounds of debugging. Writing Go test fixtures with the write tool instead of a shell heredoc avoids it, and a fixture that fails to say what it says is worth suspecting before the code under it is.
MINING LANDED in ee599ca. The bead's three criteria are now all met as far as is achievable without cgo; this is the honest final state.

CRITERION 1 (JavaScript parsed for endpoints) is met for every shape that source text can carry: quoted route literals and path-valued constants reach the frontier through the speculative phase (t5m0), and the /orders/{id} truncation that broke every templated SPA route is fixed (7dd8a5e). The cases still NOT recoverable from text alone are a CONCATENATED path (fetch(BASE + n)) and a TEMPLATE-LITERAL path (fetch(`/api/${id}`)) — the value is computed at runtime, and no string reader recovers it. Those remain recorded in js_extract_baseline_test.go as tests that assert the miss and t.Skipf the day one closes, because that is what decides whether a parser is warranted. That is a cgo decision (jsluice pulls smacker/go-tree-sitter), and it belongs to the operator, not to a session.

CRITERION 2 (source maps) is now complete in both halves. 95268c1 fetched the map through perform() so the request is scope-authorised, rate-limited and captured like any other. ee599ca reads the map's sourcesContent back through the store's spans and admits the URL-shaped paths inside it through the SAME speculative gates as a comment or a script body. A route that exists ONLY inside the map is now crawled end to end.

THE DESIGN DECISION THAT MATTERS, and it is the reason this was not a five-minute change: a map's `sources` array is NEVER read. It is a file list — /src/routes/dashboard.ts is a build-tree path, not a URL — so admitting it would flood the frontier with filenames that 404. Only sourcesContent (the original human-written source) is read, and only its URL-shaped strings are admitted. A test asserts a .ts path is never requested.

TWO BUGS THE TESTS CAUGHT, recorded because both point at the wrong file when you hit them:

  - The map's fetch row is NOT the last row. mineSourceMapBody runs inside visit() before the page's own row is appended, and the map's row commonly lands at index 0. The lookup is by URL. Related trap worth knowing: a TrafficStore assigns exchange ids from 0, so ExchangeID == 0 is a REAL id and cannot be used as a "not found" sentinel. A test asserting a non-zero id here would have been wrong.
  - The body came back empty on a body that is plainly valid JSON. The FIXTURE was wrong, not the extractor: source text containing a quote or a newline cannot be pasted into a JSON string literal by hand, so the fixture marshals through encoding/json. The symptom — an extractor correct in isolation and empty in situ — sends you to the wrong file every time.

MUTATION AUDIT, reported as measured rather than as hoped: six mutations, four killed (sourcesContent→sources, mine-and-discard, admit-every-token, admit-as-ordinary-link). TWO SURVIVED and I am not going to pretend otherwise: the positional-row mutant and the map-URL-base mutant. Neither is distinguishable by any reachable fixture — in every state a crawl can reach, the positional lookup and the URL lookup coincide, and the map-URL base differs only for a cross-host map whose result the scope gate refuses anyway. The CODE is correct in both cases (position is not a valid lookup; a path inside a map is relative to the page that named it), so both stay with the reason recorded in the commit message and in the comments. Deleting correct code to make a mutation table tidy is the same honest-counting defect this bead exists to end.

A GUARD I ADDED AND THEN DELETED: if content == "" { return }. It survived mutation testing because speculativeURLFields("") already returns no candidates — it was not load-bearing. Removed, with a comment saying why, because a guard that only looks careful is one that rots.

Status: open pending the cgo decision. Everything reachable without it is landed; the remaining scope is one decision and, if the answer is yes, a parser behind the extraction seam js_extract_baseline_test.go already pins.
close_reason: Done 2026-10-05 per operator decision (union, after online research). CGO-free jsluice: github.com/Mzack9999/jsluice (the fork Katana merged in #1570, on the pure-Go tree-sitter runtime github.com/odvcencio/gotreesitter, all MIT) pinned via replace in go.mod; verified CGO_ENABLED=0 static build, output identical to the original cgo jsluice on a probe. Measured on the same sample: jsluice alone missed template-literal paths, burpsy's miner alone missed call methods and import() chunks -> UNION. internal/crawler/jsextract.go: extractJavaScript (jsluice AST pass + speculativeURLFields, panic-recovered, normalised: EXPR/${} placeholders cut to the last whole segment, dangling ?x= queries dropped, bare tokens refused), LooksLikeJavaScript. New sibling gate consumeJavaScript (before the not-HTML skip) reads external bundles, admits candidates through admit() tagged js:jsluice:<type>/js:mined (method carried in link text, never sent), follows the bundle's own source map, bounded by MaxParseBytes; Report.javascript_read/_locations_found/_parse_failures/_truncated; new phase 13-javascript. ALSO FIXED: <script src> was never followed at all, so external bundles were never fetched — now admitted as tag 'script' (kept out of the location fingerprint). Tests: jsextract_test.go incl. acceptance TestAPathOnlyAnExternalBundleNamesIsCrawled (path only in bundle crawled; bundle source map followed; route only in original sources crawled). Full crawler + web suites green. Cost: binary 41.6 -> 58.7 MB stripped (gotreesitter grammar registry). Follow-up: crawler coverage benchmark vs Katana filed (P2). NOT committed.

title: sender: no pre-request script — cannot refresh a JWT or recompute a signature before a request goes out
description:
## Claim

burpsy cannot run a script that mutates an outgoing request just before it is sent. It has a JavaScript engine and a pre-request rule tree, but neither is wired to rewrite the request on the wire, so the common auth-flow chores — refresh an expired JWT, recompute a request signature/HMAC, stamp a nonce or timestamp — cannot be automated and are done by hand in Repeater. This is Burp's Montoya pre-request handling and Caido's pre-request scripts.

## Evidence

burpsy:
- A JS engine exists but is not used for requests: internal/jsexec/jsexec.go is a "DOM-less JavaScript execution tier built on goja," used for the scanner's JS analysis, not for request scripting (its own header says what it is NOT).
- A pre-request rule tree exists but does not run scripts: internal/session/actions.go defines an `Action`/`ActionKind` tree; the closest to a hook is `ActionInvokeExtension`, which "hands the request and the last response to a loaded plugin" (actions.go:74-76). So automation before a request means writing a whole plugin, not a short script.
- No first-class pre-request script: `grep -rliE 'pre.?request|prerequest|before.?send|request.?script'` finds only repeater_options.go, api_session.go, intruder/payload.go and sender/network.go — none of which is a user script that rewrites the outgoing request.

External precedent: Caido and Burp both offer pre-request scripting to capture a token from a login response and inject it into later requests, which 2026 API-pentest guidance calls out as needed for multi-step authenticated flows (practical-devsecops, getastra). This is the companion capability noted in the access-control bead (burpsy-react-ui-cr37): authorization testing across a multi-step flow needs a fresh token per identity.

## Fix direction

A pre-request script hook that runs a short goja script (reuse internal/jsexec) with the outgoing request exposed as a mutable object (method, path, headers, body) and read access to the last response and a small persistent store for a captured token. Attach it at the Repeater tab, a session rule, and/or a scope, run it in the send path (internal/sender), and let it rewrite the request before it goes out. Sandbox it as jsexec already is: no network, no filesystem.

## Why it matters

Every API with signed requests or short-lived tokens is painful in burpsy today: each resend needs the operator to recompute the signature or paste a fresh JWT. A pre-request script does it once and applies to every send, and it is the missing piece that makes the access-control tool (cr37) usable against real multi-step auth.
acceptance_criteria: A short goja script attached to a Repeater tab / session rule / scope runs in the send path with the outgoing request as a mutable object, read access to the last response and a small token store, and can rewrite method/path/headers/body before send; sandboxed with no network or filesystem.
notes: 2026-10-05 backend done. Pre-request scripts as a session-rule action: new ActionRunScript (wire run_script, label 'Run a pre-request script'), Action.Script, mapped through the web DTO both ways. Session rules give scope + tool targeting (Repeater/Intruder/scanner/...) + persistence, so 'attach to session rule / scope' is met; a Repeater-tab-only attachment is not separate (a rule scoped to tool=repeater covers it). Runner: internal/jsexec/request_script.go RunRequestScript on the package's existing run() sandbox (fresh VM, hard interrupt, no host bindings) — request mutable, response frozen (STRICT mode program, so writes throw; sloppy mode silently ignored them — caught by test), per-rule store persisted across requests in Coordinator.scriptStores (bounded 64 entries/64KB), capped log(), pure helpers burpsy.hmacSha256Hex/Base64, sha256Hex, base64Encode/UrlEncode/Decode, randomHex. 500ms limit, 64KB source cap. Compiled at AddRule (syntax error -> 400). On throw/timeout/broken request the request is left UNCHANGED (no half-applied signature) and the trace says why; walk continues. Tests: jsexec/request_script_test.go (6), session/actions_script_test.go (3), web/session_script_api_test.go. Editor UI queued to frontend agent.
close_reason: Done: run_script session-rule action (sandboxed goja, strict mode, frozen response, per-rule store, pure crypto helpers, 500ms/64KB bounds, compiled at install, failure leaves the request unchanged). Editor textarea + reference; live: a bad script refused on its action card, fixed script saved. UI completed and driven live 2026-10-05 by the frontend-ux agent (tsc clean, bun test src/lib 802 pass, build ok, Go reachability tests ok). Full Go module build+vet+tests green. NOT committed.

title: history/intruder: no custom-extractor column — the extractor and the column model exist but never meet
description:
## Claim

burpsy has both halves of "custom extractor as a table column" but they are not connected: it can extract a value from a response (regex with a capture group, JSON path, or whole), and its history table has user-configurable columns — but there is no user-defined extractor whose output shows up as a derived column in the history or Intruder result tables. This is Caido Automate's custom-extractor feature, and it is a small gap, not a from-scratch one.

## Evidence

burpsy:
- The extraction primitive exists: internal/web/api_session.go defines `extractHowSpec` and `extractHow` — a regex with a capture group, a JSON path, or "whole" (api_session.go:37,84-133). The sequencer has its own extractor too (api_sequencer_capture.go:124-129 `extract`).
- The column machinery exists: internal/web/ui/src/pages/history.tsx uses `Column` and `VisibilityState` from ui/table, a column-visibility menu (ui/column-visibility-menu), and per-column filters (burpsy-react-ui-8sa, history.tsx:116+).
- What is missing: nothing lets an operator define an extractor and have its captured value rendered as a column across the rows. The two systems never meet.

External precedent: Caido's June 2026 release (v0.57.0) added custom extractors in Automate — "extract response sections and view them as a custom column in the result tables by adding an extractor and defining a regex with a capture group" (caido.io 2026-06-05 release notes).

## Fix direction

Let an operator define one or more named extractors (reuse `extractHowSpec`: regex+group / JSON path) and register each as a derived column in the history table and the Intruder result table. Each row runs the extractor against its stored response and shows the captured value; the value is filterable and sortable like any other column. No new extraction engine — this is a binding from the existing extractor to the existing column model.

## Why it matters

Reading one field out of every response — a CSRF token, a user id, a version string, a rate-limit header — is a constant manual chore today: open each response and look. A derived column turns that into one glance across the whole table, and burpsy already owns both pieces it needs.
acceptance_criteria: An operator defines a named extractor (regex+group or JSON path) and it appears as a derived column in the history and Intruder result tables; each row shows the value captured from its stored response, and the column is filterable and sortable.
close_reason: Extractor columns: GET/PUT /api/history/extractors (persisted), POST /api/history/extract; History UI columns+manager+client-side filters

title: dom: no DOM Invader — a tester browsing a page cannot set a canary, watch or spoof its postMessages, or scan for prototype-pollution gadgets; DOM testing is only what a scan decides to run
description:
## Claim

Burp loads DOM Invader into its own browser: a Manifest V3 extension with a DevTools panel, driven by the tester while they browse. They set a canary, and it reports every source that carried the canary and every sink it reached, frame by frame. It logs, intercepts, replays and origin-spoofs postMessages, and can inject the canary into them. It scans for prototype-pollution sources and gadgets, tests for DOM clobbering, and can block or break on client-side redirects. Burp's own scanner sends testers to it: "We recommend using DOM Invader ... to confirm this vulnerability and scan for gadgets." burpsy has no operator-side counterpart. Its DOM testing is all scanner-side (domexec). That tier matches Burp's scanner-side dynamic JS analysis, not DOM Invader. It runs only when a scan chooses to, on a canary the operator never sees, in a Chrome that refuses extensions.

## Evidence

Burp:
- Launch path: out/readable/root/Zi9a.java:57 passes `--load-extension=`. The list comes from Zugr.ZT (failed to decompile), whose names are only in the string map: out/strings/map_merged.tsv:30169 `resources/Browser/DomInvader` and :30171 `dom-invader`. So DOM Invader exists only inside the pre-wired browser (see burpsy-react-ui-bufa).
- in/extract/resources/Browser/DomInvader/manifest.json:3-4 names "DOM Invader" at version 2.0.10. :6-32 registers content scripts at `document_start` in all frames: MAIN-world `postmessage-instrumentation.js` and `augmented-dom-instrumentation.js` (:14, :18), and ISOLATED-world `connection.js`, `postmessage.js` and `augmented-dom.js` (:27, :31). :35 is the service worker, :38 the `devtools_page`, :41 the settings popup, and :58 the CSP `connect-src https://burp/` it uses to reach Burp. The DevTools panels are panels/dom-invader.html, panels/postmessage.html and panels/augmented-dom.html. The postMessage panel has a "Replay Postmessage" modal (:35-46) with a Send button (:198).
- The settings panel, in/extract/resources/Browser/DomInvader/settings/settings.html, gives each control a stable id:
  - :246 on/off.
  - :502-507 operator canary (set, randomize, copy).
  - :40-85 sink, custom-sink, source and message tracking tabs; :153 "look for canary" on a custom sink.
  - postMessage: :254 interception, :261 spoof origin, :266 inject canary into messages, :271 duplicate values.
  - :299 DOM clobbering.
  - Prototype pollution: :396 on/off, :337 discover properties, :354 nested, :358/:362/:366 query-string, hash and JSON techniques, :370 verify, :374 CSP, :378 X-Frame-Options, :382 separate frame, :388 show techniques.
  - :417-432 filter stack, fire events, prevent redirection, redirect breakpoint.
  - :485 source injection; :493 permissions policy.
- Scanner hand-off: out/strings/map_root.tsv:14712 (burp.Zwud), the client-side prototype pollution advisory's DOM Invader recommendation. out/readable/root/Zbjf.java:600 is `BURP_BROWSER_DOM_INVADER_INVOKED`.
- Not DOM Invader: out/readable/root/Zp7.java:62-70 is the scanner's `BurpDynamicJavaScriptAnalysis` option block (`postMessageEnabled`, `prototypePollutionEnabled`, `invadeSources/Sinks`). That is the tier burpsy's domexec corresponds to.

burpsy (partial overlap, all scanner-side):
- internal/domexec/taint.go:16-32 has five plantable sources, postMessage among them, and :160-181 has a 21-entry sink table that includes `postmessage` and `prototype-pollution`. The wrappers live in `instrumentationJS` (:237).
- The canary is minted per call by internal/scanner/checks_dom.go:189-192 (`domCanary`, random). The operator cannot set, see or search for it.
- postMessage is only a planted source. taint.go:520-525 posts one self-message with target origin `'*'`, and checks_dom.go:184 uses it for the reflected variant. The page's real messages are never logged or intercepted, and nothing spoofs an origin.
- Prototype pollution: internal/scanner/checks_dom_extra.go:23-45 confirms the source only. In its own words (:44), it defers gadget discovery "to DOM Invader".
- DOM clobbering: checks_dom.go:17-25 and docs/SCANNER-COVERAGE.md:41-63 record it as "not detected, stated". Closed bead 0zma chose that disposition.
- There is no extension anywhere. burpsy-go contains no `manifest_version` JSON, and domexec/browser.go:238 launches with `disable-extensions`. A grep of internal/web/ui/src for DOM Invader, postMessage, prototype pollution, clobbering and augmented DOM finds no feature code; the only hit is an unrelated comment at pages/logger.tsx:189.

## Fix direction

This depends on burpsy-react-ui-bufa: Burp's shape is an extension in the pre-wired browser, and there is no such browser yet. Ship an MV3 extension embedded in the binary and add it to bufa's `--load-extension` list. For the MAIN-world content script, reuse domexec's `instrumentationJS` sink wrappers so the scanner and the operator share one sink list. Keep domexec's own copy extension-free. Report hits to a local burpsy endpoint, as Burp does with `https://burp/`, and add a DevTools panel plus a console view per tab. Stage it:
1. Operator canary with source/sink hits and stack traces.
2. postMessage log, intercept and replay, spoof origin, inject canary.
3. Prototype-pollution source scan plus gadget scan. Then point checks_dom_extra.go's deferral at it.
4. Clobbering. Then update SCANNER-COVERAGE.md's disposition.

## Why it matters

DOM XSS, web-message and prototype-pollution bugs are found by browsing with the instrumentation on, not by waiting for a scan. burpsy's scanner checks can report a pollution source but, by their own statement, cannot find the gadget that makes it exploitable. Without an in-browser tool, a tester has no way to follow up the findings burpsy's scanner raises, or to test the flows it never crawled.
acceptance_criteria: In the browser from burpsy-react-ui-bufa, a burpsy extension is loaded by default. The operator sets a canary and sees, per tab and frame, each source that carried it and each sink it reached, with a stack. The operator can view the page's postMessages, intercept and replay them with an edited body or spoofed origin, and inject the canary into them. The operator can run a prototype-pollution scan that reports the source and any gadget found. checks_dom_extra.go's gadget deferral and SCANNER-COVERAGE.md's clobbering disposition both point at this feature rather than at Burp's DOM Invader.
notes: 2026-10-06: not continued in the implement-all-open-beads session. Left open for an operator decision on scope and approach; no changes made.

title: proxy: there is no Open browser — every session starts by hand-wiring a browser's proxy and CA, and anything missed never reaches history
description:
## Claim

Burp ships a pre-wired Chromium: Proxy > Intercept "Open browser" launches it on its own profile, pointed at a live Proxy listener, with `--ignore-certificate-errors` so Burp's per-host certificates load without any CA install, and with Burp's extensions (DOM Invader among them) already loaded. It has its own settings (sandbox, GPU, data folder, logging), a launch-failure diagnostic, and a Help > health check. burpsy has no launcher of any kind. Its only Chrome is the scanner's headless one, which runs with extensions disabled and no proxy. Every "open in browser" action in the console is a `window.open` into whatever browser the console is in, and the toast says outright that the traffic is captured only if that browser was proxied by hand.

## Evidence

Burp (line numbers are for the `out/readable/root/` variant; `root/` and `merged/` differ):
- out/readable/root/Zrxt.java:220-221: the Intercept panel button, "Open browser" / "Open pre-configured browser" (the same panel's `interceptToggleButton` is at :173). Zw5t.java:66 is the empty-state "Open browser"; Zmbv.java:36 is "Open URL in Burp's browser".
- out/readable/root/Zpk5.java:535-538 `launchPreWiredBrowser`; :797-806 takes the first Proxy listener and passes its port (`Zsls.ZY()`, Zsls.java:27) into the launcher, or fails with "Unable to start Burp Browser - no Proxy listeners available."
- out/readable/root/Zi9a.java:51-58, the launch builder: profile dir `.ZC(...)` (:52), proxy port `.ZB(var1)` (:54), sandbox mode from settings (:56), flags `--class=burp-browser`, `--ignore-certificate-errors` and `--load-extension=` (:57). The port-to-Chromium-flag translation happens inside `net.portswigger.browser`, which exists only as class files (in/extract/net/portswigger/browser/, including chromium/ChromiumBinaryInstaller.class). Its strings were never decrypted, so no `--proxy-server` literal appears in any recovered string map.
- out/readable/root/Zugr.java:32-49 and :147-151: the profile is seeded with `Default/Preferences` from `/resources/Browser/Preferences` (in/extract/resources/Browser/Preferences:1-19 pins two extensions and turns off search suggest and leak detection). Zugr.ZT (:50-124, which failed to decompile) builds the comma-joined `--load-extension` list from out/strings/map_merged.tsv:30169-30179: `resources/Browser/NewTab`, `resources/Browser/NavigationRecorder` and `resources/Browser/DomInvader`.
- Settings keys, out/readable/root/Zblz.java:2656-2658 (`user_options.misc.embedded_browser.allow_saving_browser_settings`, `.browser_data_directory`) and :2776-2777 (`project_options.misc.embedded_browser.allow_running_without_sandbox`, `.disable_gpu`). The panels are Zrgu.java:32-94 ("Browser running": sandbox, GPU), Zrg5.java:43-142 ("Browser data": store, folder, clear all) and Zrgf.java:34-94 ("Browser logging").
- out/readable/root/Zn8.java:26-61: launch-failure dialog with sandbox and root-user diagnosis. Its AppArmor fix-up text (`/etc/apparmor.d/burpbrowser`, `apparmor_parser -r`) is at out/strings/map_root.tsv:26978-26988. Zup4.java:107 is Help > "Health check for Burp's browser". Zp3x.java:76-79 and :148-151: every proxied connection records `PROXY_EXTERNAL_BROWSER_USED` unless the built-in browser has been launched (`Zi9a.ZH`, set at Zi9a.java:59), so Burp itself treats the two paths as distinct.
- Montoya: there is no browser surface. Nothing under out/burp/api/montoya mentions a browser, and out/montoya_api/API-TYPES.tsv and API-METHODS.tsv have 0 matches.

burpsy:
- internal/web/ui/src/pages/intercept.tsx: the toolbar has no "Open browser". The only browser action is :973-978 "Open URL in browser", a `window.open` with the toast "it is captured only if that browser uses burpsy's proxy". The same pattern is at pages/contentdiscovery.tsx:316-320 and lib/actions.ts:469, 779.
- internal/domexec/browser.go:1-2 and :214-250: the only Chrome launch is the scanner's headless DOM harness. It has `disable-extensions` (:238), headless by default (:250) and no proxy flag. `Headed` (:83-91) is set only by tests.
- A grep of burpsy-go (*.go) for `proxy-server`, `load-extension`, `user-data-dir` and `ignore-certificate-errors` matches nothing. cmd/xsschallenge has its own chromedp demo, and it is not a launcher.
- internal/web/ui/src/lib/settings-sections.ts:96-99: the only browser setting is "Browser engine", which picks the headless engine for the DOM checks.
- internal/web/server.go:846: the CA reaches a browser only by a manual `/ca.crt` download and install (:851-853 cover status, import and regenerate).
- Closed bead 7rk0 (Request in browser) shipped a URL that "the operator copies and pastes" into their own browser, so it relies on the same hand-wired setup.

## Fix direction

Add a browser launcher under internal/ (not domexec, which must stay headless and extension-free for the scanner). It resolves Chromium the way `resolveChromePath` does, creates a per-project `--user-data-dir`, sets `--proxy-server=127.0.0.1:<first live listener>` (refusing with Burp's "no Proxy listeners" message when there is none), and either passes `--ignore-certificate-errors` as Burp does or the narrower `--ignore-certificate-errors-spki-list` pinned to burpsy's own CA. `--load-extension` should be a list so DOM Invader-style extensions can join it later. Expose it as POST /api/browser/launch and an Intercept toolbar "Open browser", and point the existing "Open URL in browser" actions at it. Add a Settings section for data folder, store/clear data, sandbox and GPU. Report launch failures by name, following domexec's honest-failure contract. It must run where the console's backend runs; desktop (cmd/desktop) is the natural home.

## Why it matters

Opening the pre-wired browser is the first thing a Burp user does. Without it, every burpsy session starts with hand-configuring a browser's proxy and importing a CA into its trust store, which is a machine-wide change on most platforms. A tester who skips a step gets silent gaps: traffic that never reaches history, or TLS errors mistaken for the target's. It also blocks DOM Invader parity, since Burp loads that extension through this launcher.
acceptance_criteria: One Intercept toolbar action (and POST /api/browser/launch) starts Chromium on a dedicated profile, pointed at a live proxy listener. It refuses by name when no listener or no Chromium binary exists. An HTTPS page loaded in it lands in HTTP history with no certificate warning, and without any manual proxy setting or CA import. The existing 'Open URL in browser' actions open in that browser. Settings expose data folder, store/clear data, sandbox and GPU. domexec stays headless and extension-free.
notes: 2026-09-27 filing check: the --ignore-certificate-errors-spki-list option in Fix direction works only if the presented chain contains the pinned key. burpsy's MITM already sends the CA with every leaf (internal/proxy/proxy.go:271, Certificate: [][]byte{leafDER, e.caCert.Raw}), so pinning the CA's SPKI would match. A launcher test should still assert the warning is absent, not assume it.
close_reason: Done: internal/browser launcher (domexec untouched, shares only the binary lookup): own profile (per-project default, follows project switch), --proxy-server at the first usable listener, loopback bypass removed, CA pinned by SPKI (narrower than Burp's blanket ignore), named refusals (no listener / no Chromium / root with sandbox / no display), handed-off detection, ClearData refused while running. REAL-Chromium test: pinned launch loads an HTTPS page into history; unpinned launch (negative control) never reaches the origin. Routes /api/browser/launch (riskEgress), /settings (Burp's 4 keys, persisted), /clear (riskDestructive). Intercept 'Open browser', the 3 'Open URL in browser' actions, Settings -> Browser; live: root refusal shown verbatim, launch through proxy after allowing no-sandbox, Clear disabled while running. UI completed and driven live 2026-10-05 by the frontend-ux agent (tsc clean, bun test src/lib 802 pass, build ok, Go reachability tests ok). Full Go module build+vet+tests green. NOT committed.

title: proxy/editor: gRPC and protobuf bodies are opaque — cannot read or tamper with a single field
description:
## Claim

burpsy cannot decode gRPC / protobuf request or response bodies, so a growing class of API traffic is opaque in the proxy, the editor, and Repeater: the operator sees length-delimited binary, cannot read a field, and cannot edit one and resend.

## Evidence

burpsy:
- Effectively no support: `grep -rliE 'grpc|protobuf'` over internal/ and pkg/ (Go and TSX) returns 0 files (one incidental match at most), against, for comparison, 18 files for GraphQL and a whole pkg/graphqlmap crate. So the protocol has a first-class tool and gRPC has none.
- The editor and message-viewer layer that would host a decoder exists: internal/web/ui/src/ui/editor.tsx and typed-views.tsx already special-case content types.

External precedent: gRPC/protobuf is a mainstream API transport in 2026; API-pentest guidance treats binary/gRPC APIs as a coverage gap for HTTP-only tooling (getastra, practical-devsecops 2026). Burp addresses it through extensions (e.g. protobuf decoders) precisely because raw protobuf is unreadable.

## Fix direction

1. A message-editor codec that decodes length-delimited protobuf into a readable field tree (wire types, field numbers, nested messages) without a .proto, and re-encodes edits — the "raw protobuf" view every protobuf decoder offers.
2. When a .proto or a gRPC reflection response is available, resolve field names and types.
3. Recognize the gRPC framing (the 5-byte length prefix, `application/grpc*` content types) in the proxy so bodies are decoded in history and Repeater, not just the editor.

## Why it matters

Any target with a gRPC-web or gRPC backend is currently a wall in burpsy: you cannot see or tamper with a single field. This is the difference between "can test this API" and "cannot," for a transport that is only becoming more common.
acceptance_criteria: The message editor decodes length-delimited protobuf into a field tree and re-encodes edits without a .proto; the proxy recognises application/grpc framing so bodies decode in history and Repeater; field names resolve when a .proto or reflection is available.
notes: FOUNDATION + READ VIEW LANDED (commit 5aa38e4): internal/grpcproto schemaless codec (decode/encode, every wire type, nested messages, byte-exact round-trip, garbage-rejection) + gRPC 5-byte frame recognition (incl gRPC-web trailer/compression flags); POST /api/protobuf/{decode,encode} (riskLocal); a Protobuf tab in the message editor decodes bodies whose Content-Type names grpc/protobuf, reading body_base64 (now passed to the request pane too) not lossy text. Live-verified: a captured application/x-protobuf response decodes to its fields. REMAINING (why this stays open): (1) field NAME/TYPE resolution from a .proto or gRPC reflection — the view shows field numbers + wire types only; (2) in-place EDITING — the encode path and ProtobufView Apply are wired but unreachable because no editable editor holds a faithful binary body: Repeater carries a request as a TEXT STRING, already lossy for non-UTF-8 bytes, so editing a binary protobuf there would corrupt it. Editing needs Repeater (or another editable surface) to hold the body as faithful bytes (body_base64) first.
close_reason: Closed on W3's verification from the 0rrb seat + commit evidence: substance landed as 5aa38e40 (schemaless codec grpcproto.go, gRPC 5-byte framing incl gRPC-web, POST /api/protobuf/{decode,encode}) + 8b62526f (3pco half: schema.go .proto parser + Annotate), suite green -count=1 at bfc6e7ca. Status was stale-in_progress since 10-06. The reflection note is 47id's, enabled by 0rrb's reflection client (in flight, W3).

title: intruder/scanner: no Unicode-normalization testing — the #4 web technique of 2025 cannot be expressed
description:
## Claim

burpsy has no Unicode-normalization testing: neither an Intruder payload processor that emits normalization variants of a payload, nor a passive/active check for normalization-based filter and WAF bypass. This was #4 in PortSwigger's Top 10 Web Hacking Techniques of 2025 ("Lost in Translation: Exploiting Unicode Normalization"), and ActiveScan++ shipped updates for it.

## Evidence

burpsy:
- No coverage: `grep -rliE 'unicode normali'` over internal/ (Go and TSX) returns 0.
- The place it belongs already exists: internal/intruder/process.go is the payload-processing chain, and the byte-codec layer (internal/tools codecs) is described in-repo as "the byte layer the payload-processing chain runs on." A normalization processor slots in beside the existing encoders.

External precedent: PortSwigger Top 10 of 2025, rank #4, Ryan & Isabella Barnett — normalization inconsistencies (NFC/NFD/NFKC/NFKD, and server-side case folding) used to smuggle characters past filters that normalize after they validate. (portswigger.net/research/top-10-web-hacking-techniques-of-2025)

## Fix direction

1. An Intruder payload processor "Unicode normalization variant" that, given a base payload, emits its NFC/NFD/NFKC/NFKD forms and common homoglyph/fullwidth substitutions, so a marked injection point can be swept for a filter that normalizes post-validation.
2. Optionally a passive check that flags responses reflecting a normalized form of an input different from what was sent (evidence the server normalized), which is the tell for the class.

## Why it matters

This is a current, high-signal bypass technique that burpsy cannot express at all. It is cheap because the payload-processing chain it belongs in already exists; the work is the transform table and a check, not new infrastructure.
acceptance_criteria: An Intruder payload processor emits NFC/NFD/NFKC/NFKD and fullwidth/homoglyph variants of a base payload; a target that normalizes after validating is reachable by sweeping a marked point with it. Optional passive check flags a response reflecting a normalized form differing from the input.
close_reason: normalize payload processor: nfc/nfd/nfkc/nfkd + fullwidth + homoglyph, in the chain and the Intruder editor; fullwidth NFKC round-trip tested; config-file format carries form. Optional server-normalization passive check filed separately.

title: history: cannot import a HAR file — traffic captured elsewhere can only enter burpsy by live proxying
description:
## Claim

burpsy cannot import a HAR file. Burp, ZAP, and Caido all can. HAR import is how traffic captured elsewhere — a browser's DevTools export, a CI run, a colleague's session — gets into the tool for replay and analysis without re-proxying it live.

## Evidence

burpsy:
- No HAR path: `grep -rniE 'har (file|import|export)|\.har'` over internal/ (Go and TSX), excluding the "harvest"/"harmless"/"chart" false positives, returns nothing. The tokens that matched were all unrelated words.
- burpsy already has the ingest target it would feed: a traffic store and history (internal/web history routes), so import is a parser plus a bulk-insert, not new storage.

External precedent: HAR import is standard across the field — Burp (Proxy history import), ZAP, and Caido all accept HAR. It is a routine ask for offline replay and for feeding CI-captured traffic into a manual review.

## Fix direction

A HAR (HTTP Archive 1.2 JSON) importer that parses `log.entries[]` into request/response pairs and inserts them into the history/traffic store as if proxied, preserving timing where present. Expose it as a menu action ("Import HAR") and an API route. Round-trip is a bonus (export selected history as HAR) but import is the ask.

## Why it matters

Without it, the only way traffic reaches burpsy is through its own proxy, live. That blocks the common workflows of "here is a HAR of the bug, reproduce it" and "load the traffic our CI captured," both of which every competitor supports.
acceptance_criteria: Importing a HAR 1.2 file inserts its entries into history as request/response pairs viewable and re-sendable in Repeater, timing preserved where present, via a menu action and an API route.
notes: UI done 2026-10-05 (frontend-ux agent): Import HAR action in HTTP History toolbar. Full web suite (minus unrelated WIP api_project_open_test.go/api_ca_export_test.go) green including ui_route_reachability + route manifest. Acceptance met: HAR 1.2 import via menu action AND API route, rows viewable/resendable, timing preserved. NOT committed.

Backend tests (api_har_import_test.go, 6) + full web suite green; full module suite green (SourceImport no fallout). UI verified by frontend-ux agent incl. driven flow. NOT committed.

title: access control: no way to replay a request as another identity and diff — the BOLA/IDOR class burpsy cannot test
description:
## Claim

burpsy has no way to test access control: it cannot replay a request as a second identity and diff the two responses. This is the Autorize / AuthMatrix capability, and the vulnerability class it targets — broken object-level authorization (BOLA/IDOR), function-level auth bypass, privilege escalation — is the one automated scanners most reliably miss and the one bug-bounty programs pay most for. It is not in Burp's core either (Autorize is a BApp), so this is a capability addition, not strict parity.

## Evidence

burpsy:
- No authorization-testing surface exists: `grep -rliE 'autorize|role.?matrix|authz.?matrix|replay.?as|compare.?roles'` over internal/ (Go and TSX) returns 0.
- The building blocks are already present:
  - Session/identity handling and macros: internal/session/session.go, internal/session/actions.go, internal/session/absorb.go (cookie/token absorb), internal/session/macro_analyze.go.
  - An authorized request sender: internal/sender/authorised.go.
  - A response comparer: internal/web/api_compare_sitemaps.go and the Comparer page (internal/web/ui/src/pages/comparer.tsx).

External precedent: Autorize and AuthMatrix are consistently named the top authorization BApps for bug bounty (PortSwigger "best extensions" blog; multiple 2026 "must-have extensions" roundups). API-pentest coverage in 2026 stresses BOLA/auth-bypass as what scanners miss (practical-devsecops, getastra).

## Fix direction

A new tool ("Authorization" / "Access control") that, for each request seen in history or sent from Repeater:
1. Holds N named identities (a high-priv baseline plus one or more low-priv / no-auth), each an entry in the existing session store — reuse internal/session rather than a new credential store.
2. Re-sends the request under each identity through internal/sender, stripping/substituting the identity's cookies and auth headers.
3. Classifies each result against the baseline: Enforced (access denied / different), Bypassed (same privileged content returned), Ambiguous (needs a human). Burp-Autorize's three-state model.
4. Surfaces a per-request table with the verdict and a one-click diff into the existing Comparer.

Pre-request scripting (capture a JWT from a login response, inject it into later requests) is the natural companion and should be filed or scoped alongside, because multi-step auth flows need it.

## Why it matters

Every serious web engagement tests access control by hand today in burpsy — resend, swap the cookie, eyeball the response. That is slow, unrecorded, and easy to get wrong. This turns the suite's single most valuable manual workflow into a recorded, repeatable one, and it reuses machinery burpsy already has.
acceptance_criteria: For a request in history or Repeater, burpsy re-sends it under N named identities from the session store and returns a per-identity verdict (Enforced/Bypassed/Ambiguous) with a one-click diff; a baseline-vs-low-priv test where the low-priv identity receives the privileged body is flagged Bypassed.
notes:
PARTIAL LANDED in 3c1cc04, and this bead is NOT closed by it — recording exactly what exists and what does not, because the close criteria here are a UI surface the landed work does not provide.

WHAT LANDED: the comparison ENGINE this bead's claim rests on. baseline.go (396 lines, previously untracked for 8 days) implements N-sample calibration — CalibrateBaseline over observed BaselineSamples recording modal status, mean body length, mean duration and body-hash variance; Compare flagging a response that deviates on status, length, normalised-body hash or timing; DiffAccessControl reporting a MATCH when identity B receives what identity A can see, which is the BOLA verdict this bead is named for; and RunBaselineCalibration as the sender seam that sends the N benign requests and reports the REAL count of samples it collected when some fail. Its header states the relation to the existing two-request check honestly: this generalises infra_authdiff.go's comparison from one sample to N, which is what stops an endpoint whose body varies by a timestamp from reading as an anomaly on every request.

VERIFIED, because it landed from an author who is gone: five mutations, all killed — empty calibration returning a zero Baseline (4 tests), the zero-variance relative floor removed (1), the access-control polarity INVERTED (4, the one that matters most since the same comparison read backwards reports a protected endpoint as broken and a broken one as fine), a partial calibration reporting the requested rather than the actual sample count (2), and the nil-module skip removed. Seven guard tests added at adoption for claims the code's own comments made and no test enforced.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT DELIVER, stated plainly because it is what keeps this bead open:
  1. NO SURFACE. The engine is a library. This bead's criteria ask for a Repeater control that re-sends a request under N named identities from the session store, a per-identity verdict (Enforced/Bypassed/Ambassed/Ambiguous), and a one-click diff. None of that exists — it needs a web surface, which is a peer-held package and a separate piece of work from this primitive.
  2. RunBaselineCalibration takes a BaselineSender interface rather than sending itself. The wiring a caller must write — building a sender over the shared one, sourcing identities from the session store — is exactly the work a surface would own.

The honest characterisation: this bead's CLAIM (the BOLA/IDOR class cannot be tested) is only partly addressed. What now exists is the primitive that makes the verdict correct; what is missing is anything an operator can click.

RECOMMENDED NEXT STEP for whoever picks this up: wire RunAccessControlBaselineDiff behind a Repeater action, with the identity list coming from the session store's existing rules, and have the per-identity verdict render the existing Deviation.Reasons rather than inventing new prose. The engine's Reasons field already names which signal tripped, so the UI does not need to re-derive anything.
close_reason: Access control tool: named identities (baseline + low-priv/no-auth, cookie/strip/headers) project-persisted; /api/authz/test re-sends via shared sender and classifies Enforced/Bypassed/Ambiguous (correct polarity); per-row one-click Comparer diff; timing neutered. Live-tested real sender/target. Session-sourced identities + pre-request scripting filed separately.

title: integration: no MCP server transport — the risk-gated API cannot be driven by an external AI assistant
description:
## Claim

burpsy exposes an MCP-shaped JSON API — every route is classified by a risk class and dangerous routes are gated behind a confirm — but there is no actual Model Context Protocol server transport, so an external AI assistant (Claude Desktop, Cursor, an SDK agent) cannot drive burpsy the way it can now drive ZAP. The hard part (a safety model over the tool surface) is already built; the missing piece is the transport.

## Evidence

burpsy:
- The risk model exists: internal/web/route_manifest.go defines `riskClass` per route (riskRead / riskAttack, "the field MCP-02 needs: what an unattended caller can do with a route"), and the confirm gate is referenced there and in crates/web/src/lib.rs (MCP-02: "a model driving this API unattended must confirm before widening").
- No MCP transport: `grep -rlE 'stdio|jsonrpc|json-rpc|tools/list|tools/call'` over internal/ and pkg/ Go returns only internal/extension/protocol.go (the plugin protocol, not an MCP server). There is no `tools/list`/`tools/call` handler and no stdio server binary.

External precedent: ZAP shipped an MCP add-on in 2026 — AI assistants can spider, active-scan, and retrieve alerts over MCP in natural language (zaproxy.org updates, cybersecuritynews). Caido shipped a Client SDK and an AI skill for the same purpose (caido.io 2026-03 "Announcing AI-driven Caido"). Burp AT enforces scope/tool-access/approval "in the tooling layer, architecturally separate from the model" (portswigger.net/blog/introducing-burp-at) — which is exactly the shape burpsy's riskClass already has.

## Fix direction

A thin MCP server (stdio, optionally SSE/HTTP) that:
1. Enumerates the existing route manifest as MCP tools, one tool per safe operation, carrying the route's `riskClass` in the tool description.
2. For a riskAttack tool, requires the existing confirm before executing, or refuses when the caller has not been granted attack scope — reuse the MCP-02 gate rather than reimplement it.
3. Maps tool results to MCP content.
4. Ships as a separate binary or subcommand so the console API is unchanged.

## Why it matters

burpsy already did the expensive, security-critical part: deciding, per route, what an unattended model may do and where a human must confirm. Without the transport, that work is only reachable by burpsy's own UI. With it, burpsy becomes drivable by any MCP client while keeping its own scope/approval enforcement — the "agents propose, the tool enforces" model the whole industry moved to in 2026.
acceptance_criteria: An MCP client (stdio) can list burpsy routes as tools carrying their riskClass, call a riskRead tool and get its result, and is refused or forced through the existing confirm on a riskAttack tool without a separate reimplementation of the gate.
notes:
CORRECTION (2026-09-27): this bead's claim that 'the risk/confirm gating already exists, so this is mostly a transport shim' is WRONG. Verified: route_manifest.go does not exist (only the test file); the riskClass taxonomy is test-asserted + doc comments, and the ONLY confirmation is a UI dialog (crates/web/lib.rs:393) that a direct/MCP caller never sees. There is no runtime server-side gate. The runtime gate must be BUILT first — filed as burpsy-react-ui-ejp5, now a dependency. Exposing routes over MCP before ejp5 lands hands every riskAttack route to a model with no enforcement.
2026-10-01: resumed after the two earlier agent attempts errored out; no leftover work from them (internal/mcp does not exist). Ownership for concurrent agents: I edit only NEW files (internal/mcp/**, internal/web/mcp_export.go, one dispatch case in cmd/burpsy/cli.go, MCP sections of gaps.md/PORT_STATUS.md). Not editing: route_manifest.go, confirm_gate.go, server.go, any api_*.go, ui/**, proxy/**, domexec/**. Architecture: MCP server = stdio JSON-RPC, HTTP client of the running console on loopback so the real server-side confirm gate (HEAD cc972e0) stays in the path — refusal surfaces to the MCP client as isError naming the confirm pattern; confirm tokens minted only by an explicit burpsy_confirm tool call, never auto-supplied. Coordination notes for me go in this bead's notes.
COLLISION NOTE (2026-10-02, from the session that landed 46bba66): the shared working tree now holds a SECOND, still-in-progress implementation of this bead alongside the committed one. Evidence: internal/mcp/server.go (new, appeared ~00:20), internal/mcp/tools.go (184 lines, tool-per-route-VERB naming api_pools_get, type tool{route web.RouteInfo}), internal/mcp/doc.go, and a rewritten internal/web/mcp_export.go (symbols ConfirmGateInfo/ConfirmRequired); none of these are in 46bba66. Consequence: go build ./internal/mcp/ currently fails with 'Server redeclared in this block (server.go:19 vs mcp.go:142)' and undefined web.MCPRouteInfo/MCPRoutes, because committed mcp.go + mcp_test.go sit in the same directory as that unfinished revision. The committed implementation alone is green: verified in /root/q31t-verify (HEAD + working-tree dependency fixes) - go build ./..., go vet, gofmt clean, 19/19 tests in internal/mcp pass. I did NOT delete or edit the uncommitted files, because doing that to a peer's in-flight work is exactly how my own internal/web/mcp_export.go was lost earlier today. Whoever is writing it: pick one implementation and remove the other two files, or the package cannot build. My commit 46bba66 and its export commit 0465a6a are pushed (branch ui-react-comparison, in sync at 2d07837).
2026-10-02 verification pass (session resumed after the earlier attempts errored): found the work already landed at 46bba66 and the bead CLOSED — no code written this session beyond scratch that was discarded byte-exact to HEAD. Re-verified the landed surface end to end against a live console: go build ./... clean, go test ./internal/mcp/ -count=1 ok (19 tests), and a full stdio smoke — initialize (protocol 2024-11-05, server burpsy, tools capability), tools/list (126 tools: 120 manifest routes + burpsy_confirm; risk distribution read 45 / local-write 33 / attack 12 / credential 10 / egress 7 / scope 7 / destructive 7 / asset 2 / execute 2 / confirm-mint 1), tools/call api_advisories → HTTP 200 with the real catalogue (loaded=true count=183, 00100200 present), tools/call api_audit without confirm → isError with the gate's verbatim 428 body (confirm_with, X-Burpsy-Confirm, risk:attack, mint path), burpsy_confirm → token bound to /api/audit/, immediate retry with the token → HTTP 200 POST /api/audit/999999, replay of the same token → 428 again (one-time property holds live, real confirmStore). Smoke scaffolding removed; tree clean for internal/mcp, internal/web/mcp_export.go, cmd/burpsy-mcp.

Console API unchanged (no manifest route added). Verified: go build ./..., go vet, gofmt, 19 tests in internal/mcp green against a real web.NewServer gated chain on httptest (real confirmStore mints/spends), 4 mutations each kill a named test (token relay dropped, route binding dropped, 428-as-success, collision disambiguation dropped), plus a live stdio session against a real console: initialize -> tools/list 123 -> read call 200 (183 advisories) -> attack 428 -> mint -> 200 -> replay 428. HONEST CAVEATS: (1) HEAD does not compile independently of uncommitted working-tree files (pre-existing, not touched), so verification ran in a scratch tree reconstructed from the working tree with one scratch-only rename (s.config.loginPage -> LoginPagePattern) in internal/proxy, not committed; (2) a concurrent implementation of this same bead had already written internal/web/mcp_export.go - its declarations are preserved as written and only Tier/Hints, MCPRouteForPath, MCPMethodMutates and MCPConfirmTTLSeconds were added; (3) stdio only, no SSE/HTTP; 1 MiB result cap reported in the result; streaming routes refused rather than left to hang; (4) the gate's own 428 text renders a subtree pattern with a doubled slash (POST /api/audit//confirm) - the transport prints the corrected path it POSTs to instead of editing internal/web/confirm_gate.go, which this change does not own. Also: burpsy-mcp silently exited with 'no input stream' until the smoke run caught that Options.In/Out never applied their documented os.Stdin/os.Stdout default - fixed and re-verified.

title: extender: no plugin can register a hotkey, so a plugin's only triggers are three menus and a tab
description:
## Claim
Burp's `registerHotKeyHandler` (3 overloads across 5 `HotKeyContext`s) has no counterpart in burpsy's plugin protocol — the four live kinds are context-menu, menu, editor-tab and session-action. Bead u7h closed the *UI* half of this (Extender JMenu items); the protocol half never landed.

## Evidence
- Burp: `out/burp/api/montoya/ui/hotkey/HotKeyContext.java:12-18` (the 5 contexts); `ui/UserInterface.java:100-123` (the three overloads).
- burpsy: `internal/extension/protocol.go:114-116` (4 kinds, hotkey absent) and `views.go:156-168`; `u7h` CLOSED.

## Fix direction
Add a `KindHotKey` plus a `hotkey.invoke` entry to `MethodSpecs` (the protocol file's own test reads the spec table, so the kind and its method must land together), then have `ui/src/lib/shortcuts.ts` install the registered chord through the existing keymap.

## Why it matters
Every serious Burp extension binds a key. Without the kind, a plugin can only be reached by clicking through a menu — which for an extension that runs on every request defeats the point.
notes: 2026-09-27 review of the uncommitted wsu4 diff found three defects, filed as children wsu4.1 (no hotkey can fire: the handler matches handler.keys, which the library strips of modifiers), wsu4.2 (the chord the host accepts is not the chord the UI binds) and wsu4.3 (chords that collide with the shell, other plugins or editor keys). Do not close wsu4 while they are open. They are not formally blocking deps, because bd treats --parent children as depending on the parent, so parent-blocked-by-child makes a cycle.
close_reason:
Closed as fixed in 53f4874.

Protocol half: KindHotKey joins the closed set (the kind-count tripwire
failed with its own message until the fifth was recorded); Registration
gains a chord field in Burp's Settings format ("Ctrl+Shift+K"), validated
at load through the existing per-registration refusal machinery — a hotkey
with no chord or an unspellable one is refused and counted, never accepted
as an inert row. hotkey.invoke is the method (menu.invoke's shape: a
hotkey fires with no selection behind it). NormaliseChord translates
Burp's lenient spelling and refuses what cannot honestly bind: meta/
super, bare keys, modifiers alone, function keys.

UI half: plugin-hotkeys.ts carries the same normaliser in TypeScript (the
two spellings must agree or a chord the host accepted would die in the
console), and usePluginHotkeys installs every loaded plugin's normalised
chord at the shell, one useHotkeys call over the joined list, handler =
the palette's. The Extensions page shows the declared chord beside the
kind and gains the Run button a menu action has.

Declined with reason: Burp's five HotKeyContexts are NOT modelled. A DOM
keydown cannot be scoped to one table's rows without every surface opting
in, and a binding that fires only on some pages is worse than one that
fires everywhere. A plugin hotkey here is suite-wide, which is what
Burp's context-less overload means ("it will fire for any supported
context"). Recorded in both files so the next audit does not re-file it.

Tests: the protocol's three-way check (documented = dispatched, one method
per kind, count = 5), the real-plugin kind-method test asserting "key"
reaches hotkey.invoke, 21 NormaliseChord spellings, the bad-hotkeys
load-refusal test (1 accepted / 2 refused / console names both), and 6
UI tests over the normaliser and the install walk. Mutation-checked three
directions: chord guards removed -> refusal test fails with the exact
count; hotkey dispatched to menu.invoke -> real-plugin test fails naming
the wrong method; raw Burp spelling installed -> two UI tests fail
including the never-fire meta case.

Verification: clean extraction of 53f4874 — go build ./..., go vet,
full internal/extension green (real-plugin process tests), tsc clean,
bun run check green at 772/0. Also gated with the peer session's unstaged
WIP stashed and restored.

title: ui: Settings has no Suite page — Performance, Startup, Shutdown, Temp files, Updates and Early adopter are all absent
description:
## Claim
Six of Burp's seven Suite-level settings have no section in burpsy's 20-section Settings page, and none of the six is named as declined, so the absence reads as "burpsy cannot do this" rather than "not built yet".

## Evidence
- Burp: `map_root.tsv:8846` (`user_options.misc.temporary_files_location`); `:5445-5447` (`user_options.auto_update.enabled`); `:6939-6940` (`suppress_confirm_on_close`); `:6946` (`enable_proxy_interception_at_startup` — this one IS built, at `POST /api/intercept/startup`).
- burpsy: `ui/src/lib/settings-sections.ts:52-167` (20 sections, no suite-level id); `internal/proxy/proxy.go:42-47` (the CA directory is hard-coded to `~/.burpsy/ca`, i.e. a temp location with no control).

## Fix direction
Add a `suite` section to `SETTINGS_SECTIONS` + the component map. Make the two buildable items real — a configurable temp/CA directory read by `proxy.go:38-47`, and a close-confirmation preference — and state the other four (Performance, Startup tuning, Updates, Early adopter) as declined with reasons, the way the settings page already declines its All/User/Project filter buttons.

## Why it matters
The settings surface is the migration path for an operator leaving Burp. A silently missing section is indistinguishable from an unimplemented feature, and one of these (where state lives on disk) is a real operational question.
close_reason: Suite settings section: startup interception cross-ref (built, under Proxy); new persisted 'ask before closing' pref installing a beforeunload guard; read-only CA/state-on-disk location (restart-time relocation, runtime declined to avoid desyncing the live engine); Performance/Startup-tuning/Updates/Early-adopter declined with reasons. /api/proxy/ca gained a directory field (no new route). Live-verified render + switch; snapshot-green.

title: collaborator: a payload cannot carry custom data and the server location cannot be excluded
description:
## Claim
Burp's `generatePayload(String customData, ...)` attaches up to 16 alphanumeric characters recoverable from any resulting interaction, and `PayloadOption.WITHOUT_SERVER_LOCATION` drops the location field. burpsy's mint takes a count only, so a payload is never self-identifying and every payload looks alike in the interaction log.

## Evidence
- Burp: `out/burp/api/montoya/collaborator/CollaboratorClient.java:42-54` (`customData`, its length rule, and the option parameter); `PayloadOption.java:19` (`WITHOUT_SERVER_LOCATION`).
- burpsy: `internal/web/api_collaborator.go:619-638` — the mint request is `struct{ Count int }`.

## Fix direction
Accept `custom_data` (alphanumeric, <=16 chars, reject with 400 otherwise) and `without_server_location bool`; splice the custom data into the minted marker so the existing `attributeTo` correlation still resolves the interaction to its payload, and carry both fields on the wire and through the UI.

## Why it matters
An operator minting five payloads for five parameters cannot tell which one fired without custom data. It is the difference between "something interacted" and "the search parameter is the injectable one".
close_reason:
Implemented and verified, commit 1fa90a9. Backend + wire + status view, with both halves of Burp's payload options.

CUSTOM DATA: POST /api/collaborator/payload accepts custom_data (<=16 alphanumeric) and echoes it per payload in the mint response's new "payloads" list. Validation is REFUSAL, not sanitisation — the value rides inside the payload's own address, so a separator or non-ASCII character would either be dropped (silently mislabelling the operator's payload) or change the address's shape; both cases are 400 with the reason, and the length bound is named rather than truncated.

WITHOUT_SERVER_LOCATION: the domain is omitted from the mint response AND from the status view, which is what the page renders. That second half came out of my own mutation check: I implemented the field in the mint response alone, and the mutation "ignore it in the status view" SURVIVED the first version of the test, because the page re-added the very fact the option exists to withhold. After strengthening the assertion to read the status rows, the mutation fails with the offending row attached. The status view carries a without_server_location flag so the page can explain the missing domain, and derives the domain from the address for every other payload.

VERIFIED by mutation three ways: dropping custom_data from the status view fails the attribution test; bypassing validation fails both refusal tests; ignoring without_server_location in the status view now fails the location test (it did not before). The default path is asserted to be unchanged in both the mint response and the status view, because the existing single-mint and batch clients depend on that shape.

SCOPE: this adds the two payload options. It does NOT add the per-payload custom data to the INTERACTION rows (the list an operator reads when something calls back) — the attribution path still matches on the marker, which is what makes a callback identifiable at all, and surfacing custom_data on the interaction row is a UI change with its own bead-worthy reasoning about which label wins when a marker is reused. Stated so the boundary is explicit.

Tests use the package's fake provider (mintableOOB), so they run everywhere; the real registration chain stays covered by api_collaborator_batch_test.go. gofmt clean, go build ./... clean, go vet clean, internal/web green (44s).

title: sequencer: no Analysis settings tab — the tests cannot be individually enabled or the analysis re-run
description:
## Claim
Burp's Analysis settings tab lets an operator switch individual statistical tests off and press "Redo analysis". burpsy runs a fixed battery, so a test that does not apply to a token class cannot be excluded from the verdict, and a re-analysis cannot be requested on its own.

## Evidence
- Burp: `settings/tools/sequencer.html:91-111` (per-test enable + Redo analysis).
- burpsy: `internal/sequencer/advanced.go:182-217` (four tests hard-wired, no toggles); `internal/sequencer/report.go` (`AnalyseWith` takes only the significance threshold); `ui/src/pages/sequencer.tsx` has no per-test surface.

## Fix direction
Add a `tests []string` (or `disabled_tests`) field to the analyse request, thread it into `advancedFor` and `AnalyseFips`, and expose it as checkboxes plus a Redo button. Test to write: disabling the compression test removes it from `advanced.tests` while `Grade` and `Fips` stay byte-identical.

## Why it matters
A test that is inapplicable to a token class currently drags the verdict toward a false negative with no way for the operator to say so — the same failure shape the honest-counting rule exists to prevent.
notes:
PARTIAL in the commit above: the ENGINE half only. Options.DisabledTests, the filter in advancedFor, the Disabled/DisableReason wire fields and the summary accounting are all landed and tested (7 tests, 3 mutations killed).

NOT DONE: the HTTP surface. disabled_tests is not threaded through internal/web/api_tools.go's analyse request, so an operator cannot yet send it, and ui/src/pages/sequencer.tsx has no per-test checkboxes and no Redo button. That half touches internal/web, which another agent is actively editing (46 dirty files), so it is left rather than collided into. The engine is complete and callable; only the plumbing to it is missing.
close_reason: Done: GET/PUT /api/sequencer/settings carries the ten Burp keys under Burp's names (count readable, refused off with a reason), saved with the project and reloaded on switch; analyses that name no tests use them; POST /api/sequencer/analyse gained disabled_tests (unknown ids refused; [] runs all); switched-off tests stay in the report marked not run with the name; grade unchanged (tested). Analysis settings card + Redo analysis; live: Poker+Spectral off -> marked not run. UI completed and driven live 2026-10-05 by the frontend-ux agent (tsc clean, bun test src/lib 802 pass, build ok, Go reachability tests ok). Full Go module build+vet+tests green. NOT committed.

title: repeater: no per-tab "Restore global default" and no default tab group, so a group send silently uses per-tab options
description:
## Claim
Burp lets a tab override the global send settings wholesale, marks the tab while it does, and offers "Restore global default". burpsy's per-tab options are always live, so a tab looks overridden even when it holds nothing but the defaults, and a group send silently uses whatever each tab carries.

## Evidence
- Burp: `tools/repeater/tab-settings.html:56-59` (the blue override icon and the restore item); `settings/tools/repeater.html:182-199` (the global settings it restores to).
- burpsy: `internal/web/repeater_options.go:26-47` (5 fields; no `inherits_global`); `ui/src/pages/repeater.tsx:1599-1653` (SendOptionsPanel always live).

## Fix direction
An `inherits_global bool` on the tab's options: the panel shows a "Restore global default" row that sets it, `repeaterSendSpec` skips per-tab options when it is set, and the tab strip marks the tab while overridden (Burp's blue icon).

## Why it matters
Today an operator cannot tell "this tab uses the defaults" from "this tab was tuned last week", which is exactly the state a group send depends on — and a silent per-tab override in a group send is the kind of difference that makes one request in five behave unlike its siblings.
close_reason: RepeaterTab.inheritsGlobal: sends skip per-tab options unless overriding; config panel flips to override on any change + Restore global default row; tab strip accent dot marks overrides. All send sites use sendOptionsFor(tab). Live-driven.

title: proxy settings: TLS passthrough cannot be applied to out-of-scope items, and never auto-adds on a TLS failure
description:
## Claim
Burp couples the passthrough list to scope ("Apply to out-of-scope items", only enabled when out-of-scope logging is on) and can add a server to it automatically when a client TLS negotiation fails. burpsy's `TlsPolicy` is a flat host+port list with neither behaviour.

## Evidence
- Burp: `settings/tools/proxy.html:408-412` (scope coupling), `:448-474` (the auto-add flow).
- burpsy: `internal/proxy/proxy.go:69-146` (`passthrough []string`, `passthroughPorts []uint16`, no scope check, no auto-add); UI `ui/src/lib/data.policy.ts:368-389`.

## Fix direction
Add `ApplyOutOfScope bool` to `TlsPolicy`, consulted in `interceptTLS` alongside the existing pattern/port match, and `NoteFailedNegotiation(host)` called from the handshake-error branch that writes the pattern through the existing Add path (with a counter so the auto-add is visible rather than silent).

## Why it matters
A client with pinned certificates currently costs a probe-and-retry loop started by hand; Burp turns the failure itself into the passthrough entry. And a passthrough list that ignores scope means an operator who wants out-of-scope traffic tunnelled opaque has to enumerate hosts.
notes: Backend done+committed f11e265 (2026-10-05). TlsPolicy gains applyOutOfScope + autoAddOnFailure + autoAdded counter with accessors and NoteFailedNegotiation (adds the exact host once, on, logged on the transition). Wired: handleConnect passthrough decision also tunnels an out-of-scope host when the switch is on (scope.MayContainHost at the call site); interceptTLS's client-handshake-failure branch calls NoteFailedNegotiation. PUT /api/proxy/passthrough sets the two switches, GET reports them + auto_added count, both persisted (tls.passthrough.mode) and restored at startup. Live tests: out-of-scope host tunnels opaque with only the switch on (client sees origin cert, no request bytes); auto-add adds once, no sibling. UI: two toggles in the TLS-passthrough settings panel (data.policy.ts + settings) — queued to the frontend agent with the extractor-columns UI to avoid a second concurrent ui/src editor.
close_reason: Backend f11e265 (scope-coupled passthrough + auto-add on handshake failure, persisted); UI switches in the TLS passthrough card, live-driven
